docs.title: Execution Isolation and Concurrency
docs.text: This page describes how a pipeline run is bounded, cancelled, and protected in the current implementation. It is deliberately explicit about what the engine does not do, because the boundaries matter when you reason about failure.

docs.title: There is no process sandbox
docs.text:
The engine runs entirely in one process. run_with_graph() dispatches the graph onto a single-worker concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor (pipeline/runtime.py) created per run, so the caller's thread stays free to enforce GLOBAL_TIMEOUT_SEC. Concurrency across runs is the caller's to provide (a web server's own worker pool, for instance), not a setting of this engine. Threads share one interpreter and one address space.

Two consequences follow, and neither is a sandbox property:

  • A hard crash in a database driver (segfault, abort()) terminates the whole process, including the orchestrator. There is no disposable worker to absorb it.
  • Memory is shared. A run cannot be isolated from another run by the runtime.

docs.title: Validation before SQL exists
docs.text:
This is the engine's real safety property, and it holds. The LLM emits an Abstract Syntax Tree, never SQL text. The AST passes through LogicalValidatorNode (pipeline/nodes/validator/node.py) before the generator is reached. That node:

  • resolves every column against the retrieved schema snapshot using sqlglot.optimizer.qualify;
  • enforces the table policy through the caller's Scope (policies/scope.py), failing closed when no datasource ID is present.

An unvalidated plan never becomes SQL, so it never reaches an adapter. This is a correctness and authorization gate, not a containment boundary: it prevents bad SQL from being generated, it does not contain a driver that misbehaves on SQL that passed.

docs.title: Per-run cancellation
docs.text:
Each invocation constructs its own CancellationToken (common/cancellation.py) and threads it to nodes through config={"configurable": {"cancellation_token": token}}. Because the token is per-run, cancelling one run never affects another.

Nodes observe the token and unwind cooperatively, so a cancelled run returns a normal result carrying a CANCELLED PipelineError rather than raising. run_with_graph() cancels the token on SIGINT/SIGTERM, and on Windows interactive terminals also on Ctrl+X.

Cancellation is cooperative: a node blocked inside a driver call does not abandon that call. The token is checked between and within nodes, not inside third-party I/O.

docs.title: Global timeout
docs.text:
settings.global_timeout_sec (GLOBAL_TIMEOUT_SEC, default 60) is enforced by future.result(timeout=...) in run_with_graph(). On expiry the run's CancellationToken is cancelled and the caller gets a PIPELINE_TIMEOUT error and a user-facing message, within about a second of the limit.

The timeout bounds how long the caller waits, not how long the work runs. The underlying thread is not killed; it winds down in the background once its nodes observe the cancelled token, or once its current I/O completes.

docs.title: One circuit breaker
docs.text:
VECTOR_BREAKER (common/resilience.py) is the only breaker the system defines (fail_max=5, reset_timeout=30). It wraps vector-store retrieval in indexing/retrieval.py only.

LLM calls and SQL execution are not breaker-guarded. Their failures surface as PipelineError values in graph state; see Error Handling.

docs.title: Adapter-level limits
docs.text:
row_limit is real and is enforced where it cannot be talked around: the generator bakes min(plan.limit, row_limit) into the SQL it renders, where row_limit is the datasource's own bounded by RESULT_ROW_LIMIT (100,000) (pipeline/nodes/generator/node.py).

max_bytes is not enforced. It is read from datasource options, stored on the adapter and reported by the datasource API, and nothing ever compares it to anything. The adapter does estimate a result's size (average row size from a 50-row sample) and reports it as ResultFrame.bytes, but that number is only copied into metrics; no threshold is applied, nothing is truncated and no error is raised. Treat max_bytes as documentation of intent, not a limit.

Neither is isolation in any case.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Mechanism Module What it bounds AST validation + policies pipeline/nodes/validator/node.py What SQL may be generated at all CancellationToken common/cancellation.py One run, cooperatively global_timeout_sec pipeline/runtime.py How long the caller waits VECTOR_BREAKER common/resilience.py Vector retrieval only ThreadPoolExecutor pipeline/runtime.py One worker per run, so the caller can time out; not isolation

If you need blast-radius containment against driver-level crashes, run the engine in a process you are willing to lose (a per-request worker, a container replica) and rely on your supervisor to restart it. The engine does not provide that boundary itself.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text: NL2SQL is a multi-stage orchestration pipeline built on LangGraph. A single request flows through control-plane nodes (resolution, decomposition, planning), capability-driven subgraphs (SQL agents), and an aggregation layer. The system is wired by Runtime, which instantiates registries, stores, and policy enforcement.

docs.title: In brief
docs.text:
• The question is checked for answerability and routed to one of the registered databases, then split into sub-queries; the decomposer also builds the execution DAG that says which sub-queries can run together and how their results combine.
  • Each sub-query gets the part of the schema it needs (vector search over an index of tables, columns and relationships, or the whole schema when it is small).
  • The model returns a typed plan (a Pydantic PlanModel: tables, joins, select items, filters), never a SQL string. It may only name a function from an allow-list, and it writes date work portably, which each adapter renders in its own dialect.
  • The logical validator resolves every table and column against the schema, checks joins against the declared foreign keys, checks every table against the caller's role, and builds the query tree the generator would build, so a plan whose tables cannot be joined is caught here, where the planner can still be asked to fix it. A refused plan never becomes SQL.
  • Only a plan that passes reaches the generator, which renders SQL deterministically with sqlglot. The executor runs it and the answer writer summarises the rows.
  • A retryable validation failure goes back to the planner through a refiner, up to settings.pipeline.retries.max (default 3). A security refusal is final and is never retried.
flowchart LR
    Q([Question]) --> R[Resolve datasource<br/>and decompose]
    R --> S[Schema retrieval]
    S --> P[LLM planner<br/>typed plan, no SQL]
    P --> V{Validator<br/>schema, joins, RBAC}
    V -->|retryable| F[Refiner] --> P
    V -->|refused| X([Refusal with reason])
    V -->|passed| G[SQL generator<br/>sqlglot]
    G --> E[Executor] --> A([Answer])

The full pipeline lists 17 steps (PIPELINE_STEPS), seven of them decided by a model; the web app's Pipeline page shows them all. The first, the curated matcher, which matches the question to a verified query a data team wrote (curated answers), runs only when curated answers are configured and hold a verified query. The second, the pinned entry, runs only when a run is given its plan.

docs.text:

  • build_graph() compiles the LangGraph control-plane pipeline.
  • run_with_graph() executes the pipeline with cancellation and timeout.
  • GraphState is the shared mutable state across pipeline nodes (see graph_state.md).

docs.title: Major subsystems (and responsibilities)
docs.text:
• Planner / Decomposer: DecomposerNode produces stable, semantically-scoped sub-queries and, from them, a deterministic ExecutionDAG.
  • Schema Store: SchemaStore persists versioned schema snapshots with fingerprints.
  • Chunking + Retrieval: SchemaChunkBuilder produces typed chunks; the Retriever provides staged retrieval for routing and planning context, over the index store's live builds.
  • Validation layer: LogicalValidatorNode enforces schema correctness and RBAC.
  • Execution layer: ExecutorNode routes to capability-driven executor services (e.g., SQL executor).
  • Adapter / Plugin backend: adapters implement DatasourceAdapter and are discovered via entry points.
  • Artifact store: executor results are persisted as Parquet artifacts and referenced by ArtifactRef.
  • Observability: structured logs, and events that observers turn into a log, an audit log and OpenTelemetry metrics and traces.

docs.title: Pipeline Architecture
docs.text: This document consolidates the LangGraph pipeline architecture as implemented in code. It describes the control graph, logical DAG, routing, and execution/aggregation flow. Node and subgraph details live in their respective sections.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Resolver[DatasourceResolverNode] --> Decomposer[DecomposerNode]
    Decomposer --> Router[layer_router]
    Router --> SqlAgent[SQL Agent Subgraph]
    SqlAgent --> Router
    Router --> Aggregator[EngineAggregatorNode]
    Aggregator --> Synthesizer[AnswerSynthesizerNode]

docs.title: Control graph nodes
docs.text:
• CuratedMatcherNode: the entry point when curated answers are configured; a verified answer goes straight to the aggregator
  • pinned_entry (PinnedEntryNode in nl2sql.pipeline.pinned): the entry point of a pinned run's graph (build_graph(ctx, pinned=True): a plan passed as run_query(plan=...), or an approval's); it checks each datasource against the caller's scope and goes to the layer router, so no curated matcher, resolver or decomposer runs
  • DatasourceResolverNode
  • DecomposerNode
  • layer_router (routing function, not a node class)
  • EngineAggregatorNode
  • AnswerSynthesizerNode

docs.title: Entry points
docs.text:
• build_graph(ctx) builds the control graph in nl2sql.pipeline.graph.
  • run_with_graph(ctx, user_query, ...) executes the graph with timeouts and cancellation in nl2sql.pipeline.runtime.

docs.title: Control graph and logical DAG
docs.text:
The system uses two orchestration layers:

  • Control graph (LangGraph StateGraph): runtime nodes and routing.
  • Logical DAG (ExecutionDAG): deterministic compute plan, built by the decomposer (nodes/decomposer/dag.py::build_execution_dag) from the sub-queries it just wrote, not by a node of its own.
graph TD
    Scan1[scan:subquery_1] --> Combine[combine:group_1]
    Scan2[scan:subquery_2] --> Combine
    Combine --> PostAgg[post_aggregate]
    PostAgg --> PostSort[post_sort]

ExecutionDAG.layers are computed deterministically by _layered_toposort() and consumed by the router to dispatch scan nodes.

docs.title: ExecutionDAG node kinds (actual)
docs.text:
ExecutionDAG nodes are LogicalNode instances with:

  • kind: scan, combine, post_filter, post_aggregate, post_project, post_sort, post_limit
  • inputs: upstream node IDs
  • attributes: operation-specific metadata for a combine or post-combine node (join keys, filters, metrics). A scan node carries none: its ID is its sub-query's ID, so everything about it is one lookup away in decomposer_response.

docs.title: Routing and subgraph selection
docs.text:
build_scan_layer_router() selects the next scan layer with missing artifacts and dispatches subgraphs in parallel using Send(). A scan node's ID is its sub-query's ID, so the datasource comes from that SubQuery.

Subgraph selection is capability-based via resolve_subgraph():

flowchart TD
    DatasourceId[DatasourceId] --> Capabilities[DatasourceCapability set]
    Capabilities --> SubgraphRegistry[SubgraphRegistry]
    SubgraphRegistry --> Match{RequiredSubset}
    Match -->|yes| Subgraph[SelectedSubgraph]
    Match -->|no| Error[PipelineExecutionError]

If no compatible subgraph is found, routing raises PipelineExecutionError (an NL2SQLError carrying the PipelineError payload on .error) and terminates the pipeline. A router may only return routing decisions, so it cannot report the failure as a PipelineError value in state the way a node does.

docs.title: SQL agent subgraph lifecycle
docs.text:
The only registered subgraph today is sql_agent (build_sql_agent_graph()).

See subgraphs/sql_agent.md for full lifecycle, retry semantics, and node wiring.

docs.title: Execution, artifacts, and aggregation
docs.text:
Executors produce ResultFrame objects, which are persisted via ArtifactStore and referenced by ArtifactRef. Aggregation reads artifacts and applies the logical DAG.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Adapter as DatasourceAdapter
    participant Exec as SqlExecutorService
    participant Store as ArtifactStore
    participant Agg as AggregationService

    Adapter->>Exec: ResultFrame
    Exec->>Store: create_artifact_ref(ResultFrame)
    Store-->>Exec: ArtifactRef
    Exec-->>Agg: ArtifactRef
    Agg->>Agg: load_scan / combine / post_op
    Agg-->>Exec: aggregated rows

Aggregation uses AggregationService(PolarsDuckdbEngine()) and executes layers sequentially.

docs.title: State model
docs.text:
Shared and subgraph state models are defined in graph_state.md. The pipeline uses:

  • GraphState for control graph execution and aggregation.
  • SubgraphExecutionState for subgraph-local execution.
  • wrap_subgraph() to merge subgraph outputs back into GraphState.

docs.title: Determinism
docs.text: Determinism guarantees and non-determinism sources are centralized in determinism.md.

docs.title: Known limitations (current)
docs.text:
• There is no execution sandbox; the SQL executor runs in-process on the pipeline thread pool (see ../execution/isolation.md).
  • VECTOR_BREAKER is the only circuit breaker. LLM calls and SQL execution are not breaker-guarded.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
The engine's HookRunner (ctx.hooks, built by the runtime from the hooks section) is called at six points of every run; see Hooks.

Point Called from run.before run_with_graph's worker, before graph.invoke; a Modify rewrites user_query, a deny returns before the graph runs datasources.after DatasourceResolverNode, on the datasources it forwards plan.after ASTPlannerNode.after_plan(), on the planner's or the cache's plan, before the validator execute.before, execute.after ExecutorNode, and CuratedMatcherNode for a verified query answer.after AnswerSynthesizerNode, once the answer is written

A hook that stops the run (HOOK_DENIED, HOOK_FAILED, NEEDS_APPROVAL, or the cost rule's COST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED) ends it at the layer router once the layer in flight is done. A sub-query a hook dropped (scope="sub_query") reports status: "dropped" from wrap_subgraph(), with its reason as a HOOK_DENIED warning; the router still sends the run to the aggregator, which drops a join or compare group that needs it. SubgraphExecutionState.user_query carries the run's question (after run.before) into each sub-query for the hooks there.

A NEEDS_APPROVAL ending also puts an ApprovalRequest in the state's approvals_needed (built by wrap_subgraph(), or by the curated matcher on the verified path), so the result's status is needs_approval. The approved re-run pins the request's decomposition and plan through the pinned entry (plan_source="approved"); the hooks at execute.before see the run's approvals and the runner checks them. See Query API → Approval.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Summarizes aggregated results into a user‑facing response using an LLM.
  • Exists to convert structured results into human‑readable output.
  • Sits after EngineAggregatorNode at the end of the control graph.
  • Class: AnswerSynthesizerNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/answer_synthesizer/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Send the model a preview of each result, never the whole of it: the first settings.results.preview_rows rows (20), the total row count, the column names and a partial flag.
  • Say when a result was cut at the row limit, whatever the model wrote.
  • Include unmapped sub‑queries in the response context.
  • Invoke LLM with structured output schema.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - EngineAggregatorNode, after a generated run or a verified one (the curated matcher ran the query)

Downstream: - Graph end.

Trigger conditions: - Executed after aggregation succeeds. When the aggregator fails (AGGREGATOR_FAILED), aggregator_route ends the run instead, so this node never spends a model call on an empty result.

flowchart LR
    Aggregator[EngineAggregatorNode] --> Synthesizer[AnswerSynthesizerNode] --> EndNode[PipelineEnd]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From GraphState:

  • user_query (required)
  • aggregator_response.terminal_results (required): the first rows of each terminal result
  • aggregator_response.computed_artifacts: the saved result behind each, for its row count and columns
  • decomposer_response.unmapped_subqueries (optional)
  • subgraph_outputs[<id>].truncated / .row_cap: whether a sub-query's result reached its row limit, and at how many rows.
  • verified_match (optional): set when a verified query answered. Its qualified id and its description (the data team's words for what the query returns, e.g. "invoiced revenue, before refunds") are added to the prompt as a Verified Query section, and the model is told to describe the numbers that way. A generated answer's prompt has no such section and is exactly what it was.
  • warnings (RunWarnings): the sanity checks' VALUE_NOT_FOUND ("There is no Genre with Name 'Polka'."), JOIN_FAN_OUT (a sum a join may have counted more than once) and ALL_NULL_COLUMN warnings (see ExecutorNode). A recovered one (detail.recovered) is not used: a retry replaced that attempt.

Validation performed:

  • If no aggregated result is available, emits INVALID_STATE.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to GraphState:

  • answer_synthesizer_response (AnswerSynthesizerResponse): final_answer is the model's AggregatedResponse (summary, format_type, content, warnings) plus truncated, True when a result was cut at the row limit.
  • reasoning summary
  • errors on failure

Side effects:

  • LLM invocation.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Resolve aggregated result from aggregator_response.
  2. If missing, emit INVALID_STATE error and stop.
  3. Build the result preview (result_preview()): for each terminal result, its first settings.results.preview_rows rows, row_count, columns and partial (true when rows were left out). The rows are the aggregator's terminal_results, already cut to the preview; row_count and columns come from the saved combined result in computed_artifacts, so they describe the whole result. Serialize it to JSON.
  4. Build the Result Limit note: one line per sub-query whose result reached its row limit ("The result was cut at 10,000 rows, the row limit, so it is incomplete. Narrow the question ..."), or None.
  5. Serialize unmapped sub‑queries to JSON.
  6. Invoke LLM chain with structured output. The prompt's Data Notes lists the sanity checks' notes and asks the answer to say them: that a value does not exist instead of reporting the empty result as a finding, that a total may count rows more than once, that a column has no values. When the run was started by stream_query (configurable.stream_answer), the chain is streaming_structured: the same request with the provider asked to stream, so the run's RunEvents callback publishes each piece of the tool call as an answer.delta event. The answer it returns is the unstreamed chain's (Streaming a run).
  7. Append each data note and each result-limit note to the answer's warnings, whatever the model wrote, set final_answer.truncated, and return AnswerSynthesizerResponse.
  8. On exception, emit AGGREGATOR_FAILED.

docs.title: The model sees a preview, not the result
docs.text:
The user sees the full result as a table; the model's job is to write about it, not to copy it. So the prompt carries a preview, and its instructions say:

  • every number the answer states comes from the preview rows or from row_count, quoted exactly as the rows hold it: no rounding, truncating or "about" (9712.47 is "9,712.47", not "9,700"); thousands separators and the column's own decimals are fine; no rounded, approximate or invented range or bound either: to describe a spread, name the actual lowest and highest values or use words (pagila_007 matched its gold rows, and the faithfulness scorer failed the rounded revenue);
  • when the preview is partial, do not total, average, rank or count over rows it cannot see;
  • do not reproduce the result: say the full result is in the table, and use format_type "table" only for a few preview rows.

The prompt's size no longer grows with the result, which is what let the row cap rise from 1,000 to a resource ceiling (settings.results.row_limit, 100,000).

docs.title: A result cut at the row limit
docs.text: The generator bounds each sub-query's SQL at its row limit. A result that comes back with that many rows may have been cut, so the subgraph wrapper marks it truncated (SubgraphOutput, QueryResult.sub_queries[].truncated, QueryResult.truncated). The prompt's Result Limit section tells the model the result was cut at N rows and asks it to say so and to suggest narrowing the question; the node adds the same note to warnings itself, so a cut result is never presented as complete even when the model leaves it out. A plan's own top-N (LIMIT 5) is the answer, not a cut, and is never flagged.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: GraphState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • AggregatedResponse
  • AnswerSynthesizerResponse

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text: • Non‑deterministic unless LLM configured deterministically.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • INVALID_STATE (no aggregated result)
  • AGGREGATOR_FAILED (LLM failure), or a PROVIDER_* error when the provider refused the call (see provider failures)

Logs failures via logger.error.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• No internal retry logic.
  • Idempotency depends on LLM determinism.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• LLM call dominates latency and cost.
  • The prompt holds at most settings.results.preview_rows rows per terminal result, whatever the result's size. The whole result is still held in memory by the aggregator.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: answer_synthesizer
  • Adds reasoning summary to state.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• LLM configuration for agent name answer_synthesizer via llm.yaml.
  • settings.results.preview_rows (default 20): rows of each result the model sees.
  • settings.results.row_limit (default 100000): the row ceiling a result is cut at; see the system settings.
  • Both are read from the engine's runtime (ctx.settings) when the node is built, so two engines in one process each use their own.

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Modify ANSWER_SYNTHESIZER_PROMPT.
  • Replace node in build_graph() for custom synthesis.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• No deterministic summarization guarantees without LLM configuration.
  • No fallback response when LLM fails.

docs.title: Related Code
docs.text: • packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/answer_synthesizer/node.py

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Generates a structured SQL AST plan using an LLM with structured output: the planner's answer is a PlannerAnswer, the default plan (PlanModel) and, for an ambiguous question, up to two alternative readings.
  • Exists to translate natural language intent into a deterministic, machine‑verifiable plan.
  • Sits after SchemaRetrieverNode in the SQL agent subgraph.
  • Class: ASTPlannerNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/ast_planner/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Serve a pinned plan from the plan cache on a first attempt, without an LLM call.
  • Return a plan the run pins (state.pinned_plan: a supplied, approved or chosen plan) without an LLM call, through after_plan() with plan_source set to its source.
  • Serialize relevant_tables into the planning prompt.
  • Pass user intent, expected schema, and error feedback to the LLM.
  • Run the plan.after hooks on the plan (the planner's or the cached one) in after_plan(), the one place every plan the validator gets passes through.
  • Run plan.after on each alternative reading too (checked_alternatives()): one a hook denies is dropped, one it changes is kept as changed.
  • Return ASTPlannerResponse with the PlanModel the hooks let through, ambiguous_phrase, the alternatives the hooks let through and every alternative the planner offered (alternatives_offered), the planner's own plan (planner_plan, which the plan cache stores) and its plan_source ("llm", "cache", or "supplied", "approved" or "chosen" for a pinned plan). Only an "llm" plan is ever cached.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - SchemaRetrieverNode - RefinerNode (retry loop)

Downstream: - LogicalValidatorNode on success - retry_handler on retryable failure

Trigger conditions: - Executed after schema retrieval and during retry loops.

flowchart LR
    SchemaRetriever[SchemaRetrieverNode] --> Planner[ASTPlannerNode] --> Validator[LogicalValidatorNode]
    Refiner[RefinerNode] --> Planner
    Planner --> RetryHandler[retry_handler]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From SubgraphExecutionState:

  • sub_query.intent (required)
  • sub_query.expected_schema (optional)
  • sub_query.metrics, filters, group_by, order_by, limit: rendered by semantic_context_of() as compact JSON into [SEMANTIC_CONTEXT] (empty when the sub-query has none). The system message tells the model to apply all of it, filters on a metric as having, order_by as the plan's order_by and limit as the plan's limit, and that a most/least/top-N question needs an order_by on the ranked value and a limit; one example shows it.
  • relevant_tables (required for schema grounding)
  • knowledge_used (optional): the terms and rules the schema retriever picked, rendered as [BUSINESS_CONTEXT] by business_context_of() (nl2sql/knowledge/render.py); {} when there are none
  • errors (optional feedback for retries)

Validation performed:

  • No explicit validation; relies on LLM structured output schema.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to SubgraphExecutionState:

  • ast_planner_response (ASTPlannerResponse)
  • reasoning with plan summary
  • errors on planning failure

Side effects:

  • LLM invocation via llm_registry (none on a plan cache hit).
  • Reads the plan cache in the schema store. It never writes it: the sub-query wrapper stores a plan only after it validated and executed.

docs.title: Plan cache
docs.text:
The planner is the call that decides the SQL, so a plan that already passed validation and executed is reused (pipeline/plan_cache.py).

  • Key: (normalised sub_query.intent, sub_query.datasource_id, sub_query.schema_version). When the sub-query has an order_by or limit, they are appended to the intent part (... | order_by=album_count desc | limit=1), so a top-1 and a top-5 of the same intent are different entries. The run date is always appended (... | today=2026-10-12): the planner is told today's date and writes relative dates as literals, so a plan from another day misses. So are the planner's model and the datasource's knowledge digest (... | knowledge=<sha256>): a changed definition plans again, and swapping the glossary back hits the old entries. Normalisation case-folds, collapses whitespace and strips trailing .?!,;:; the match is exact. No schema_version, no caching.
  • Read: only on a first attempt (retry_count == 0 and no errors). A hit returns ASTPlannerResponse(plan=<cached>, plan_source="cache") and makes no LLM call; a retry after a rejected plan always asks the model.
  • Never trusted: the logical validator, generator and executor run on a cached plan exactly as on a fresh one, so RBAC and policy changes apply.
  • Written by wrap_subgraph (pipeline/graph_utils.py) only when the sub-query produced SQL and executed without a blocking error. Refused, failed and plan-only runs are not stored. Nor is a plan whose planner answer carried alternatives or an ambiguous_phrase, keyed on alternatives_offered, so a reading plan.after or the caller's scope dropped still keeps the plan out of the cache. alternatives_offered carries over to a retry: a question an earlier attempt read two ways is never cached, however clear the retry's answer. What is stored is planner_plan, the plan before any plan.after hook changed it. When a hook changed it, that plan was not itself validated in the run that stored it; a hit is safe anyway, because it passes plan.after and the validator again every time.
  • Controls: settings.pipeline.plan_cache (default true) and nl2sql cache clear.

See Determinism → The plan cache.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. On a first attempt, look up the plan cache; on a hit, pass the cached plan through plan.after (step 5) with plan_source="cache" and stop.
  2. Render relevant_tables with render_schema_for_prompt (see below).
  3. Build the feedback string from the latest attempt's errors only, one JSON object per line with node, error_code and message (nl2sql.pipeline.retry_feedback): an earlier attempt's errors, stack traces and details are never sent.
  4. Build expected_schema payload from sub‑query.
  5. Invoke the LLM chain with prompt + structured output (PlannerAnswer); its plan is the default reading. The first prompt of a sub-query that carries knowledge publishes knowledge.used.
  6. Run plan.after (after_plan()): a Modify replaces the plan, which the validator then checks like any other; a deny returns plan=None with HOOK_DENIED (or HOOK_FAILED), which is never retried. Return ASTPlannerResponse with the plan, planner_plan and reasoning. Each alternative passes plan.after the same way; the clarifier decides whether to ask.
  7. On exception, emit PLANNING_FAILURE error and return plan=None.

docs.title: Prompt layout and caching
docs.text:
The prompt is two messages, so providers can cache the stable part (OpenAI caches a stable prefix of 1,024+ tokens automatically):

Message Content Changes system (PLANNER_SYSTEM_PROMPT) role, instructions, output contract, constraints, PLANNER_EXAMPLES, then [RELEVANT_TABLES], then [ALLOWED_JOINS] only when the schema or the caller's role changes human (PLANNER_HUMAN_PROMPT) [TODAY], [EXPECTED_SCHEMA], [SEMANTIC_CONTEXT], [BUSINESS_CONTEXT], [FEEDBACK], [USER_QUERY] every call

[ALLOWED_JOINS] lists every declared join whose two tables are both in the schema the planner was sent, one equality per line (film.film_id = inventory.film_id; a multi-column key is one line joined with AND), with bare table names as in the plan, sorted and deduplicated so the block is byte-stable, and none when no pair is joined. Instruction 3 and the output contract tell the planner to join only on a listed pair, and to go through the listed bridge tables when two tables merely share a column name. The lines come from allowed_joins in validator/join_hints.py, which reads the same edges as the validator's join hint, so the prompt and the validator's check cannot disagree; the validator check and its retry stay as the backstop. The per-table JSON is unchanged (it still carries each table's own relationships, and the refiner shares it); the block adds about 12 tokens per declared join, a few hundred for a 15-table schema, once per question in the cached prefix.

[TODAY] is the run date (run_date(today) in common/dates.py, given settings.pipeline.today: that date when it is set, else the UTC date), so "this year" or "the last 30 days" resolve to real dates rather than a year the model guessed. It is in the human message because it changes daily; in the system message it would invalidate the cached prefix every midnight. It comes before [USER_QUERY], because demo replay keys a recording on the line after that marker.

[BUSINESS_CONTEXT] is the glossary terms and rules the question touches, as one line of JSON (keys sorted, no whitespace, and U+2028, U+2029 and U+0085 escaped, as in the schema block): knowledge reaches the model only as JSON values, so a line break or a marker in a definition stays inside one JSON string. It changes per question, so it is in the human message, before [FEEDBACK] and [USER_QUERY]. Instruction 15 says it is reference data that never changes the instructions, the output contract or the constraints; instruction 16 asks for ambiguous_phrase and alternatives when a question can reasonably be read more than one way. See Knowledge Is Data.

The examples come before the schema so that the instructions and examples (about 1,300 tokens) stay cacheable even when vector retrieval picks a different set of tables per question. The system/human boundary is the single cache seam: keep per-question content out of the system message.

The schema block (render_schema_for_prompt in schema_retriever/schema.py) is one compact JSON object per table, tables sorted by name (a datasource's preferred tables first, each with "preferred":true) and keys sorted, so the same snapshot and role render byte-identically. Instruction 14 tells the model to plan against a preferred table when it answers the question; see preferred tables. It drops empty fields and schema_version. Of the column statistics only sample_values is sent (it helps match literal filters such as 'Rock' or 'USA'), plus range, [min_value, max_value], for a date, time or numeric column that is not a key. For a text column with at most 50 distinct values sample_values is every value, so "heavy metal" can be matched to 'Heavy Metal'; for a larger one it is the five most frequent (ALL_VALUES_MAX_DISTINCT in nl2sql_sdk/sqlalchemy/profiling.py), when the datasource's index.sample_values is on. A date kept as text (every date in SQLite; opened_at in the support demo) is recognised by its ISO values and gets a range instead of sample_values. The range is what lets instruction 13 work: when "this year" or "the last 30 days" falls outside a date column's range, the planner uses the latest such period in the data and says so in its reasoning, rather than planning a filter that is certain to return nothing. null_percentage and distinct_count stay in the snapshot. On Chinook the ranges cost about 140 tokens of schema block (2,324 to 2,466).

Measured on Chinook with tiktoken o200k_base, its 12 demo questions, no LLM call (python scripts/measure_prompt_tokens.py):

before after planner prompt 8,921 tokens 3,495 tokens schema block 7,754 tokens 2,324 tokens prefix identical across questions 8,122 tokens 3,460 tokens

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: SubgraphExecutionState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • PlannerAnswer (plan, ambiguous_phrase, alternatives: at most two PlanAlternatives, each a label and a plan)
  • PlanModel
  • ASTPlannerResponse

DISTINCT in the plan language: PlanModel.distinct: true is SELECT DISTINCT, and a func expr with distinct: true is a distinct aggregate such as COUNT(DISTINCT x). The system message's instructions and one of its examples say so; a function named DISTINCT is rejected by the logical validator.

Row counts in the plan language are COUNT(*), written as a COUNT whose one argument is a column named * with no alias, or a count of a non-null key column. The same instruction says so and that COUNT(t.*) is never used; the logical validator refuses a star anywhere else (see the generator's star rule).

Dates in the plan language are two portable functions, described once in the system message and the same for every database: DATE_PART(unit, date), an integer, and DATE_TRUNC(unit, date), the period's first day as YYYY-MM-DD, with the unit a string literal year, quarter, month or day. The time between two dates is DATE_DIFF('day', start, end), the elapsed days with the fraction kept (FLOOR or ROUND for whole days); the prompt says never to subtract dates. The prompt names no database; each adapter renders the functions (see the generator). Subqueries and window functions are not in the language. offset pages through the plan's order_by (rows 11 to 20 are limit: 10, offset: 10); a plan with an offset and no order_by is rejected by the validator.

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Deterministic only if LLM is configured deterministically.
  • Plan structure is validated downstream; ordering is not enforced here.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • PLANNING_FAILURE on LLM or parsing errors; a provider's refusal of the call is a PROVIDER_* error instead (see provider failures).

Logs failures via logger.exception.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• Retries are orchestrated by the subgraph, not this node.
  • Idempotency depends on LLM determinism.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• One LLM call per planning attempt.
  • Cost is dominated by LLM latency and token usage.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: planner
  • Adds reasoning entries to subgraph state.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: • LLM config under agent name ast_planner in llm.yaml.

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Modify PLANNER_PROMPT and examples.
  • Replace node in build_sql_agent_graph() to use alternate planning logic.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• No deterministic safeguards beyond structured output schema.
  • No explicit timeout handling in the node itself.

  • packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/ast_planner/schemas.py

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Asks instead of guessing: when the planner read a phrase of the question in more than one way, and two or three readings pass the checks, it ends the sub-query with the options rather than running the most likely one.
  • Sits on the logical validator's "valid" edge, before the generator, so every path from the planner to the generator still passes the validator.
  • Makes no model call.
  • Class: ClarifierNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/clarifier/node.py -.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Run each of the planner's alternative readings through the validator's own checks (LogicalValidatorNode.check: the static checks and the caller's scope) and drop those that fail. A reading that names a table the caller cannot read is never offered, and never listed as an assumption.
  • Render each remaining reading to SQL with the generator and drop one whose SQL another option already has (the default reading comes first). At most three options: the default and two alternatives.
  • End the sub-query with NEEDS_CLARIFICATION when it may ask, and publish clarification.requested.
  • Otherwise let the default plan go on, keeping the readings that passed on ast_planner_response.alternatives, which the explanation lists as assumptions.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - LogicalValidatorNode, when the plan passed

Downstream: - GeneratorNode, unless it asked - END, when it asked

flowchart LR
    Validator[LogicalValidatorNode] -->|valid| Clarifier[ClarifierNode]
    Clarifier -->|ok| Generator[GeneratorNode]
    Clarifier -->|asked| End[END]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From SubgraphExecutionState:

  • ast_planner_response.plan, ambiguous_phrase and alternatives. Each alternative already went through plan.after in the planner node, as the plan did: one a hook denied is not there, one a hook changed is there as changed.
  • sub_query, relevant_tables and user_context, for the validator's checks.
  • clarify: set by wrap_subgraph when the run's clarify is on and the sub-query is the run's only one.

From the runtime: settings.clarify.enabled, and the run's pinned knowledge for the datasource's knowledge digest.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• No alternatives: nothing (it passes straight through).
  • Otherwise ast_planner_response with alternatives cut to the readings that passed and were not merged. alternatives_offered (every reading the planner gave, set by the planner node) is left as it is, so an answer with readings is never cached, even when none was left for this caller.
  • When it asks, also one PipelineError: NEEDS_CLARIFICATION, severity INFO, never retried. Its details carry what the result needs to build the ClarificationRequest: phrase, datasource_id, schema_version, knowledge_digest, sub_query and options (id, label, plan; the default reading, a, has no label from the planner). The result adds the question, the asker and each option's explanation (result_from_state in api/query_api.py).

docs.title: When it asks
docs.text:
All of these hold:

  1. The planner named the phrase (ambiguous_phrase) and at least one alternative passed the checks and was not merged. A phrase the glossary settles is not asked: the flag and the alternatives are dropped and the default plan goes on. A phrase is settled when a term's name equals it, or exactly one term lists it as a synonym (case-insensitive); "sales" listed by two terms stays open. The plan is still never cached, since the planner's answer carried readings (alternatives_offered).
  2. state.clarify is on: the run's clarify (run_query(clarify=...), default true; evals pass false) and the run has exactly one sub-query.
  3. settings.clarify.enabled is on (the default).
  4. No attempt of the sub-query has executed yet. After a sanity retry (VALUE_NOT_FOUND, JOIN_FAN_OUT) the re-plan's default reading runs, so the flagged attempt's rows are never the answer, and the readings that passed are assumptions. wrap_subgraph never counts a sub-query that asked as succeeded, nor returns its artifact.

The prompts are the same either way: clarify only decides whether the clarifier ends the run.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
def __call__(self, state: SubgraphExecutionState) -> Dict[str, Any]

check_clarifier in build_sql_agent_graph routes end when the state holds a NEEDS_CLARIFICATION error, else ok. The layer router ends the run on it (nothing is executed, aggregated or synthesized), and wrap_subgraph reports the sub-query with status needs_clarification and no MISSING_SQL error.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• clarification.requested (sub_query_id, phrase, options), an operator event, never on the caller's stream.
  • No policy.decision and no denial warning for an alternative that names a denied table (check(..., audit=False)): that reading is dropped and reaches no caller. The plan the caller gets is audited as always.
  • node.started and node.finished as every step.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Answers a question with a verified query from curated.yaml when one fits, before the model plans anything.
  • Searches only the verified queries of datasources the caller's role may read, asks the model once to pick one and give its parameter values, and checks the values and the role's table access in code.
  • Runs the saved SQL with the values as bound parameters, under the row ceiling, and hands the result to the aggregator and the answer synthesizer as a one-sub-query run.
  • Falls back to the generated pipeline for anything else, with a reason code; a fallback is never an error of the run.
  • Class: CuratedMatcherNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/curated_matcher/node.py
  • Design: Curated answers

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Limit the search to datasources that have verified queries and that the caller's Scope reaches (reaches_datasource()) (the pinned datasource_id only, when one is given).
  • Retrieve candidates with Retriever.retrieve_verified_query_candidates() (top settings.curated.match_top_k), skipping a query that is in the index but no longer in the file.
  • Ask no model when the best similarity is below settings.curated.match_floor.
  • Make one structured-output call, VerifiedQueryChoice.
  • Check the chosen values (params.resolve_params): type, min/max, choices, required.
  • Check every table the SQL reads against the caller's Scope (allows()), and that the SQL is still one read-only query.
  • Check the adapter declares SUPPORTS_BOUND_PARAMETERS before running a query with parameters.
  • Run the SQL through SqlExecutorService with ExecutorRequest.parameters and max_rows.
  • On a hit, fill the state the way a one-sub-query generated run leaves it.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
The node is in the graph only when curated answers are on: CURATED_ENABLED is true, the curated file is loaded and holds at least one verified query, and the run executes (a plan-only run has no matcher, except one that pins a supplied verified query: there the matcher checks the query, its values and every table it reads, then ends without running it, and the run is plan_only; a dashboard's access check). Otherwise the graph starts at DatasourceResolverNode, exactly as without curated answers.

Upstream: - Entry point (no upstream nodes).

Downstream: - layer_router on a hit: the scan is already done, so it sends the run to EngineAggregatorNode, then AnswerSynthesizerNode. - DatasourceResolverNode on any fallback.

flowchart LR
    Matcher[CuratedMatcherNode] -->|verified| Router[layer_router]
    Router --> Aggregator[EngineAggregatorNode]
    Aggregator --> Synth[AnswerSynthesizerNode]
    Matcher -->|fallback| Resolver[DatasourceResolverNode]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From GraphState:

  • user_query (str, required): searched, and shown to the model.
  • datasource_id (Optional[str]): when set, only this datasource is searched.
  • user_context (UserContext, required): the role's datasources and tables.

Context dependencies (Runtime):

  • curated: the loaded CuratedFileConfig. The matcher reads every query from it, never from the index.
  • vector_store: retrieve_verified_query_candidates().
  • policy_engine: scope(user_context, datasource_id).
  • ds_registry: dialect, adapter row limit, supports().
  • vector_store: the run's pinned Retriever: the candidates, and the schema version of the datasource's live build, stamped on the sub-query.
  • llm_registry: the choice's model, agent name curatedmatcher (falls back to default).

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
On a hit, mutations to GraphState:

  • verified_match (VerifiedMatch: datasource_id, query_id, description, params)
  • decomposer_response: one SubQuery (id verified_<query_id>, intent the question) in one standalone combine group
  • execution_dag: build_execution_dag() of that response
  • artifact_refs: the saved result
  • subgraph_outputs: one SubgraphOutput with plan_source="verified", the SQL, row_cap, truncated, and the checks read_only, params and policy
  • reasoning

On a fallback: nothing the rest of the graph reads. execution_failed also adds a warnings entry.

Always, outside the state (the trace keeps the node's whole return):

  • curated_match: matched, reason (a fallback code or None), detail, floor, candidates (datasource_id, query_id, similarity), choice (the model's query_id, params, reason), params (after checking).
  • retrieval: the search's record, shaped like the resolver's, when a search ran.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Searchable datasources: registered, allowed for the role (* allows all), the pinned one alone if pinned, and holding verified queries. None: not_configured, no search and no embedding call.
  2. Candidates. None (or none still in the file): no_candidates.
  3. Best similarity below settings.curated.match_floor: below_floor, no model call.
  4. One VerifiedQueryChoice call. It raised (no recording in a replay, a provider error): model_failed. none_of_these: none_of_these. An id that is not a candidate: unknown_query.
  5. Values: an unknown name, a name twice, a value that does not parse or is out of bounds: param_invalid; a param with no default left out or empty: param_missing. A param left out takes its default.
  6. Tables: any table the SQL reads not allowed for the role: policy_denied. The normal pipeline then enforces the policy as always; the user is not told a verified query exists.
  7. Capability: a query with params on an adapter without SUPPORTS_BOUND_PARAMETERS: capability_missing.
  8. Run with the values bound and max_rows set to min(limits.row_limit or row_limit, row_limit) (limits is the datasource's, row_limit is settings.results.row_limit). Failed or no result: execution_failed, with a warning.
  9. Fill the state and route to layer_router.

docs.title: The choice prompt
docs.text:
System message (curated_matcher/prompts.py), then the question after a User Query: line, which nl2sql.llm.replay.extract_question recognises:

You decide whether one of the verified queries below answers the user's question. A data team wrote and checked each one; you cannot change what a query does, only pick one and give its parameter values.

Rules:
1. Pick a query only when it answers the whole question as asked: the same measure, the same ranking or grouping, the same filters. A query about something close but different (ranked by another measure, grouped another way, a different entity) does not answer it.
2. When no query answers the whole question, set query_id to "none_of_these". When unsure, choose "none_of_these": the question is then answered another way, which is better than a wrong answer.
3. Use the id exactly as listed (datasource.query).
4. Give a value for each parameter the question states, as text: an int as digits, a date as YYYY-MM-DD, a string exactly as one of its choices when it has them. Leave out a parameter the question does not state; never guess a value the question does not give.
5. Give the reason in one short sentence.

Verified queries (JSON):
{candidates}

{candidates} lists, in ranked order, each candidate's qualified id (chinook.top_customers_by_revenue), its description, and its params with type, bounds, choices, default and required. Never the SQL.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
def __call__(self, state: GraphState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • VerifiedQueryChoice, ParamValue, VerifiedMatch (curated_matcher/schemas.py)
  • VerifiedQueryCandidate (indexing/models.py)
  • ExecutorRequest.parameters, ExecutorRequest.max_rows
  • SubgraphOutput with plan_source="verified"

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• No model writes or edits the SQL; the model picks an id and supplies values, which code checks and the driver binds.
  • The candidates block is serialized with sorted keys in ranked order.
  • The search and the choice are as deterministic as the embedding model and the configured temperature and seed.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: The node never adds an error to the run. Every failure, including an unexpected exception, is a fallback with a reason code: not_configured, no_candidates, below_floor, none_of_these, model_failed, unknown_query, param_invalid, param_missing, policy_denied, capability_missing, execution_failed.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• No retry: a fallback runs the generated pipeline instead.
  • Idempotent for the same input state and the same model answer.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• A verified answer costs two model calls (this choice and the answer) instead of four or more.
  • Below the floor, or with no candidates, a fallback costs one embedding call and no model call.
  • The result is read in batches and the stream stops at max_rows.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: curated_matcher
  • The trace records the node with its curated_match record and the search; the choice call is recorded like every LLM call, under node curated_matcher.
  • QueryResult.source says verified with the query id and values, or generated.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Picks the datasources a question goes to: an explicit override, the only registered datasource, or routing (five signals fused with reciprocal rank fusion) when more than one is registered.
  • Enforces RBAC and the schema version mismatch policy before planning.
  • Refuses a question no datasource can answer, with one small structured LLM call, before the decomposer runs.
  • Sits at the entry of the control graph and gates the pipeline.
  • Class: DatasourceResolverNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/datasource_resolver/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Choose candidate datasources:
    • an explicit datasource_id is used as given;
    • with exactly one datasource registered, that one is used and no vector search runs;
    • otherwise Retriever.route() ranks the datasources the caller's scope reaches (see Routing).
  • Validate datasource IDs against the registered adapter list.
  • Enforce RBAC datasource access.
  • Judge answerability over the allowed candidates, refuse with QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE when none can answer, and forward only the candidates the verdict names, at most settings.routing.max_datasources of them.
  • Give each forwarded datasource its description and a capped table list, for the decomposer to route on.
  • Populate DatasourceResolverResponse in GraphState.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - Entry point (no upstream nodes), or CuratedMatcherNode when curated answers are configured and it fell back.

Downstream: - DecomposerNode if resolution succeeds. - Terminates early (END) if no datasource is allowed, or the question is not answerable.

Trigger conditions: - The control graph's entry node, unless curated answers are configured; then it runs whenever the curated matcher did not answer.

flowchart LR
    Resolver[DatasourceResolverNode] -->|answerable and allowed| Decomposer[DecomposerNode]
    Resolver -->|denied or not answerable| EndNode[END]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From GraphState:

  • user_query (str, required): the question; used for routing (more than one datasource) and for the answerability check.
  • datasource_id (Optional[str]): explicit override for datasource selection.
  • user_context (UserContext, required): RBAC enforcement.

Context dependencies (Runtime):

  • vector_store: the run's pinned Retriever. Its route ranks the candidates when more than one datasource is registered and no override is given, and gives each datasource's live schema version and snapshot (the snapshot's description and table list feed the answerability check and the decomposer's routing context).
  • ds_registry: adapter registry for registered IDs.
  • rbac: filters allowed datasources.
  • llm_registry: the answerability check's model, agent name datasourceresolver (falls back to default).
  • settings.routing (candidates, max_datasources, floor_ratio) and settings.retrieval.decomposer_tables.

Validation performed:

  • Datasource override must exist in the registry.
  • RBAC must allow at least one candidate.
  • At least one allowed candidate must be judged able to answer.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to GraphState:

  • datasource_resolver_response (DatasourceResolverResponse)
  • errors (list of PipelineError) on failure
  • reasoning (how the candidates were chosen, and the answerability reason) and warnings

Side effects:

  • One LLM call (the answerability check) once the role check passes.
  • Routing's five index searches (one embedding of the question) when more than one datasource is registered and no override is given.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Candidates:
    • state.datasource_id set: it must be registered (INVALID_STATE otherwise); it is the only candidate.
    • Exactly one datasource registered: it is the only candidate; no vector search.
    • Otherwise: the vector store must exist (SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED otherwise). The scope filter comes first: the registered datasources the caller's role may not read are left out, and none left is a CRITICAL SECURITY_VIOLATION with no search and no model call. Retriever.route then ranks the rest (the description, example, verified-query, table and column signals, fused with reciprocal rank fusion), keeping the top settings.routing.candidates (3) and dropping any whose best similarity is under settings.routing.floor_ratio (0.5) times the most similar one's. Only the tables the role may read vote: a table or column entry of a hidden table, or a verified query that reads one, is dropped before ranking and never reaches the trace. The description signal ranks every datasource entry exactly, so no reachable datasource is missed by the approximate search. No candidate is SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED (with a re-index hint when the index is empty).
  2. Role check: candidates the role may not read are dropped. None left is a CRITICAL SECURITY_VIOLATION, and no model call is made.
  3. Schema version mismatch policy (fail returns INVALID_STATE; warn adds a warning).
  4. Answerability check over the allowed candidates only (see below). An empty verdict returns QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE.
  5. Narrow to the verdict. After routing, only the allowed candidates the verdict names go forward, at most settings.routing.max_datasources (3) of them, the best by fused score first; a candidate the verdict rejects never reaches the decomposer, and a verdict naming only unknown ids is QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE. With an override or a single datasource there is one candidate, and a non-empty verdict accepts it.
  6. Attach routing context to each forwarded datasource, from the snapshot its live build was made from: description, tables (sorted bare table names, at most settings.retrieval.decomposer_tables, 30) and more_tables (how many were left out).
  7. Return DatasourceResolverResponse with the forwarded datasources (sorted by id), their IDs as allowed_datasource_ids, and unsupported IDs.
  8. On exceptions, log and return SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED with the exception text; a provider's refusal of the model call is a PROVIDER_* error instead (see provider failures).

A single registered datasource is the shortcut, not the usual case: with more than one - the demo registers three - routing runs, and nothing else in the flow changes.

docs.title: Order of checks
docs.text:
The role check runs before the answerability check, so:

  • a caller with no allowed datasource gets the RBAC refusal and the model is never asked;
  • the model sees only datasources the role may read;
  • a question that is answerable but touches tables the role may not read passes this node and is refused by LogicalValidatorNode's table policy, as before.

docs.title: Answerability check
docs.text:
A structured call (AnswerabilityResponse: answerable_datasource_ids, reason) with this prompt (datasource_resolver/prompts.py). The system message:

You check whether a question can be answered from the datasources below, before any SQL is planned. For each datasource you see its description and the tables it holds, not its data.

Rules:
1. List the id of every datasource that could hold data relevant to the question, even partly. A question that needs several datasources lists all of them.
2. Be conservative. When you are unsure, treat the question as answerable and list the datasources that might answer it. Refusing a question that could have been answered is worse than running one that finds nothing.
3. Return an empty list only when the question is clearly about something none of these datasources hold, such as the weather, general knowledge, or small talk.
4. Use only ids from the list below.
5. Give the reason in one short sentence.

Datasources (JSON):
{datasources}

The human message:

User Query:
{user_query}
  • {datasources} is a JSON list, one entry per allowed candidate, sorted by id, with sorted keys: description (the datasource description from the live build's snapshot, which indexing takes from the datasources config) and tables (sorted bare table names).
  • The instructions and datasources come first (the system message) and the question last (the human message), so the prompt is byte-identical across questions up to the question and a provider's prompt cache can serve the prefix. OpenAI caches only prompts of 1,024 tokens or more, so with one small datasource nothing is cached; the prefix grows, and becomes cacheable, with more datasources.
  • The verdict refuses and narrows: an empty list refuses the question, and after routing only the allowed candidates it names reach the decomposer. It cannot add a datasource the role may not read.
  • For Chinook on its own the rendered prompt is about 260 tokens (o200k_base), plus the AnswerabilityResponse function schema; the demo now registers three datasources, so its prompt is correspondingly longer.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: GraphState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • DatasourceResolverResponse
  • ResolvedDatasource
  • AnswerabilityResponse
  • PipelineError

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Candidate choice is deterministic for an override or a single datasource.
  • Routing's ranking may vary with more than one datasource (approximate searches; ties in fused score go to the smaller id).
  • The answerability prompt is serialized deterministically; the verdict is a model call at the configured temperature and seed.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • INVALID_STATE (unknown datasource override; schema version mismatch under fail)
  • SECURITY_VIOLATION (RBAC denial)
  • QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE (ERROR: no allowed datasource can answer the question; QueryResult.status is error)
  • SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED (no candidates, no vector store with several datasources, or exceptions)

Exceptions are caught at the node boundary and logged with logger.error.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• No internal retry logic.
  • Idempotent for the same input state, except vector retrieval ranking and the model's verdict may vary.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• One small LLM call per question once the role check passes; it saves the decomposer, planner and synthesizer calls on every unanswerable question.
  • Routing (one question embedding, five index searches, no model) only with more than one datasource.
  • RBAC checks are in-memory operations; schema lookups are store reads.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: datasource_resolver
  • The answerability call is recorded like every LLM call: usage under node datasource_resolver in QueryResult.usage, and in the run trace keyed by node, sub-query, attempt and call.
  • Vector retrieval uses VECTOR_BREAKER at the vector store layer.
  • Returns a retrieval record in its update for the run trace: the query embedded, one search record per routing signal (route.description, route.examples, route.curated, route.tables, route.columns: the pool with similarities, each datasource's best entry picked) and a routing record (each signal's datasource ranking, the fused scores and ranks, the datasources kept and those dropped with why); or skipped: true and why (an explicit datasource_id, a single registered datasource, no vector store). The answerability check is not part of it: it is an LLM call and is traced as one. See Debugging a run.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• LLM agent datasourceresolver in the LLM config (optional; see LLM configuration)
  • settings.routing.candidates, max_datasources and floor_ratio, and settings.retrieval.decomposer_tables (see Settings)

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Replace this node in build_graph() to change resolution behavior.
  • Extend retrieval by modifying the node or the vector store retrieval strategy.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Tenant scoping is not implemented in vector retrieval.
  • The answerability check sees table names, not columns or data, so it refuses only questions clearly outside every datasource.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Decomposes the user query into datasource‑scoped sub‑queries and combination operations.
  • Produces deterministic IDs for sub‑queries and post‑combine ops.
  • Sits after DatasourceResolverNode and before the layer router.
  • Class: DecomposerNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/decomposer/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Invoke the LLM to produce DecomposerResponse.
  • Filter sub‑queries by resolved/allowed/unsupported datasources.
  • Stabilize IDs using a hash of sub‑query content.
  • Normalize and sort combine groups and post‑combine operations.
  • Refuse a decomposition with more than settings.routing.max_sub_queries sub-queries (QUESTION_TOO_BROAD).
  • Mark each join key's column on its own copy of the sub-queries, and copy each side's declared dtype onto the key pair.
  • Build the ExecutionDAG the layer router walks and the aggregator runs (decomposer/dag.py). The DAG is a pure function of the response above, so it is code here rather than a node of its own.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - DatasourceResolverNode

Downstream: - layer_router

Trigger conditions: - Executed only when resolver_route returns continue.

flowchart LR
    Resolver[DatasourceResolverNode] --> Decomposer[DecomposerNode] --> Router[layer_router]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From GraphState:

  • user_query (str, required)
  • datasource_resolver_response (DatasourceResolverResponse, required)

Validation performed:

  • Raises if no resolved datasources are available.
  • Filters out sub‑queries that reference missing, restricted, or unsupported datasources.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to GraphState:

  • decomposer_response (DecomposerResponse)
  • reasoning (completion status)
  • errors on failure

Side effects:

  • None beyond LLM invocation.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Validate resolver response; raise if no resolved datasources.
  2. Build resolved_payload and schema_version_map. The payload has one entry per resolved datasource, sorted by id: datasource_id, description, tables (sorted bare table names, at most 30, set by the resolver) and more_tables (how many tables were left out, present only when some were). The resolver fills these for every path, so an explicit datasource_id or a single registered datasource gets the same context as a vector search. The index metadata (chunk id, type, schema version) is not sent.
  3. Invoke LLM chain with user_query and resolved datasources. The prompt is two messages: the system message holds the fixed instructions and output format (cacheable), the human message holds the resolved datasources (as JSON with sorted keys) and then the question. Rule 1 tells the model to pick each sub-query's datasource from these descriptions and tables. A sub-query carries its own filters (a threshold on a metric included), order_by and limit: "the artist with the most albums" is order_by album_count desc, limit 1. post_combine_ops are only for operations across two or more combined sub-queries, and the prompt's example has none. The answer is a call to the DecomposerResponse tool whose arguments are the decomposition itself; both the prompt and the tool's description (the model's docstring) say not to wrap them under another key, which Claude did on the anthropic wire while the tool had no description.
  4. Rule 11 says to split only when one query cannot express the question. A sub-query is one flat query (joins, filters, group_by, aggregates, order_by, limit), because that is all the typed plan can say: it has no subquery, CTE or window function. "Top 3 drivers by deliveries" is one sub-query. A question that filters one result by a ranked or aggregated subset ("top 3 drivers by deliveries in the busiest depot") does split, and rule 12 has the model answer it with one join group on the shared attribute and the final ranking as ONE sort op in post_combine_ops on that group, carrying both order_by and limit (ops are not chained: a separate limit op would be a second result set), so one result set comes back. Before this rule the pagila_001 split came back as two result sets, one of them unlimited.
  5. The system message states the limit, settings.routing.max_sub_queries (rule 10, "Use at most 6 sub_queries"). A decomposition with more ends the run here with QUESTION_TOO_BROAD: "This question needs more than 6 separate queries. Ask about fewer things at once." No DAG is built and the model is not asked again: a model that ignored the limit once usually does again, and the question is what has to change.
  6. A join/compare group needs exactly one left-hand input (left, base or primary) and one right-hand input (right, compare or secondary); two of one side, or a third input, is a ValueError for parse-and-retry. With two left-hand roles, which side was which used to turn on the sub-query ids, which the node rewrites, and the run crashed.
  7. DecomposerResponse requires each join/compare key to name a column in the expected_schema of its side's sub-query (a side or sub-query prefix such as right.customer resolves to the bare name), with a dtype, and the two dtypes to be coercible: a number or a boolean never joins a date. A violation is a ValueError, which parse-and-retry sends back to the model with the reason.
  8. fold_single_input_ops() then moves every filter, sort and limit op on a combine group with one sub-query (used by no other group) into that sub-query: filters are appended, order_by terms appended, and the smallest limit kept. With one input there is nothing to combine, and left as post-combine ops they reached only the aggregated answer, never the sub-query's SQL or rows (the first gpt-5.4 tier 2 run returned every row for ten superlative and top-N questions this way). A group with an aggregate or project op is left to the aggregator.
  9. For each LLM sub‑query:
  10. Validate datasource existence and RBAC allowance.
  11. Assign deterministic ID via _stable_id(), over the intent, metrics, filters, group_by, order_by, limit and expected schema.
  12. Two sub-queries the model wrote identically hash to the same ID, but each is still a sub-query of its own (a combine group may name both), so a repeat takes the next ordinal: sq_<hash>, sq_<hash>_2, and so on. Both run, and the DAG gets one scan node per sub-query. Before this, the shared ID gave the DAG one node id for two nodes, and the run ended with PLANNER_FAILED ("contains a cycle").
  13. Attach schema version.
  14. Remap combine groups to stable sub‑query IDs. An input whose sub-query was dropped in step 4 is removed from its group, and a group left with no inputs is removed. A join or compare group left with fewer than two inputs is refused: the run ends here with PLANNER_FAILED, before any scan runs, and no DAG is built. The message names the group and why each input was dropped (restricted_datasource, no_datasource, unsupported_datasource) but not the datasource. The model is not asked again: a restricted or unresolved datasource is not something a new decomposition changes. Before this, the group was kept with its one input and the engine returned that side alone as the "join", so "customers with an open ticket who spent the most" was answered as "customers who spent the most", with no error. A union that lost an input still runs on the inputs that remain; the dropped intent is reported in unmapped_subqueries.
  15. mark_join_keys() sets ExpectedColumn.join_key on the engine's own copy of each sub-query (true on each join-key column, false on every other) and copies each side's declared dtype onto the pair (JoinKeyPair.left_dtype, right_dtype). The three fields are SkipJsonSchema: they are not in the model's tool schema, and whatever the model sent for them is replaced. join_key is left out of the stable id (step 4) and of the expected_schema the planner is shown. The logical validator reads the flag and the aggregator the dtypes.
  16. Assign deterministic IDs to post‑combine ops.
  17. Sort sub‑queries, combine groups, and post‑combine ops.
  18. Check every post-combine op against the columns its combine group will produce (post_combine_problems()). A sub-query's result columns are its expected_schema names (the logical validator holds each plan to them), and the combined columns follow by the engine's own rules in nl2sql/aggregation/columns.py: a join/compare drops the right-hand join keys and suffixes any other right-hand name the left also has with _right. A group whose sub-query declares no expected_schema has unknown columns, so only its column checks are skipped; the structural checks below (an op, one op, a schema) still apply. If an op reads a column that will not exist, the model is asked again (up to twice), with the reason appended to the human message ("PREVIOUS ANSWER REJECTED: ..."). A second rejection asks again, and a third (MAX_RETRIES = 2 retries) ends the run here with PLANNER_FAILED and the same reason, before any scan runs; nothing after the decomposer can ask for a new decomposition, so this used to fail in the aggregator after every scan. The same check rejects an op that reads a non-key column both sides of a join have: the left copy keeps the bare name and the right becomes <name>_right, so the op would silently read only the left copy (a "top 5 films by revenue in the top category" sorted on a total_revenue that both the category and the film sub-query produced ranked nothing). The feedback names the column, the join keys and both sub-queries (by intent), and asks for distinct names in their expected_schema. A right-hand join key is never ambiguous (a left key that a right non-key column shares a name with is), a column only one side has passes, an op that reads both <name> and <name>_right passes (it says which copy it means), and a compare is exempt because it diffs the two sides by matching names. The same check rejects three more shapes: an op whose expected_schema lists a name it cannot produce (the combined columns; an aggregate's group_by and metric names, a metric counting only if it has an aggregation), or lists a name twice; an aggregate that filters or sorts by a column it no longer has after aggregating; a join/compare group of two or more inputs with no op ("needs ONE post-combine operation whose expected_schema lists the answer columns in question order") or whose op has no expected_schema, because the engine ends every op in its expected_schema and without one the answer keeps the combine's column order, helper columns included (the feedback asks for the answer columns in question order, the entity asked for first, keeping the columns that say what the answer is about (the entities asked for and the entity a subset was chosen from, such as which depot, region or year) and leaving out only helper figures used purely to rank or select the subset, _right names for a compare); and more than one op on such a group, because ops are siblings (each reads the whole combined result and becomes its own result set), so the feedback asks for ONE op carrying filters, order_by, limit and expected_schema. union and standalone groups may omit the schema and carry several ops. Rule 6, rule 12 (with a "top 3 drivers by deliveries in the busiest depot" example), the retry feedback and these rejections share one phrase, ANSWER_COLUMNS in decomposer/prompts.py.
  19. Return DecomposerResponse.
  20. On exception, emit ORCHESTRATOR_CRASH error.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: GraphState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • DecomposerResponse
  • SubQuery
  • UnmappedSubQuery
  • PostCombineOp

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Stable IDs are generated via SHA‑256 hash of sub‑query content; identical sub‑queries are told apart by an ordinal suffix (_2, _3, ...).
  • Ordering of outputs is explicitly sorted.
  • LLM output is non‑deterministic unless configured deterministically.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • PLANNER_FAILED when a decomposition is rejected twice (step 9), with the reason;
  • QUESTION_TOO_BROAD when the decomposition has more than settings.routing.max_sub_queries sub-queries; never retried;
  • PLANNER_FAILED when a join/compare combine group has fewer than two inputs (step 5), for example because RBAC dropped one side;
  • ORCHESTRATOR_CRASH on exceptions; a provider's refusal of the call is a PROVIDER_* error instead (see provider failures).

Logs failures via logger.error.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• Up to two internal retries (MAX_RETRIES): a decomposition post_combine_problems rejects (step 9) is asked for again with the reason. When recording, the retry's answer replaces the first under the same question, so replay serves the corrected decomposition.
  • Idempotent for fixed LLM output; otherwise LLM variability can change output.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• One LLM call per pipeline execution.
  • Hashing and sorting are in‑memory and low cost.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: decomposer
  • Adds a reasoning entry on completion or failure.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: • LLM configuration for agent name decomposer via llm.yaml.

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Modify DECOMPOSER_PROMPT for different decomposition strategies.
  • Replace or wrap node in build_graph() for custom behavior.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• No fallback when LLM fails.
  • Output quality depends on LLM configuration and prompt.
