docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Executes the ExecutionDAG over persisted artifacts using the aggregation engine.
  • Exists to combine scan results deterministically into final result sets.
  • Sits after layer_router and before AnswerSynthesizerNode.
  • Class: EngineAggregatorNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/aggregator/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Load scan artifacts from artifact_refs, lazily, as polars scans.
  • Execute combine and post‑operation nodes in DAG order, as one lazy plan.
  • Save each terminal result as its own artifact, and produce AggregatorResponse with those artifacts and a preview of each.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - layer_router (after all scan artifacts are available)

Downstream: - AnswerSynthesizerNode, when aggregation succeeded - End of run, when it failed (aggregator_route in pipeline/routes.py)

Trigger conditions: - Router dispatches to aggregator when no pending scan nodes remain.

flowchart LR
    Router[layer_router] --> Aggregator[EngineAggregatorNode] --> Synth[AnswerSynthesizerNode]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From GraphState:

  • execution_dag (required)
  • artifact_refs (required)

Validation performed:

  • None in node; aggregation service raises on missing artifacts.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to GraphState:

  • aggregator_response (AggregatorResponse)
  • reasoning and errors

Side effects:

  • Reads artifacts from the artifact store.
  • Writes one artifact per terminal result, in the run's folder: <tenant_id>/<request_id>/result_<node_id>.parquet with the default template (see Artifact Store).
  • Writes the run's result manifest beside them, <tenant_id>/<request_id>/manifest.json (see Artifact Store).

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Read execution_dag and artifact_refs.
  2. Check every combine input against its row cap (see Row cap before a combine below). A capped input to a join/compare ends the run here with RESULT_TRUNCATED; a capped input to a union adds a RESULT_TRUNCATED warning and aggregation goes on.
  3. Invoke AggregationService.execute(dag, artifact_refs).
  4. A join/compare combine casts both sides of each key to one type before the join, in polars, non-strictly. The types are the ones the decomposer declared (JoinKeyPair.left_dtype, right_dtype): each side is cast first to its own, then both to the type they meet as (nl2sql/aggregation/join_keys.py: text is parsed as the other side's type, two numbers meet as a whole number, a date and a datetime as a datetime, a number and a boolean as a boolean by 0 and 1). A number goes straight to the number type, and two keys declared float whose frames hold integers join as integers: a float cannot tell ids above 2^53 apart. A cast never changes a value, it nulls it: 7.9 or a decimal 7.50 cast to a whole number is null, not 7 or 8. Text is stripped of surrounding spaces, on both sides of a text key too. Timestamps of any unit and zone become naive UTC microseconds; text becomes a date or timestamp only by the ISO formats (2024-01-02, 2024-01-02 13:00[:00[.fff]], the same with T, a trailing Z or a +02:00 offset), never by inference, and a TIME key declared a date or timestamp is null. Text parsed as a number loses its padding, so "007" and "7" both match 7: a key of zero-padded codes should be joined as text, or it may fan out. A value that does not convert becomes null and matches nothing; AggregationService.execute counts them per side (PolarsDuckdbEngine.unconverted_join_keys) and the node adds a JOIN_KEY_UNCONVERTED warning for each, carried to QueryResult.warnings: "3 of 412 support.customer_ref values are not numbers and joined nothing." No dialect is involved: this is compute on result frames.
  5. A join/compare combine resolves each join key against its frame's columns. A key written with a side or sub-query prefix (right.customer, sq_2.customer) resolves to the bare column when only that exists; an unknown key is left for polars to report. A join/compare with fewer than two inputs raises (AGGREGATOR_FAILED) instead of returning the one frame it has; the decomposer refuses such a group before anything runs, so this is the last line of defence.
  6. A post-combine op (PolarsDuckdbEngine.post_op) applies every field it carries, in SQL's order: the reshaping its operation names (aggregate groups with polars' group_by), then its filters (after an aggregate they filter the aggregated rows, as HAVING does), its order_by, its limit, and last its expected_schema when it has one, for every operation type: the answer's columns in that order, so a filter or sort may read a column the answer leaves out. A schema name the op cannot produce is refused with the columns it does have. A filter op with order_by and limit, as the decomposer's prompt used to show, keeps all three.
  7. Before polars is asked for any column, a post-combine op's attributes (group_by, metrics, filters, order_by) are checked against the combined frame. An attribute the frame does not have is refused with the columns it does have, and a side-qualified one (right.customer) with the reason — see No anti-join below. The decomposer runs the same check on the decomposition before anything executes (nl2sql/aggregation/columns.py, shared with this engine) and asks the model again (up to twice), so here it is the last line of defence.
  8. AggregationService.execute returns each terminal node as a polars LazyFrame: the scans are ArtifactStore.scan_parquet, and the combines and post-combine ops only add to the plan, so no sub-query result is loaded whole before it is written.
  9. Save each terminal result with ArtifactStore.write_lazy, which streams the plan into a parquet artifact, and build AggregatorResponse:
  10. computed_artifacts[node_id]: the saved result's ArtifactRef, with the whole result's row_count and columns (sub_query_id unset).
  11. results: one ResultSummary per saved result (node_id, columns, row_count, and truncated: a sub-query upstream of the node in the DAG was cut at its row cap), also written as the run's manifest.json. QueryResult.result_manifest carries it, and the facade's paging and CSV export read the result by it.
  12. terminal_results[node_id]: the first settings.results.preview_rows rows, read back from that artifact. This is what the answer model is shown; it is not the whole result.
  13. Return success reasoning.
  14. On exception, emit AGGREGATOR_FAILED, on the state's errors and on AggregatorResponse.errors. The graph's aggregator_route then ends the run: the answer synthesizer is not called on the empty result, so the aggregator's error is the run's outcome and no model call is spent explaining {}.

docs.title: Row cap before a combine
docs.text:
The generator caps every sub-query at its datasource's row_limit, bounded by the settings.results.row_limit ceiling (100,000, also the cap when none is set), unless the plan asks for fewer rows itself, and records that cap as row_cap on its response and on the sub-query's SubgraphOutput. The cap is applied in each sub-query's SQL, before the combine: a join input with 2240 rows under a row_limit of 1000 reaches the aggregator as 1000, and every match the other 1240 held is silently lost. The wrapper marks such a sub-query's SubgraphOutput.truncated, which QueryResult and the answer carry (see AnswerSynthesizerNode).

So before combining, the aggregator looks at each combine input whose result has row_cap rows or more:

  • join / compare: refused. The run ends with RESULT_TRUNCATED (through aggregator_route, so no answer is synthesized), naming the sub-query and the cap. Missing rows mean missing matches, so the combined answer could be wrong, and a wrong answer is worse than none.
  • union: a warning. The rows a union returns are still right, only possibly incomplete, so it runs and a RESULT_TRUNCATED warning with the sub-query's id is carried to QueryResult.warnings.

A result of exactly row_cap rows may be complete; telling the two apart would mean fetching one row more, so it is treated as cut short. A plan's own top-N (LIMIT 5) is the answer, not truncation, and is never flagged. To answer such a question, ask something narrower (aggregate in the sub-query) or raise the datasource's row_limit.

docs.title: No anti-join: what "bought X but never Y" does here
docs.text:
CombineGroup.operation is one of standalone, compare, join and union. join and compare are both inner joins (how="inner" in PolarsDuckdbEngine.combine), and FilterSpec has no null or existence operator, so there is no way to express "present on the left and absent on the right". This is a capability gap in the plan language, not a bug in the engine.

Asked "Which customers bought jazz tracks but never rock?", the model decomposes it into the two sets and then reaches for a right-hand column to negate against — right.customer. That column does not exist: an inner join keyed on the shared column drops the right-hand copy, and the other right-hand columns are suffixed _right. Every tier 2 run has failed this question, and what reached the caller was polars' own unable to find column "right.customer"; valid columns: ["customer"].

Resolving the prefix away would be worse. right.customer would become customer, the filter would run against the intersection, and the answer would be the customers who bought both genres — wrong, and silently so. So the attribute check refuses the question and says why. The decomposer now makes this check first and asks the model again with the same message; a second answer with the same problem ends the run in the decomposer with it, before any scan runs. A recording run also met the made-up variant, a filter on bought_rock, which the same check catches. The message reads:

Aggregator failed: Post-combine operation references 'right.customer', which
the combined result does not have. Available columns: customer. A column
qualified by side does not survive the combine: ... it cannot be expressed:
the plan language has no anti-join or set-difference operation ... so the
question is refused rather than answered with the intersection.

The same gap has a second shape: the decomposer sometimes emits the two sub-queries uncombined, and AggregationService.execute then returns two terminal result sets, which the run reports as "expected one result set, got 2" (2026-09-22_27cad30). Both are the same missing operation.

Closing it properly means adding an anti-join (or except) to CombineGroup.operation, the decomposer prompt, the DAG and the engine. That is a feature, not a fix, and is deliberately not done here.

Key contracts:

docs.text:

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • AGGREGATOR_FAILED
  • JOIN_KEY_UNCONVERTED, a warning: join-key values that did not convert to the key's type
  • RESULT_TRUNCATED, an error when a join/compare input hit its row cap, a warning when a union input did

Logs failures via logger.error.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• No internal retry logic.
  • Idempotent for a fixed DAG and artifacts.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• Scans Parquet artifacts lazily and executes joins/aggregations in polars; the combined result is streamed to its artifact (sink_parquet), and only the preview rows are collected into Python.
  • Cost grows with artifact size and DAG complexity. A join, sort or group-by may still need its inputs in memory as polars columns, never as Python rows.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: aggregator
  • Adds reasoning entries for success and failure.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• Uses PolarsDuckdbEngine.
  • settings.results.preview_rows: rows of each terminal result kept in terminal_results.
  • The combined result is written to the runtime's results store (ctx.artifact_store, <storage.path>/results/), as the sub-query artifacts are.

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Replace aggregation engine by modifying node to use a different AggregationService.
  • Replace node in build_graph() for alternate aggregation behavior.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Fails if required artifacts are missing.
  • Several post-combine ops on one combine group are siblings, not a chain: each reads the combine's output and is its own terminal result.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Delegates SQL execution to an executor service based on datasource capabilities.
  • Persists results via the artifact store and returns ExecutorResponse.
  • Sits after GeneratorNode in the SQL agent subgraph.
  • Class: ExecutorNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/executor/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Validate required execution inputs (SQL and datasource ID).
  • Gate execution on the datasource declaring supports_sql.
  • Build and submit ExecutorRequest.
  • Return executor response and propagate errors.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - GeneratorNode

Downstream: - Subgraph end (artifacts returned to control graph).

Trigger conditions: - Executed when SQL generation succeeds.

flowchart LR
    Generator[GeneratorNode] --> Executor[ExecutorNode] --> EndNode[SubgraphEnd]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From SubgraphExecutionState:

  • generator_response.sql_draft (required)
  • sub_query.datasource_id (required)
  • sub_query.schema_version (optional)
  • trace_id, subgraph_name, user_context

From Runtime:

  • ds_registry
  • tenant_id

Validation performed:

  • Missing SQL → MISSING_SQL
  • Missing datasource ID → MISSING_DATASOURCE_ID
  • No executor for datasource → INVALID_STATE

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to SubgraphExecutionState:

  • executor_response (ExecutorResponse)
  • errors and reasoning

Side effects:

  • Executes SQL against datasource via executor service.
  • Reads the result a batch at a time when the adapter has execute_batches (StreamingAdapterProtocol), settings.results.fetch_batch_size rows per batch, and writes each batch to the artifact as it arrives (ArtifactStore.write_batches); an adapter without it is called through execute and its one frame is written the same way. A failure the adapter reports between batches fails the sub-query as a failed execute would, and nothing is written (see artifact store). metrics.row_count and metrics.bytes_returned are summed over the batches.
  • SqlExecutorService also takes ExecutorRequest.parameters and max_rows, which this node never sets: generated SQL carries no parameters and its LIMIT is in the text. The curated matcher sets both for a verified query: the parameters reach the adapter in AdapterRequest.parameters and are bound, and the stream stops after max_rows rows, cutting the last batch and closing the adapter's stream.
  • Persists results to artifact store, one artifact per sub-query: the request's node_id (the sub-query id) is passed to the store as sub_query_id and dag_node_id, so two sub-queries of one run never write the same file (see artifact store). The ArtifactRef records it as sub_query_id.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Validate SQL and datasource ID.
  2. Check the adapter declares supports_sql; otherwise return INVALID_STATE.
  3. Build ExecutorRequest with trace/subgraph identifiers and schema version.
  4. Run execute.before (the cost rule's built-in policy.cost first, when policies.cost is set), execute the request, and run execute.after on the result's summary. The cost rule's estimate, when it asked for one, is returned as estimate and reaches SubQueryResult.estimate, even when the SQL was then stopped.
  5. After execute.after, run the answer sanity checks on the result (below), unless settings.pipeline.sanity_checks is false; a result a hook stopped is never checked.
  6. On exception, emit EXECUTOR_CRASH.

docs.title: Answer sanity checks
docs.text:
Cheap checks on each sub-query's result, before the aggregator, in pipeline/nodes/executor/sanity/: the filter values of an empty result (values.py), join fan-out (fanout.py) and all-null columns (nulls.py). Every probe is a sqlglot tree built from the plan and rendered by the adapter (render_sql), bounded, and never run on a table the caller's scope denies; a check that fails to run reports nothing, and a failure in the checks never fails the run. A verified query is not checked: it runs in the curated matcher, not through this node.

Probes and hooks. A probe (the value check's and the fan-out check's) is SQL the hooks never see: it runs outside execute.before and execute.after, and nothing publishes it. So when any hook is attached at execute.before (an operator gating the SQL that reaches the database), no probe runs; only the all-null check, which reads the saved result and sends nothing to the database. None runs either for a caller the cost rule gives a limit, since a probe would bypass it; a caller with no limit keeps them. settings.pipeline.sanity_checks: false turns every check off. A probe is bounded by the datasource's timeout; one that times out is skipped silently.

Check Runs on Code Then Missing filter value an empty result VALUE_NOT_FOUND A close value and a retry left: an ERROR, retried once. Otherwise a WARNING. Join fan-out a result with rows JOIN_FAN_OUT Under COUNT, confirmed, with a retry left: an ERROR, retried once. Under SUM or AVG, or with no retry left: a WARNING. All-null column a result with rows ALL_NULL_COLUMN Always a WARNING.

Each check retries at most once per sub-query, within settings.pipeline.retries.max, and a pinned plan (supplied, approved or chosen) is never retried, so its findings are warnings. Each finding carries details.attempt, which the SQL agent routes on, and publishes sanity.flagged (code, sub_query_id, retry; see Events). A warning reaches the result's warnings as a RunWarning, and the answer synthesizer says it (see AnswerSynthesizerNode).

docs.title: Join fan-out
docs.text:
Joining Customer to Invoice on Invoice.CustomerId repeats each customer once per invoice, so COUNT(c.CustomerId) counts invoices and SUM(c.Credit) adds each customer's credit several times. A table's rows are repeated when a join in the plan reaches, on its far side, a key that is not the far table's whole primary key (from the snapshot, through the sub-query's relevant_tables); every table on the near side of that join is repeated. One table joined to two others on their many side (a many-to-many sum: invoices and tickets of one customer) is the same case. A table with no known primary key is taken as unique, so it is never suspected: a warehouse that declares no keys (Snowflake or BigQuery often do not, nor do views) gets no fan-out check.

A suspected COUNT, SUM or AVG over a column of a repeated table (not already DISTINCT) is confirmed by one probe over the plan's own FROM, joins, WHERE and GROUP BY: does any group hold one row of that table more than once?

SELECT 1 FROM <the plan's FROM and joins>
WHERE <the plan's WHERE> AND NOT <alias>.<primary key> IS NULL
GROUP BY <the plan's groups>, <alias>.<primary key>
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 LIMIT 1

A row confirms it. The rows an outer join null-extends have no key, so they never count, and a row that appears once in each of several groups (which a grouped aggregate counts rightly) never counts either. The probe needs a single-column primary key and every table of the plan readable by the caller. The key keeps its case as reflected and is spelled as the generator spells a column, rendered by the adapter in its dialect.

Under COUNT the planner is told to count distinct values, which the plan can say (Expr.distinct). Under SUM or AVG the repair (aggregate the many side first) needs a derived table the plan cannot express, so it is a warning: "SUM(Customer.Credit) may count some Customer rows more than once: joining Invoice repeats them." Messages name tables and columns, never values.

docs.title: All-null columns
docs.text: A result with rows whose column holds only nulls (usually an outer join that matched nothing, or the wrong column) is a warning. It reads the saved result's null counts, never its values; there is no probe and no fix to suggest.

docs.title: An empty result's filter values
docs.text:
"Which customers bought Metal?" planned as Genre.Name = 'Metal' returns no rows because Chinook's genre is 'Heavy Metal'. Reported as is, the answer says nobody bought any. So when a query succeeds with zero rows, sanity/values.py's check_values() looks at every string literal the plan's WHERE compares a bare column to with =, IN or LIKE, through AND and OR only (a negated or != comparison, a column inside a function, and a number are left alone), at most five per sub-query:

  1. Does it exist? SELECT 1 FROM <table> WHERE <column> = '<value>' LIMIT 1 (LIKE for a pattern). If yes, nothing is said: the empty result stands.
  2. The closest values. From the column's sample values in the snapshot when one of them is close (a case-insensitive match, then by similarity), with no query. Otherwise a case-insensitive match first (LOWER(column) = LOWER('value'), DISTINCT, LIMIT 3); failing that, a bounded SELECT DISTINCT column ... LIMIT n (n is 500, or the adapter's row_limit if lower) and the three most similar by difflib (cutoff 0.6).
  3. What it reports, as VALUE_NOT_FOUND:
  4. With a close value and a retry left, an ERROR telling the planner which values exist: "No Genre.Name value is 'Jaz', so the query returned no rows. The closest existing values are 'Jazz'; use one of them if it is what the question means." The SQL agent sends it back through the refiner (see SQL agent). It is raised once per sub-query: an empty result after that retry is reported as a warning instead.
  5. Otherwise a WARNING: "There is no Genre with Name 'Polka'." (with "; the closest is ..." when there is one). The sub-query still succeeds with its empty result, and the answer synthesizer is told the value does not exist (see AnswerSynthesizerNode).

Every probe is a SELECT built with sqlglot and rendered by the adapter (render_sql), so no dialect is named here; each has a LIMIT no higher than the adapter's row cap. A table the role may not read (RBAC, as the logical validator checks it) is never probed, a probe the database refuses claims nothing, and a failure in the check never fails the run.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: SubgraphExecutionState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • ExecutorRequest
  • ExecutorResponse

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Deterministic request construction.
  • Execution results depend on external datasource state and are not deterministic.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • MISSING_SQL
  • MISSING_DATASOURCE_ID
  • INVALID_STATE
  • EXECUTION_FAILED: the database rejected the query as wrong (the adapter's retryable); the SQL agent sends it back to the refiner while retries remain
  • DB_EXECUTION_ERROR: the database refused or could not run the query (permission, timeout, connection); fatal
  • EXECUTOR_CRASH: an exception escaped the adapter
  • VALUE_NOT_FOUND: an empty result filtered on a value its column does not have; an ERROR (retried once) when a close value exists, a WARNING otherwise
  • JOIN_FAN_OUT: an aggregate over rows a join repeated, confirmed by the probe; an ERROR (retried once) under COUNT, a WARNING under SUM or AVG
  • ALL_NULL_COLUMN: a result column with no value; a WARNING

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• No internal retry logic. The SQL agent's check_execution routes a retryable EXECUTION_FAILED, and this attempt's VALUE_NOT_FOUND or JOIN_FAN_OUT ERROR, back to the refiner (see SQL agent).
  • Idempotency depends on datasource and query semantics.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• External I/O dominates (database execution).
  • Artifact persistence writes Parquet results.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: executor (and sanity, sanity.values, sanity.fanout for skipped checks)
  • sanity.flagged for each sanity finding
  • Propagates executor response reasoning and errors.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• tenant_id from settings.
  • settings.pipeline.sanity_checks (default true): false turns the sanity checks off.
  • Executor selection based on adapter capabilities.

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Extend SqlExecutorService to alter execution behavior.
  • Replace node in build_sql_agent_graph() to alter execution behavior.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Executes in‑process on the pipeline thread pool; there is no process sandbox (see ../../execution/isolation.md).
  • No built‑in retries on transient execution failures.
  • The fan-out check reads only the select list's COUNT, SUM and AVG of a plain column, and confirms with the plan's whole WHERE but no GROUP BY; a SUM or AVG fan-out is reported, not repaired.
  • The filter-value check covers string literals in WHERE only, not HAVING, and reads at most 500 distinct values to find a similar one, so on a high-cardinality column a near miss can go unsuggested (the value is then reported as missing).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Converts the AST plan into SQL using sqlglot.
  • Enforces adapter row limits and dialect selection.
  • Sits between LogicalValidatorNode and ExecutorNode.
  • Class: GeneratorNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/generator/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Convert PlanModel expressions into sqlglot expressions.
  • Build a SQL query with ordered selects, joins, filters, groupings, and limits.
  • Apply adapter dialect and row limit.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - ClarifierNode, after LogicalValidatorNode passed the plan

Downstream: - ExecutorNode

Trigger conditions: - Executed when logical validation passes and the clarifier did not ask which reading was meant.

flowchart LR
    Validator[LogicalValidatorNode] --> Clarifier[ClarifierNode] --> Generator[GeneratorNode] --> Executor[ExecutorNode]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From SubgraphExecutionState:

  • ast_planner_response.plan (required)
  • sub_query.datasource_id (required)

From Runtime:

  • ds_registry (adapter dialect and row limits)

Validation performed:

  • Raises if datasource ID or plan is missing.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to SubgraphExecutionState:

  • generator_response (GeneratorResponse with sql_draft, and row_cap: the adapter's row_limit when it, not the plan's own LIMIT, bounds the query; None when the plan asked for that many rows or fewer). The aggregator uses it to tell a sub-query cut short by the cap from a complete one (see EngineAggregatorNode).
  • reasoning
  • errors on failure

Side effects:

  • Adapter registry access for dialect/limits.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Validate presence of datasource ID and plan.
  2. Resolve adapter and dialect.
  3. Compute effective limit from plan/adapter row limit: row_limit is the datasource's row_limit bounded by the settings.results.row_limit ceiling (100,000), or the ceiling when the datasource sets none; the limit is min(plan.limit or row_limit, row_limit). When the cap is what bounds the query, record it as row_cap.
  4. Traverse AST with SqlVisitor to build sqlglot expression tree.
  5. Every operator becomes the node sqlglot's parser would build (+ -> exp.Add, * -> exp.Mul, IS NOT -> NOT ... IS ..., and so on), wherever it is nested. An operator with no mapping raises; it is never rendered as a function named after the operator.
  6. An operand that is itself an operator is parenthesised, because sqlglot prints a hand-built tree without adding the parentheses its parser would have seen ((a + b) * c would otherwise print as a + b * c).
  7. / is sqlglot's true division, so on SQLite it renders as CAST(a AS REAL) / b rather than integer division.
  8. || is string concatenation, rendered as the dialect's own: a || b on SQLite and Postgres, CONCAT(a, b) on MySQL, a + b on T-SQL. A + with a string operand (a non-numeric string literal, or another concatenation) renders the same way, because on SQLite 'Jane' + ' ' is numeric addition and returns 0. A + between two columns stays addition: their types are not known here.
  9. A column named * is the wildcard, never an identifier, and it is allowed in two places only: a whole select item with no alias (*, or t1.* for a declared alias) and COUNT(*) (the single, non-DISTINCT argument, unqualified). Both render with a bare star on every dialect. Anywhere else SqlVisitor raises MisplacedStar (a ValueError), and the logical validator, which builds its tree through the same visitor, reports it as a retryable INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE asking for COUNT(*) or a count of a non-null column such as the key. COUNT(t1.*) is refused rather than rewritten to COUNT(*): SQLite and T-SQL reject it, and on Postgres under an outer join it counts the NULL-extended rows of t1 as 0 where COUNT(*) counts them as 1.
  10. Select aliases and column names are quoted, the dialect's way, only when they are not bare identifiers. The decomposer names result columns in plain words and the planner must use those names as aliases, so an alias such as sales support agent renders as AS "sales support agent" (and AS `sales support agent` on MySQL), in the select list and in the ORDER BY tie-breakers.
  11. A func expr with distinct: true wraps its arguments in exp.Distinct, so {"kind": "func", "func_name": "COUNT", "is_aggregate": true, "distinct": true, "args": [x]} renders as COUNT(DISTINCT x). PlanModel.distinct: true renders SELECT DISTINCT.
  12. A func expr is built with sqlglot.exp.func(name, *args), so a function sqlglot knows becomes its typed node and each dialect renders it its own way (LENGTH is LEN on T-SQL, COUNT is COUNT_BIG on T-SQL). A name sqlglot does not know (such as STRFTIME) stays as written; the logical validator has already limited names to ast_planner.functions.ALLOWED_FUNCTIONS. A function sqlglot builds as an operator (MOD(a, b) is a % b) keeps its operands' grouping.
  13. Dates are portable: DATE_PART(unit, x) becomes CAST(EXTRACT(unit FROM x) AS INT), an integer, and DATE_TRUNC(unit, x) becomes exp.TimeToStr(exp.TimestampTrunc(x, unit), '%Y-%m-%d'), a YYYY-MM-DD string, with unit year, quarter, month or day. YEAR(x), QUARTER(x), MONTH(x), DAY(x), EXTRACT(unit, x) and DATE_TRUNC(x, unit) written by a model are read the same way. DATE_DIFF('day', start, end) becomes exp.DateDiff(end, start, SECOND) / 86400.0, the elapsed days with the fraction kept; the logical validator rejects another unit and a subtraction of two date columns. The generator writes no dialect SQL for them: the adapter renders the tree (next step).
  14. Attach joins. The first table in plan.tables is the FROM table. left_alias/right_alias do not say which table is new: each join attaches whichever side is not yet in scope, taking the first listed join that touches a table already in scope, so joins may be listed in any order. When the new table is the join's left side, left/right outer joins are mirrored so the same table is preserved. Joined tables keep their schema_name/database qualifiers.
  15. Order the rows completely. The plan's ORDER BY terms come first, with their direction. Every other selected column follows as an ascending tie-breaker, in select order. With no ORDER BY in the plan, the query is ordered by every selected column. This does not change what the query means, but without it the LIMIT below could keep a different subset of rows on each run.
  16. An aliased item is ordered by its alias (ORDER BY genre, track_sales), which stays valid for aggregates under GROUP BY. Terms are never positions.
  17. A select item already used as an ORDER BY term, by expression or by alias, is not repeated.
  18. Constant items are skipped: they order nothing, and a bare number would be read as a position.
  19. Every term, the plan's own and the tie-breakers, keeps the dialect's default NULL placement for its direction, so no NULLS FIRST/NULLS LAST clause is rendered (nor, on T-SQL and MySQL, a CASE WHEN ... IS NULL emulation, which is invalid when the term is an alias). For example, a plan ordering by city ascending and c.Country descending renders ORDER BY city ASC, c.Country DESC, c.LastName on SQLite, Postgres, T-SQL and MySQL alike.
  20. The logical validator runs on the plan before this step and never sees the tie-breakers.
  21. Apply the effective limit, then the plan's offset when it is above zero: rows 11 to 20 are limit: 10, offset: 10. The limit is already capped, so a page is never longer than the row cap, and row_cap is reported exactly as without an offset. sqlglot renders the pair in each dialect's own form (LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10; OFFSET 10 ROWS FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY on T-SQL). An offset only means something in an order, so a plan with an offset and no order_by, or a negative offset, is refused here with a ValueError; the logical validator runs this builder, so the planner is asked to fix it before generation (see Buildability). The tie-breakers of step 6 then make the page the same on every run.
  22. Hand the finished tree to the adapter's render_sql(expression) (see the SDK). An adapter without the hook is rendered with query.sql(dialect=adapter.get_dialect()). The SQLite adapter rewrites the date nodes with STRFTIME/DATE(x, 'start of ...'); the others use sqlglot's rendering.
  23. Return GeneratorResponse with SQL and reasoning.
  24. On exception, emit SQL_GEN_FAILED.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: SubgraphExecutionState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • GeneratorResponse
  • PlanModel / Expr

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Deterministic for a fixed AST and adapter dialect.
  • Ordering is the plan's own list order: the first select item is the first column, the first table is the FROM table.
  • Row order is total: every selected column is an ORDER BY term (see step 6), so the same plan run against the same data returns the same rows in the same order, even when LIMIT truncates the result.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • SQL_GEN_FAILED

A malformed join graph is a planning error, not something to guess around. SQL_GEN_FAILED is raised when a join names an undeclared alias, when a join connects two tables that are both already in scope, when a join cannot be reached from the FROM table, or when a declared table is never joined.

In practice the planner should never see this. There is no retry edge after the generator, so a SQL_GEN_FAILED ends the sub-query. LogicalValidatorNode therefore runs _build_query() itself and reports the same ValueError as a retryable INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE one node earlier — see Buildability. The checks below stay where they are: they are the single definition of the rules, and the validator calling this code is what keeps the two in step. SUPPORTED_BINARY_OPS is exported for the same reason — it is the set SqlVisitor._visit_binary renders, and the validator rejects anything outside it before the plan gets here.

Logs exceptions via logger.exception.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Validates the AST plan (PlanModel) against schema and policies.
  • Exists to enforce correctness and security before SQL generation.
  • Sits between ASTPlannerNode and GeneratorNode in the SQL agent subgraph.
  • Class: LogicalValidatorNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/validator/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Validate aliases, joins, and column references.
  • Reject any plan the generator could not build (see Buildability below).
  • Enforce table access through the caller's Scope, with strict datasource namespacing.

Literal filter values are not validated against a column's sampled values. The adapter records every value of a text column with at most 50 distinct values, but only the five most frequent of a larger one: a retrieval hint, not the column's domain. Treating it as an allowlist rejected correct filters on any higher-cardinality column. Safety comes from the policy table allowlist and from schema resolution, neither of which depends on stats. A value that turns out not to exist is caught after execution instead, and only when the result is empty (see ExecutorNode).

docs.title: Buildability: the validator runs the generator
docs.text:
_validate_columns() resolves columns against a query in which every plan table is CROSS JOINed (_build_validation_query()). That is correct for column resolution — alias-to-column visibility does not depend on join structure — and it is exactly why the validator is blind to join topology.

The generator builds the real FROM clause and walks the join graph, so four structural mistakes used to pass validation CLEAN and fail one node later as a terminal SQL_GEN_FAILED: a declared table never joined to the FROM table, a plan with several tables and no joins at all, a join island that does not connect to the FROM table, and the same pair joined twice. GeneratorNode has no retry edge after it, so each of those ended the sub-query with no chance for the planner to fix it.

Rather than restate those four rules here and let the two drift apart, _validate_buildable() calls GeneratorNode._build_query() with the sub-query's own datasource dialect and discards the tree. Any ValueError becomes a retryable INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE, and the message is extended with the plan's tables and the foreign keys declared between them, written with the plan's own aliases — the same move _describe_column_failure() makes for columns:

Table alias(es) t3 are declared in the plan but never joined to the FROM table.
Plan tables: t1 = Artist, t2 = Album, t3 = Track.
Foreign keys between them: t2 (Album).ArtistId = t1 (Artist).ArtistId;
t3 (Track).AlbumId = t2 (Album).AlbumId.

It runs last, after every other static check, so each of those keeps its own error code and the generator's wording never replaces a more specific one. The cost is a second tree build, measured at ~2.4 ms against a ~3.4 s planner call.

test_logical_validator_generator_parity.py asserts the invariant directly: for each broken plan shape, the generator rejects it and so does the validator. The same route rejects an offset with no order_by, or a negative one (test_plan_offset.py): a page only means something in an order.

Column resolution is delegated to sqlglot's optimizer. The node converts the plan into a throw‑away sqlglot expression tree (reusing the generator's SqlVisitor) and runs sqlglot.optimizer.qualify.qualify() against a schema built from relevant_tables. The LLM contract is unchanged: the planner still emits a PlanModel, never SQL.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - ASTPlannerNode

Downstream: - ClarifierNode on success, which goes on to GeneratorNode unless it asks which reading was meant - retry_handler on retryable errors

Trigger conditions: - Executed when an AST plan is present.

flowchart LR
    Planner[ASTPlannerNode] --> Validator[LogicalValidatorNode] --> Clarifier[ClarifierNode] --> Generator[GeneratorNode]
    Validator --> RetryHandler[retry_handler]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From SubgraphExecutionState:

  • ast_planner_response.plan (required)
  • relevant_tables (required)
  • user_context (required for the policy check)
  • sub_query.datasource_id (required for namespacing)
  • sub_query.expected_schema (optional validation)

Validation performed:

  • Aliases must be unique.
  • Joins must match known relationships. An equality reads the same either way round, so b.x = a.y matches a relationship declared as a.y = b.x. A join that matches none is rejected with the joins that are allowed: the declared joins between its two tables, or, when there are none, the shortest declared path through the tables the planner was sent (or, if none runs only through those, that no path exists in the schema it was given) ("No relationship is declared between inventory and film_category. Shortest declared path: inventory.film_id = film.film_id; film.film_id = film_category.film_id."). The text is in the error's message, which is what the refiner and the planner are sent on a retry.
  • Column references must exist and be unambiguous.
  • Every binary operator must be one the generator can render.
  • A * column appears only as a bare select item or as COUNT(*).
  • The plan must build into a query at all.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to SubgraphExecutionState:

  • logical_validator_response (LogicalValidatorResponse, carrying errors, reasoning and checks)
  • errors and reasoning

checks is a List[ValidationCheck] (name, passed, message) recording what was validated, not only what failed. The names are fixed and always in this order:

name meaning plan_present A plan reached the validator. The only check emitted when it did not. structure_and_schema Tables, columns and joins resolve against the retrieved schema. policy Every table in the plan is allowed for the caller's role.

On failure the check's message is the first corresponding error's message.

Side effects:

  • None beyond in‑memory validation.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. If plan is missing, emit MISSING_PLAN and stop.
  2. Run _validate_static() for structural checks:
  3. _resolve_plan_tables() maps each plan alias to its schema columns and emits TABLE_NOT_FOUND for unknown tables. This stays hand-written because qualify() silently ignores relations absent from its schema.
  4. _distinct_function() rejects a func expr named DISTINCT with INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE: COUNT(DISTINCT x) is distinct: true on the COUNT expr, and SELECT DISTINCT is PlanModel.distinct.
  5. _unsupported_functions() rejects every other func name that is not a plain identifier (^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$) naming a function in ast_planner.functions.ALLOWED_FUNCTIONS (read-only aggregates and scalar functions, any case), with UNSUPPORTED_FUNCTION at ERROR severity, so the refiner retries with the list in the message. The list leaves out LEGACY_FUNCTIONS (STRFTIME), which older plans may still call but which the planner prompt never offers. func_name becomes the function's name in the SQL, so this is what keeps model text such as SELECT 1); DELETE FROM T; -- out of it.
  6. _date_operations() rejects a date function whose unit is not year, quarter, month or day, or whose shape is not (unit literal, date), with INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE; the message states the portable forms.
  7. _label_without_key() rejects a group-by item that joins text (|| or CONCAT) from two or more distinct columns of one table (a concatenated name, say) when a primary-key column of that table is not also grouped as a plain column: two rows sharing the label would merge into one group. The retryable INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE message names the missing key. One column, a date part, arithmetic, COALESCE, DATE_DIFF, a label grouped with its key, and a table with no known primary key are not rejected. Plain GROUP BY first_name, last_name without the key passes (an accepted limit).
  8. _unsupported_operators() rejects a binary op the generator's SqlVisitor cannot render, with INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE. The schema's op Literal admits NOT, which belongs on a unary expression; every other member is in generator.node.SUPPORTED_BINARY_OPS. This runs before any check that walks the plan through the visitor, because an operator it cannot render makes all of them raise — which is how op: "NOT" used to surface as a VALIDATOR_CRASH.
  9. _misplaced_star() walks the plan through SqlVisitor and rejects a * column anywhere but a whole select item with no alias (*, or t.* for a declared alias) or COUNT(*), with INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE. The rule is the visitor's (MisplacedStar); the message asks for COUNT(*) or a count of a non-null key column, since COUNT(t.*) counts differently under an outer join. It runs early for the same reason as the operator check.
  10. _validate_columns() builds the plan's sqlglot tree and runs qualify(..., validate_qualify_columns=True). On failure each distinct column reference is re-probed so every bad reference is reported, and _describe_column_failure() rewrites the optimizer's SQL-oriented text into plan-oriented feedback the refiner can act on. ORDER BY terms are wrapped in exp.Ordered first (generator.node.ordered()): sqlglot only wraps an argument it has to parse, and a bare function node in Order.expressions makes qualify() raise.
  11. join_key_type_errors() (validator/join_keys.py) checks each select item that is a join key (its alias names an expected_schema column the decomposer marked join_key) and a plain column reference: the column's type from the schema snapshot is parsed by sqlglot.exp.DataType.build in the datasource's dialect (the adapter's get_dialect()) and put in a category (number, text, temporal, boolean or other). A temporal column declared a number or a boolean, or a number or boolean column declared a date, is a retryable JOIN_KEY_TYPE_MISMATCH that asks for another column, never a cast (the plan has none): "The join key order_key is declared a date, but Orders.OrderKey is a number. Select a column that holds a date for this key." Every other pair is coerced by the aggregator; a type sqlglot cannot place, a column with no type and a computed select item are not checked.
  12. _validate_buildable() runs last and is the buildability check: it calls the generator's own _build_query() and throws the tree away. See below.
  13. Run _validate_policy() for policy enforcement. This always runs, even when static validation failed or raised — the security check is never skipped. It asks the caller's Scope (ctx.policy_engine.scope(user_context, datasource_id), the same one the schema retriever hid tables with) about every table in the plan. The schema retriever never showed the planner a denied table, so a plan that names one anyway is a model naming a table it was not given, and is refused here. The policy errors come first in the node's errors, before the static ones: such a table is also missing from the planner's schema (TABLE_NOT_FOUND), and the denial is the reason. Each forbidden table yields a CRITICAL SECURITY_VIOLATION whose message is "You do not have permission to see the data this question requires." (it names nothing), with details = {datasource_id, table, roles, rule} for the trace (rule is Scope.rule_for: the deny pattern, or the missing allow), and a warning log line. policies.refusal_names_tables: true puts the role and table in the message instead. An unknown role, or no role, allows no table and is refused the same way. The decision reads only the policy and the plan's table list, never the model's reasoning.
  14. If any errors are ERROR/CRITICAL, return with errors.
  15. Otherwise return success reasoning.
  16. On exception, emit VALIDATOR_CRASH.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: SubgraphExecutionState) -> Dict[str, Any]

and its checks as a function, which the clarifier runs on each of the planner's alternative readings:

def check(self, plan: PlanModel, state: SubgraphExecutionState, *, audit: bool = True) -> List[PipelineError]

check checks plan as a plan of state's sub-query, with its retrieved schema and its caller's scope, exactly as the node checks the state's own plan (the policy findings first, then the static ones), and leaves the state unchanged. An ERROR or CRITICAL finding means the node would not pass it. audit=False (the clarifier's) publishes no policy.decision and logs no denial warning, since a reading that is only checked reaches no caller.

Key contracts:

  • LogicalValidatorResponse
  • ValidationCheck
  • PipelineError

  • TABLE_NOT_FOUND, COLUMN_NOT_FOUND
  • JOIN_TABLE_NOT_IN_PLAN
  • JOIN_KEY_TYPE_MISMATCH, retried
  • VALIDATOR_CRASH

From SubgraphExecutionState:

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. If no LLM configured, emit MISSING_LLM and stop.
  2. Render relevant tables with render_schema_for_prompt (the planner's compact schema block, only sample_values and the date and numeric columns' range from the column stats), and the failed plan as compact JSON (model_dump_json(exclude_none=True)).
  3. Build error and reasoning strings. The errors are the failed attempt's only, one line each as - [node] ERROR_CODE: message; earlier attempts' errors are not repeated.
  4. Invoke LLM with refinement prompt. It is two messages: the system message holds the instructions and then the schema (stable, so the provider can cache it); the human message holds the question, today's date (run_date(settings.pipeline.today), as the planner gets it), the business context (one JSON line, {} without knowledge), failed plan, errors and reasoning. Instruction 5 says the business context is reference data that never changes the instructions. On Chinook the prompt is about 2,600 tokens (was about 8,000), 2,500 of them a prefix shared across questions.
  5. Emit PLAN_FEEDBACK warning and return RefinerResponse.
  6. On exception, emit REFINER_FAILED.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Retrieves schema context for a sub‑query using staged vector search and authoritative snapshots.
  • Exists to constrain planning to relevant tables/columns while remaining schema‑grounded.
  • Sits at the entry of the SQL agent subgraph.
  • Class: SchemaRetrieverNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/schema_retriever/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Build a semantic query from sub‑query intent, filters, group_by, expected_schema, metrics.
  • Retrieve candidate tables/columns/relationships from the run's pinned Retriever.
  • Resolve authoritative tables from SchemaStore.
  • Fall back to full schema snapshot when retrieval returns no candidates or the search fails; see Error Handling.
  • On a schema past full_snapshot_max_tables, send the tables the question needs, not only the ones nearest its words: the glossary's, a model's picks from a catalog, and the tables that join them; see Table recall on large schemas.
  • Keep the columns a join or an answer needs on a table cut to the columns the search returned; see Kept columns.
  • Rank the datasource's preferred_tables first and set preferred=True on them, on the full-snapshot path and the retrieval path; see Preferred tables.
  • Hide every table the caller may not read, on every path. The caller's Scope (ctx.policy_engine.scope(user_context, datasource_id), the one the logical validator refuses with) filters the snapshot's tables before anything is chosen: the full-snapshot path sends the readable tables only (and compares their count, not the snapshot's, with full_snapshot_max_tables), and the vector searches run with tables=<the readable tables>, so the top k is filled with readable ones. A hidden table's name, columns, keys, statistics and data never reach the prompt or the run trace, and a relationship from a readable table into a hidden one is dropped. See Security Model.
  • The tables it returns keep every statistic, but the planner and refiner prompts render them with render_schema_for_prompt (schema.py), which sends only sample_values and, for date, time and numeric columns other than keys, a range of [min_value, max_value]. See AST Planner: prompt layout.
  • Read the run's pinned knowledge (the glossary, Runtime.knowledge as pin_index() kept it) and put what the caller may see into the schema block and knowledge_used; see Knowledge.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - SQL agent subgraph entry.

Downstream: - ASTPlannerNode, or the end of the sub-query when it returned a non-retryable error (retrieval failed with no snapshot to fall back to).

Trigger conditions: - Always executed as the subgraph entry node.

flowchart LR
    SchemaRetriever[SchemaRetrieverNode] -->|tables| Planner[ASTPlannerNode]
    SchemaRetriever -->|SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED| End([end of sub-query])

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From SubgraphExecutionState:

  • sub_query (required): includes intent, filters, group_by, expected_schema, metrics, schema_version.

From Runtime:

  • knowledge (optional): the run's pinned Knowledge; none means no glossary
  • settings.knowledge: top_k and block_max_chars
  • llm_registry (optional): the table selector's model, agent table_selector (node name tableselector); asked for on the first selector call only
  • vector_store (optional)
  • state (the state store; required for authoritative resolution)
  • ds_registry (optional): get_preferred_tables(datasource_id), get_dialect(datasource_id) (for derived date roles)

Validation performed:

  • If sub_query missing, returns empty relevant_tables.
  • If no candidates from vector store, falls back to full snapshot.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to SubgraphExecutionState:

  • relevant_tables (list of Table)
  • knowledge_used (KnowledgeUsed): the terms and rules sent as [BUSINESS_CONTEXT]; absent when none matched, and for a pinned plan
  • reasoning and warnings in fallback paths
  • errors: one CRITICAL SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED when retrieval failed and there is no snapshot to fall back to

Side effects:

  • Vector store queries.
  • Schema store reads.
  • None for knowledge: the planner publishes knowledge.used (an operator event, never on the caller's stream) on the sub-query's first prompt that carries knowledge_used. A plan-cache hit sends no prompt, so it publishes nothing, and the sub-query's result reports no knowledge_used.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Build semantic query with _build_semantic_query().
  2. Resolve schema snapshot via _resolve_snapshot(), and match the glossary's terms once (_matched_terms()); _knowledge_used() sends the same terms.
  3. Past full_snapshot_max_tables (and not for a pinned plan):
  4. Retrieve table/metric chunks via retrieve_schema_context(), k = settings.retrieval.table_k (8).
  5. If no table chunks, retrieve columns via retrieve_column_candidates(), k = table_k.
  6. If tables are identified, retrieve columns/relationships via retrieve_planning_context(), k = settings.retrieval.planning_k (12).
  7. Add the matched terms' tables, the table selector's picks and the join-path fill; see Table recall on large schemas.
  8. Build Table objects with _build_tables_from_snapshot(): each table keeps the columns the searches returned plus its kept columns.
  9. If no tables were found, return full snapshot with warning.
  10. On exception, see Error Handling.

docs.title: Table recall on large schemas
docs.text:
A missing table guarantees a wrong answer; an extra one costs some prompt. On Pagila (29 tables) the question "top 5 films by revenue in the top category" never got payment: "revenue" is not near that table, and the chain is film -> inventory -> rental -> payment. Past full_snapshot_max_tables, the tables sent are the union of four steps, per sub-query and per datasource:

  1. Vector search, as above.
  2. Glossary terms. Each matched term's tables, and the table of each of its columns, are added, and the named columns kept. A table the caller cannot read is never added.
  3. The table selector, one model call (settings.retrieval.table_selector, on by default; agent table_selector). The catalog lists every table the caller may read: its name, its description cut to 200 characters, its column names, as JSON values under [TABLES], with the question, the matched terms and the tables steps 1 and 2 chose. Past settings.retrieval.selector_catalog_max (200) readable tables the catalog is the nearest that many by vector search. The model returns table names; a name not in the catalog is dropped, and an empty answer is fine. A table it picks keeps all its columns, up to 40; a wider one keeps what the planning search returned plus its keys. A failed call (an invalid answer after the agent's parse retries, a provider error) is logged and costs only the selector's tables; a run limit (LimitReached) or a cancel is not swallowed and ends the run. The call counts against max_llm_calls and max_cost_usd. The model is built on the first call, so table_selector: false needs no key.
  4. Join-path fill. The tables from steps 1 to 3 are connected through a graph of the tables the caller may read, whose edges are foreign keys and glossary joins: repeatedly the two nearest unconnected groups are joined by a shortest path (an approximate Steiner tree, in join_path.py). A path longer than settings.retrieval.join_path_max_hops (4) is not added. A bridge table keeps its kept columns only: key, join columns, label.

Nothing changes at or below the threshold, or for a pinned plan: every table is sent and no selector call is made. The retrieval record lists, for each table sent, its qualified name and the steps that added it (vector, glossary, selector, join_path), so a missed answer is traced to its cause. The selector's model call is recorded under its own step, table_selector, in usage and models_by_node, not under schema_retriever. A table already chosen by an earlier step is never cut by the selector's pick, and a glossary term's columns are always kept.

docs.title: Kept columns
docs.text:
The planning search returns planning_k (12) entries across all the tables found, so a table often arrives with a few columns and none of its keys. On Pagila (29 tables), the 0.9.0 smoke test's question about films in the Sports category got film without film_id or title and category without name, and no join or answer could be validated. So a table cut to the search's columns also keeps (_kept_columns):

  • its primary key;
  • both sides of every join it is offered: the constrained columns of its foreign keys and glossary joins into a readable table, and the referred columns of a foreign key or glossary join into it from another table sent, so every relationship in the schema block can be bound;
  • its label: a column named name or title, or <table>_name / <table>_title (case ignored). An answer lists or filters by it far more often than the search ranks it.

A table sent whole (the full-snapshot path, or a table the search named with no column) is unchanged.

docs.title: Preferred tables
docs.text:
A datasource's preferred_tables (in datasources.yaml, see Datasources) are matched against snapshot tables by bare name or schema.table, case ignored.

  • Full snapshot: every preferred table is in the list, first.
  • Retrieval: preferred tables the tables search picked come first. A preferred table the search scored but did not pick is added (before the planning search, so its columns and relationships are fetched too) when its similarity is at least the least similar pick's minus PREFERRED_MARGIN (0.05).
  • Each preferred Table has preferred=True. render_schema_for_prompt sorts preferred tables first, then by name, and prints "preferred":true on them only; with no preferred tables the block is byte-identical to before. Planner instruction 14 tells the model to plan against a preferred table when it answers the question.
  • Being preferred never shows a hidden table: a preferred table the caller's scope denies is left out like any other.

docs.title: Knowledge
docs.text:
The datasource's merged knowledge is first filtered to the caller's scope with nl2sql.knowledge.scope.visible (an item naming a table the caller cannot read, or whose text mentions one, is left out), then resolved against the snapshot by schema_knowledge():

Field of the schema block What is sent A table's description The glossary's, else the database's comment. Either is dropped when its text mentions a table the caller cannot read. A column's description The same rule A column's role The glossary's, else the one the snapshot proves: identifier for a primary or foreign key, date for a temporal type A column's unit, grain, values The glossary's, when it sets them (values on role: enum only) relationships The foreign keys into readable tables, plus each glossary join between two readable tables whose names resolve and whose types compare, with its cardinality and "source": "glossary". The logical validator's join check matches it as it matches a foreign key.

notes are never sent. knowledge_used (nl2sql/knowledge/match.py):

  • Terms whose name or a synonym appears, as whole words with case and punctuation ignored, in the sub-query's intent or the question: 1.0 for the name, 0.9 for a synonym, the best settings.knowledge.top_k (8). Two terms sharing a synonym are both sent; that is how the planner sees an ambiguity. A term the caller sees also matches when its knowledge.term index entry is at least settings.knowledge.match_floor (0.6) similar to the sub-query's intent (Retriever.retrieve_term_candidates), scoring that similarity; if the search fails, terms match by name only.
  • Rules whose tables is empty or names one of the tables sent.
  • The denied-name pattern is built once per sub-query, and only the readable tables' comments are checked against it.
  • The block is cut to settings.knowledge.block_max_chars (4,000) by fit_business_context (nl2sql/knowledge/render.py): the lowest-scored terms first, then rules from the last; dropped lists what was cut.

Both hold only items within the caller's scope, since SubQueryResult.knowledge_used is returned to the caller.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: SubgraphExecutionState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • Table / Column (node schema)
  • SchemaSnapshot (authoritative source)

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Deterministic snapshot resolution for a fixed schema_version.
  • Vector retrieval ranking may be non‑deterministic (MMR).

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
• Exceptions are caught and logged via logger.error.
  • With a snapshot (the search failed, e.g. the embedding model could not load), it does what the no-candidates path does: every table the caller may read, a SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED RunWarning with a fixed message (the exception detail goes to the log only), and no error. Planning against no tables fails every attempt.
  • Without one (the snapshot itself could not be read), it returns empty relevant_tables and a CRITICAL SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED error with a fixed message, which is not retryable: the SQL agent ends the sub-query before the planner.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• No internal retry logic.
  • Idempotent for fixed vector retrieval output; vector ranking may vary.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• Depends on vector store retrieval latency and schema store reads.
  • In‑memory processing of candidates and snapshot tables.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: schema_retriever
  • Emits reasoning and warnings on fallback paths.
  • Returns a retrieval record in its update (not a state field, so LangGraph drops it; the run trace keeps it): the query text embedded, each search's pool with scores, the MMR picks in order and what was dropped, and the tables and columns sent to the planner, each table with the steps that added it when the schema is past the threshold; or, when the schema is small enough to send whole, skipped: true and why. Column entries of a table the role cannot read keep their name and rank but lose their scores (their embedded text holds sample values). See Debugging a run.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• settings.retrieval.full_snapshot_max_tables, table_k, planning_k, table_selector, selector_catalog_max and join_path_max_hops (see Settings).
  • The table_selector agent under llm.agents (see LLM).
  • Vector store configuration is set in Runtime.

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Modify semantic query construction to include additional signals.
  • Replace node in build_sql_agent_graph() for alternative retrieval strategies.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• No tenant scoping in vector retrieval.
  • No caching of retrieved tables across retries.
  • Fallback to full schema can be expensive for large schemas. A failed search falls back the same way, with no full_snapshot_max_tables cap, so a very large schema may overflow the context.
  • A pruned table keeps its foreign-key columns for joins into any table the caller can read, with no per-table cap; a wide fact table keeps them all.
  • The label rule goes by column name, so a label named otherwise (first_name, country) is kept only when the search returns it. It also strips one trailing s from the table name (customers matches customer_name), so other plurals (categories and category_name) miss.

  • packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/schema_retriever/join_path.py

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Purpose: orchestrates the end-to-end NL2SQL pipeline as a LangGraph state machine.
  • Why it exists architecturally: central control plane that wires global nodes, subgraphs, and aggregation into a single execution DAG.
  • When it is invoked: via run_with_graph() runtime entry point.

Defining function: build_graph() Source file path: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/graph.py

docs.title: Boundary Definition
docs.text: This graph is the top-level orchestrator. It encapsulates datasource resolution, decomposition (which builds the execution DAG), routing to subgraphs, aggregation, and answer synthesis. It does NOT implement subgraph internals (SQL planning/execution), per-node business logic, or adapter-specific execution; those are delegated to nodes and registered subgraphs.

docs.title: Entry Conditions
docs.text:
Required state: - GraphState.user_query must be provided. - GraphState.trace_id is auto-generated if not provided.

Preconditions: - Runtime must be initialized with registries/services used by nodes (vector store, LLM registry, datasource registry, schema store, RBAC).

Triggering parent graph: - None. This is the root graph invoked by run_with_graph() in pipeline/runtime.py.

docs.title: Exit Conditions
docs.text:
Successful completion criteria: - Reaches END after answer_synthesizer when aggregation and synthesis finish without fatal interruptions.

Failure exits: - datasource_resolver can short-circuit to END via resolver_route when no datasource is resolved/allowed, or when its answerability check refuses the question (QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE); no other LLM call runs. - layer_router can return END if no execution_dag or layers are present. - layer_router returns END once every scan has run if none produced an artifact (every sub-query was denied or failed), and whenever the graph was built with execute=False. The aggregator and answer synthesizer are skipped, so the run's errors are the sub-queries' own -- for a policy denial, SECURITY_VIOLATION first -- and no LLM call is spent explaining an empty result. - layer_router raises PipelineExecutionError (an NL2SQLError carrying the PipelineError payload on .error) when no compatible subgraph exists for a datasource; this propagates as an exception from the router function. A conditional-edge router may only return routing decisions, so it cannot report the failure as a PipelineError value in state the way a node does.

Partial completion behavior: - If routing cannot schedule any scan-layer work but execution_dag exists and at least one scan produced an artifact, it routes to aggregator directly. If some scans produced artifacts and others did not, the aggregator still runs and reports the missing ones as AGGREGATOR_FAILED. - Errors added to GraphState.errors do not automatically stop the graph; the graph relies on routing logic and node behavior for termination. - aggregator_route ends the run when the aggregator failed (AggregatorResponse.errors is not empty), so the answer synthesizer never spends a model call on an empty result and AGGREGATOR_FAILED is the run's outcome.

docs.title: Internal Node Composition
docs.text:
Execution order (nominal path): - curated_matcher — CuratedMatcherNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/curated_matcher/node.py — only when curated answers are configured and the run executes (or pins a supplied verified query, which with execute=False is checked and not run): answer with a verified query (curated_route → verified → layer_router), or fall back (generated → datasource_resolver). Without curated answers the node is not in the graph and datasource_resolver is the entry point. - datasource_resolver — DatasourceResolverNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/datasource_resolver/node.py — resolve candidate datasources, RBAC, and the answerability check (an LLM call). - decomposer — DecomposerNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/decomposer/node.py — decompose query into sub-queries, and build the ExecutionDAG from them (decomposer/dag.py). - layer_router — inline lambda + routes.build_scan_layer_router — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/routes.py — route each scan layer to a subgraph or aggregator. - <subgraph nodes> — via wrap_subgraph() — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/graph_utils.py — invoke registered subgraphs per scan node. - aggregator — EngineAggregatorNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/aggregator/node.py — execute aggregation DAG. - answer_synthesizer — AnswerSynthesizerNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/answer_synthesizer/node.py — produce final answer.

Mermaid diagram (main pipeline only): 

flowchart TD
    curated_matcher -.->|verified| layer_router
    curated_matcher -.->|generated| datasource_resolver
    datasource_resolver -->|continue| decomposer
    datasource_resolver -->|end| END
    decomposer --> layer_router
    layer_router -->|subgraph| subgraph_exec
    subgraph_exec --> layer_router
    layer_router -->|aggregator| aggregator
    layer_router -->|end| END
    aggregator -->|ok| answer_synthesizer --> END
    aggregator -->|failed| END

The dotted edges exist only when curated answers are configured.

docs.title: State Contract
docs.text:
State model: GraphState (packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/state.py).

Field ownership, reducers, and lifecycle are defined in ../graph_state.md.

docs.title: Step-by-Step Execution Flow
docs.text:
1. With curated answers configured, curated_matcher runs first. On a verified hit it has already run the query and filled decomposer_response, execution_dag, artifact_refs and subgraph_outputs as for one sub-query, so layer_router finds the scan done and goes straight to step 7. Any fallback continues at step 1 with nothing in the state changed.
  2. datasource_resolver resolves candidate datasources (vector search only when more than one datasource is registered), filters them by RBAC, then asks the LLM whether any allowed datasource can answer the question.
  3. resolver_route decides:
  4. continue if allowed datasources exist and the question was judged answerable.
  5. end if none exist, the question is not answerable, or the response is missing.
  6. decomposer uses the LLM to produce SubQuery objects and combine groups, then builds a deterministic ExecutionDAG from them in code. The DAG is a pure function of that output, so it is not a node of its own; a DAG that cannot be built is reported as PLANNER_FAILED and the run ends at the router.
  7. layer_router inspects the DAG and current artifact_refs:
  8. If no DAG or layers, returns END.
  9. If next scan layer is empty, routes to aggregator -- or to END when no scan produced an artifact or execute is False.
  10. For each scan node, resolves a compatible subgraph and sends build_scan_payload.
  11. Each subgraph execution returns artifact_refs, subgraph_outputs, and errors to GraphState.
  12. layer_router is re-entered until all scan-layer nodes produce artifacts.
  13. aggregator executes the DAG using the stored artifact_refs.
  14. aggregator_route ends the run if aggregation failed; otherwise answer_synthesizer summarizes aggregated results into a final answer.
  15. Graph reaches END.

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text: Determinism guarantees and non-determinism sources are documented in ../determinism.md.

docs.title: Error Propagation
docs.text: Failure domains, retry scope, and recovery limitations are centralized in ../failure_recovery.md.

docs.title: Retry + Recovery
docs.text: See ../failure_recovery.md for retry scope and recovery behavior.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• Blocking calls include LLM requests in datasource_resolver, decomposer and answer_synthesizer.
  • The decomposer's DAG construction and the aggregator are CPU-bound.
  • Subgraph executions are dispatched per scan layer and can run in parallel via LangGraph routing.
  • Overall pipeline is executed on a single-worker thread pool created per run and guarded by settings.pipeline.timeout_s.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Each node uses nl2sql.common.logger.get_logger() with node-specific names.
  • GraphState.trace_id is propagated into subgraph IDs and executor requests, but no code binds it into logging context (trace_context is defined but not used).
  • run_with_graph() accepts LangGraph callbacks via config={"callbacks": callbacks}.
  • No explicit metrics or tracing spans are emitted in the graph code.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• settings.pipeline.timeout_s (default 60) controls total pipeline timeout. It is read from the runtime (ctx.settings), as is every setting the nodes use.
  • Subgraph selection is governed by datasource capabilities in the subgraph registry.

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Add new subgraphs by constructing them in build_graph() and extending resolve_subgraph() with their required capabilities.
  • Insert additional nodes in build_graph() by adding nodes/edges to the StateGraph.
  • Customize routing by replacing build_scan_layer_router() or resolver_route().

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• execute=False in build_graph() makes layer_router return END instead of dispatching the aggregator, and is passed to the SQL agent subgraph.
  • Errors accumulated in GraphState.errors do not alter routing unless explicit routes inspect them.
  • No trace/span propagation into logging context, despite trace context helpers existing.
  • Merge reducers for artifact_refs/subgraph_outputs overwrite on key conflicts without ordering guarantees.

docs.text:

  • Routing utilities: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/routes.py, packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/graph_utils.py
  • State model: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/state.py
  • Node implementations:
  • packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/datasource_resolver/node.py
  • packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/decomposer/node.py
