Server Sample database Generated wide schema PostgreSQL 16 Pagila, in database pagila database wide, schemas sales_01 ... ops_20 and audit MySQL 8.0 Sakila, in database sakila databases wide_s01 ... wide_s20 and wide_audit (MySQL's schemas are databases) SQL Server 2022 AdventureWorksLT, in database AdventureWorksLT2022 database wide, schemas sales_01 ... ops_20 and audit

docs.title: Local use
docs.text:
You need Docker with the compose plugin.

python testbed/passwords.py > testbed/.env               # once: random passwords, ignored by version control
docker compose -f testbed/docker-compose.yml up -d --wait
set -a; . testbed/.env; set +a                           # the tests read the same variables
REALDB=compose pytest -m realdb
docker compose -f testbed/docker-compose.yml down        # add -v to drop the data

In PowerShell, load the variables with Get-Content testbed/.env | ForEach-Object { $name, $value = $_ -split '=', 2; Set-Item "env:$name" $value } and set $env:REALDB = "compose".

The compose file has no default password, so no password is written in the repository: TESTBED_POSTGRES_PASSWORD, TESTBED_MYSQL_PASSWORD and TESTBED_MSSQL_PASSWORD are required, and up stops naming the variable if one is missing. testbed/passwords.py prints three fresh random ones. Docker Compose reads testbed/.env by itself, because it sits beside the compose file. A server keeps the password its data volume was created with, so make a new .env only together with down -v.

The first up downloads the samples, generates the wide schema and loads everything, which takes a few minutes (SQL Server wants about 2 GB of memory). Loading happens once per data volume, so a later up is quick. --wait returns only when every server is loaded.

Install the drivers the tests use with pip install -e "packages/nl2sql[postgres,mysql,mssql,duckdb]". SQL Server also needs Microsoft's ODBC Driver for SQL Server (17 or 18) on the machine; the tests use the newest one installed.

docs.title: The compose file
docs.text:
Service Image What it does samples python:3.12-slim One-shot. Runs testbed/samples.py: downloads each sample from a pinned URL, checks its SHA-256, extracts Sakila from its archive, and writes the wide schema for the three servers with testbed/wide_schema.py, all into the samples volume. Skips what is already there. postgres postgres:16 Starts after samples. On its first start, testbed/postgres/init.sh (the image's own init mechanism) loads Pagila and the wide schema and creates the reader login. mysql mysql:8.0 The same with Sakila, through testbed/mysql/init.sh. The mysql client handles Sakila's DELIMITER blocks. mssql mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest The server. Its healthcheck passes only once mssql-init has finished. It has a 60-second stop_grace_period: after Docker's default 10 seconds a stop ends in SIGKILL, and the next start then recovers every database before any can be opened. mssql-init the same image, for its sqlcmd Runs testbed/mssql/init.sh: waits up to five minutes until the server accepts logins and every sample database it already has is ONLINE in sys.databases (asked from master, since a database still in recovery cannot be opened), then restores AdventureWorksLT from the .bak, loads the wide schema and creates the reader login, skipping each database that already exists. Then it marks itself loaded for its healthcheck and idles instead of exiting.

Every server has a healthcheck that passes only once it is loaded, so up --wait is enough before running tests. --wait fails on an exited container unless another service waits for it to complete, as the servers wait for samples. Nothing waits for mssql-init, and on a later up it skips everything and would exit at once, so it stays running instead; that is what makes the same up -d --wait work on every start.

The file reads four variables:

Variable Default TESTBED_BIND 127.0.0.1 TESTBED_POSTGRES_PASSWORD none: required (testbed/passwords.py) TESTBED_MYSQL_PASSWORD none: required TESTBED_MSSQL_PASSWORD none: required Service Published port Admin user Sample database postgres 15432 postgres pagila mysql 13306 root sakila mssql 11433 sa AdventureWorksLT2022

The ports avoid a clash with a database already installed locally.

Each server also has a login nl2sql_reader, with the server's password, that may read its sample database and nothing else: not the wide schema. Tests use it where a limited login matters.

docs.title: The sample databases and their licences
docs.text:
Nothing is committed to the repository; the samples service downloads each file and refuses one whose SHA-256 differs from the pinned value, so we never redistribute the samples. If one is ever vendored, its licence file goes beside it.

Sample Files Source Licence Pagila pagila-schema.sql, pagila-insert-data.sql github.com/devrimgunduz/pagila, pinned to commit 5ba5a57, from before Pagila moved to PostgreSQL 18 PostgreSQL License (copyright Devrim Gündüz) Sakila sakila-schema.sql, sakila-data.sql, from sakila-db.tar.gz downloads.mysql.com, which is not versioned: MySQL re-publishes the archive in place (last on 2026-10-31), and then the samples service exits 1 with a checksum error until the pinned SHA-256 in testbed/samples.py is updated New BSD AdventureWorksLT 2022 AdventureWorksLT2022.bak github.com/microsoft/sql-server-samples, release adventureworks MIT

The server images have their own terms. The SQL Server image runs the free Developer edition, which needs ACCEPT_EULA=Y and is licensed for development and testing, which is all we do with it.

When an upstream file changes, samples stops with the expected and actual hashes. Check the new file, then pin its URL and hash in testbed/samples.py.

docs.title: The generated wide schema
docs.text:
python testbed/wide_schema.py --dialect postgres|mysql|tsql --seed 7 writes one SQL file. The same seed always gives the same schema:

Feature Count What it tests Schemas 20 (sales_01 ... ops_20), plus a small audit Index scope, policy globs Tables 1,200 in the 20 schemas, with 5 to 30 columns each Reflection and retrieval at scale Views 2 per schema Views are indexed Odd column types boolean, uuid, json, binary, xml and array where the server has the type; the nearest plain type where it does not Profiling never aborts Comments on about 30% of tables and columns Descriptions come from the database Foreign keys within each schema Join paths Mixed-case names 10 tables, such as CustomerAccounts Quoting Rows 3 tables with 1,000,000 rows, 50 with 1,000, the rest empty Row estimates, profiling limits

The rows are made on the server (generate_series on PostgreSQL, a cross join of digit tables on MySQL and SQL Server), so the file stays small.

Routing is measured on it too: tests/realdb/test_routing_wide.py indexes Pagila and the whole wide schema side by side on PostgreSQL, and checks that questions about films go to Pagila and questions about payroll runs or ledger entries go to the wide schema, however many tables there are to vote (the routing suite). Indexing the wide schema takes about 17 minutes on CI's runner, so the test runs on PostgreSQL only, and only when REALDB_WIDE_ROUTING is true: the workflow sets it nightly, on demand, and on pull requests that change nl2sql/indexing/ (or the test itself). It skips otherwise.

Table recall is recorded on Pagila too: tests/realdb/test_pagila_retrieval.py indexes it with local embeddings, runs the Pagila suite in mode retrieval (no model, no key, the table selector off) and gates it against the newest record in benchmarks/retrieval/pagila/. The workflow uploads its report as the eval-pagila artifact, which nl2sql eval publish records when the retriever moves on purpose. PostgreSQL only.

docs.title: The realdb marker and fixtures
docs.text:
Every test under packages/nl2sql/tests/realdb/ is marked realdb. Its fixtures find the servers from the environment:

Variable Meaning REALDB=compose The compose servers on 127.0.0.1, at the published ports, with the passwords in the three TESTBED_*_PASSWORD variables REALDB_POSTGRES, REALDB_MYSQL, REALDB_MSSQL A URL for one server, such as postgresql://postgres:<password>@127.0.0.1:15432/, with the password percent-encoded. It wins over REALDB=compose. REALDB_REQUIRED=1 A missing server is a failure, not a skip

Without a server, a realdb test skips with the fix in its message. Under REALDB_REQUIRED=1 it fails instead: a green run that skipped the real databases proves nothing.

Fixture or helper What it gives server Each of the three servers in turn (RealServer: its admin URL, its sample database, engine() for a SQLAlchemy engine) datasource(server, database=None, **fields) A Datasource for one database on the server, the sample by default engine_on(database=None, **fields) An NL2SQL engine on one database of server, with a fake LLM and no key

Test code may name dialects and use SQLAlchemy directly; the boundary tests cover packages/*/src, not the tests.

test_conformance.py runs the adapter conformance kit (nl2sql_sdk.testing) on each server. Its seed goes into schemas kit_a and kit_b of the sample database (databases of those names on MySQL), written with the admin login and dropped after each test. Its limited_login is a login nl2sql_kit the test makes, whose password holds @ : / # % and which may read kit_a only.

docs.title: CI: the realdb workflow
docs.text:
.github/workflows/realdb.yml runs the test bed on GitHub's runners. No cloud credentials are involved.

Job Runs What it does changes always Works out whether a pull request touches database-facing code (the paths below). On the nightly and on-demand runs the answer is always yes. realdb on a pull request when changes says so; nightly on main; on demand (workflow_dispatch), which is run before every release generates fresh passwords with testbed/passwords.py into the job's environment, masked in the log; docker compose ... up -d --wait, installs Microsoft's msodbcsql18 for pyodbc and packages/nl2sql[postgres,mysql,mssql,duckdb], then pytest -m realdb with REALDB=compose and REALDB_REQUIRED=1 realdb-gate always, after the other two Passes when realdb passed, or was skipped because nothing database-facing changed; fails otherwise. The decision is testbed/gate.py. This is the check to require.

The paths that make realdb run on a pull request:

packages/sdk/**
packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/adapters/**
packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/indexing/**
packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/storage/**
packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/schema/**
packages/nl2sql/tests/realdb/**
testbed/**
.github/workflows/realdb.yml

To run it by hand: Actions, "Real databases", "Run workflow", or gh workflow run realdb.yml --ref main.

The unit job in test.yml runs pytest -m "not integration and not realdb".

The scripts under testbed/ have their own unit tests, which need no database: packages/nl2sql/tests/unit/test_testbed.py (the wide schema, the checksums, skipping what is there, and the gate), packages/nl2sql/tests/unit/test_realdb_fixtures.py (the skip, the failure under REALDB_REQUIRED=1, and the variables) and packages/nl2sql/tests/unit/test_testbed_vm.py (scripts/testbed.py, against a fake gcloud on PATH).

docs.title: The GCP VM
docs.text:
The same compose file also runs on one small VM, nl2sql-testbed in project nl2sql-testbed-261014, zone us-central1-a. It is started for a session and stopped after it. There are no GitHub-to-GCP credentials: the owner, or an agent the owner asks, runs it by hand, at least once before each release.

Setting Value Machine e2-standard-2 (2 vCPU, 8 GB: SQL Server alone wants 2 GB), Debian 12 Docker Installed with the compose plugin by the VM's startup script on its first boot Disk 30 GB standard persistent disk. It keeps the images and the data volumes while the VM is stopped, so a later session skips the load. External IP Ephemeral, for outbound traffic only (image pulls, sample downloads). It is released, and free, while the VM is stopped. Network Its own VPC, nl2sql-testbed, so none of the default network's open rules apply. One firewall rule admits TCP 22, 15432, 13306 and 11433 from IAP's range 35.235.240.0/20 only: no database port is public. Access IAP: gcloud compute ssh and scp with --tunnel-through-iap, and gcloud compute start-iap-tunnel for the three servers Passwords Secret Manager: testbed-postgres-root-password, testbed-mysql-root-password and testbed-mssql-root-password

docs.title: scripts/testbed.py
docs.text:
You need the Google Cloud CLI, logged in (gcloud auth login) as an account with the access listed below. The script is Python so that it runs the same on Windows and Linux; it finds gcloud on PATH.

python scripts/testbed.py run -- pytest -m realdb    # the usual way: up, the command, down
python scripts/testbed.py up                         # or step by step
python scripts/testbed.py status
python scripts/testbed.py down
Command What it does up Reads the three passwords from Secret Manager into memory, starts the VM, copies testbed/ to it (never a local testbed/.env), waits up to five minutes for Docker (the first boot installs it), runs docker compose up -d --wait there with TESTBED_BIND=0.0.0.0, then opens the three IAP tunnels in the background and waits until localhost:15432, 13306 and 11433 answer. The first session loads the samples, which takes several minutes. run -- <cmd> up, then <cmd> with REALDB_POSTGRES, REALDB_MYSQL and REALDB_MSSQL pointing at the tunnels, then down in a finally: also after Ctrl-C, a failing command or a failed up. It exits with the command's code. down Closes the tunnels it opened, runs docker compose stop on the VM so every server shuts down cleanly, then stops the VM. Stopping the VM alone kills SQL Server, and the next session then waits for its databases to recover. If the servers cannot be stopped within three minutes (the VM is unreachable or already stopped), it says so and stops the VM anyway. Safe to run again. status The VM's state, how long it has been running, and whether each tunnel answers. Never a password.

--project, --zone and --instance override the defaults above.

The passwords reach the VM on the stdin of the docker compose command, so they live only in that command's environment there, and reach <cmd> through its own environment. They are never written to a file, put on a command line or printed, and the script never changes its own environment. The tunnels' process ids are kept in nl2sql-testbed/tunnels.json in the system's temporary folder, so a later down can close them.

Every gcloud compute ssh and scp call passes --strict-host-key-checking=no and --tunnel-through-iap. Right after a start, the first connection can fail while the VM boots and its new SSH key propagates (plink says Remote side unexpectedly closed network connection); the copy and the Docker wait retry such a connection failure, and only that, up to five times about a minute in all, then give up, and run still stops the VM.

On Windows, gcloud uses PuTTY's plink and pscp, and by default answers their host-key question by feeding them y on stdin instead of passing the caller's stdin on. The copy and the Docker wait keep that default, which stores the VM's host key in PuTTY's cache; the docker compose step sets CLOUDSDK_SSH_PUTTY_FORCE_CONNECT=false in gcloud's environment only, so the passwords on its stdin reach the VM. OpenSSH ignores the setting.

The script writes that stdin as bytes, one password per line ending in a bare newline: in text mode Windows would end each line with a carriage return, and the servers would be initialised with every password plus \r while the tests use the password alone (MySQL then answers 1045 and SQL Server 18456). The command on the VM also drops a trailing carriage return from each password it reads. A server keeps the password its data volume was created with, so if one was ever initialised with a wrong password, drop the volumes once while the VM is up, then down and up again, which loads the samples afresh:

gcloud compute ssh nl2sql-testbed --project=nl2sql-testbed-261014 --zone=us-central1-a --tunnel-through-iap \
  --command="sudo TESTBED_POSTGRES_PASSWORD=unused TESTBED_MYSQL_PASSWORD=unused TESTBED_MSSQL_PASSWORD=unused docker compose -f testbed/docker-compose.yml down -v"

After up on its own, remember down: a running VM bills by the hour. If the script is killed hard or the VM is started by hand, the nightly stop job below stops it at 03:00 UTC. That stop does not stop the servers first, so SQL Server is killed; the next up then waits while it recovers its databases, which mssql-init allows for.

docs.title: Cost controls
docs.text: Control Why The VM is stopped whenever no session runs A running VM bills by the hour Ephemeral external IP only Released, and free, while stopped No public database port; IAP's range only Nothing else can reach the servers run always stops the VM in a finally A failed test cannot leave it running The nightly stop at 03:00 UTC The backstop for everything above A budget of $10 a month with alerts The last line Item Approximate cost (check the billing report after the first month) Stopped the 30 GB disk: about $1 to $2 a month Running about $0.07 an hour The scheduler job free: one job is inside Cloud Scheduler's free tier

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
The owner's account holds roles/owner on the project, which covers both the set-up below and scripts/testbed.py. Anyone else who runs the script needs:

Role For roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1 starting, stopping and describing the VM, and the SSH key gcloud compute ssh adds to it roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor --tunnel-through-iap and start-iap-tunnel roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor on the three secrets the passwords

docs.title: One-time set-up
docs.text:
Nothing in the repository creates cloud resources. The owner runs these once, in a bash shell (Git Bash on Windows) logged in to gcloud. The three secrets already exist.

PROJECT=nl2sql-testbed-261014
REGION=us-central1
ZONE=us-central1-a
VM=nl2sql-testbed
STOPPER=testbed-stopper@$PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com

# 1. The APIs.
gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com iap.googleapis.com cloudscheduler.googleapis.com \
    billingbudgets.googleapis.com --project=$PROJECT

# 2. A network of its own, so the default network's open SSH and RDP rules do not apply.
gcloud compute networks create nl2sql-testbed --subnet-mode=custom --project=$PROJECT
gcloud compute networks subnets create nl2sql-testbed --network=nl2sql-testbed \
    --region=$REGION --range=10.10.0.0/24 --project=$PROJECT

# 3. The one inbound rule: SSH and the three servers, from IAP's range only.
gcloud compute firewall-rules create nl2sql-testbed-allow-iap --network=nl2sql-testbed \
    --direction=INGRESS --action=ALLOW --rules=tcp:22,tcp:15432,tcp:13306,tcp:11433 \
    --source-ranges=35.235.240.0/20 --target-tags=nl2sql-testbed --project=$PROJECT

# 4. The VM: e2-standard-2, Debian 12, a 30 GB standard disk, an ephemeral external IP,
#    no service account. Its startup script installs Docker and the compose plugin once.
#    printf writes it with LF line endings, which an inline script typed in Git Bash on
#    Windows does not get: with CRLF the VM fails to run it (exit 127) and Docker never arrives.
printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' \
    'command -v docker >/dev/null || curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh' > startup.sh
gcloud compute instances create $VM --project=$PROJECT --zone=$ZONE \
    --machine-type=e2-standard-2 --image-family=debian-12 --image-project=debian-cloud \
    --boot-disk-size=30GB --boot-disk-type=pd-standard \
    --network=nl2sql-testbed --subnet=nl2sql-testbed --tags=nl2sql-testbed \
    --no-service-account --no-scopes \
    --metadata-from-file=startup-script=startup.sh
gcloud compute instances stop $VM --zone=$ZONE --project=$PROJECT    # stopped until a session needs it

# 5. The nightly stop: a service account that may only stop this VM, and a scheduler job
#    that calls the Compute Engine API with its token at 03:00 UTC.
gcloud iam service-accounts create testbed-stopper --display-name="Stops the test-bed VM" --project=$PROJECT
gcloud iam roles create testbedStopper --project=$PROJECT --title="Test-bed stopper" \
    --permissions=compute.instances.stop --stage=GA
gcloud compute instances add-iam-policy-binding $VM --zone=$ZONE --project=$PROJECT \
    --member=serviceAccount:$STOPPER --role=projects/$PROJECT/roles/testbedStopper
gcloud scheduler jobs create http nl2sql-testbed-nightly-stop --project=$PROJECT --location=$REGION \
    --schedule="0 3 * * *" --time-zone=Etc/UTC --http-method=POST \
    --uri=https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/$PROJECT/zones/$ZONE/instances/$VM/stop \
    --oauth-service-account-email=$STOPPER \
    --oauth-token-scope=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform

# 6. The budget: $10 a month, with alerts at 50%, 90% and 100%.
BILLING=$(gcloud billing projects describe $PROJECT --format='value(billingAccountName)')
gcloud billing budgets create --billing-account=${BILLING#billingAccounts/} \
    --display-name="nl2sql test bed" --budget-amount=10USD \
    --filter-projects=projects/$PROJECT \
    --threshold-rule=percent=0.5 --threshold-rule=percent=0.9 --threshold-rule=percent=1.0

To check the set-up, run python scripts/testbed.py run -- pytest -m realdb. To check the nightly job, start the VM with python scripts/testbed.py up, run gcloud scheduler jobs run nl2sql-testbed-nightly-stop --location=$REGION --project=$PROJECT, and python scripts/testbed.py status should then show it stopped; finish with python scripts/testbed.py down to close the tunnels.

docs.title: Testing Architecture
docs.text: Tests are organized by scope and live under packages/**/tests. The core engine has unit, integration, and end-to-end tests.

docs.title: Test layout
docs.text:
packages/nl2sql/tests/
  unit/             # Node-level tests, registries, stores
  integration/      # Pipeline components with real data
  e2e/              # End-to-end flows
  cli/              # CLI command tests
  adapters/         # Cross-dialect adapter contract tests
  sqlalchemy_base/  # tests of the SDK's SQLAlchemy base (nl2sql_sdk.sqlalchemy)
  realdb/           # Against real PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server (the test bed)
packages/api/tests/ # FastAPI route and service tests (stubbed engine)

pytest.ini is the single source of truth for pytest configuration - test paths, markers, and addopts. Do not add a [tool.pytest.ini_options] table to pyproject.toml: pytest reads only one config file, and pytest.ini wins, so such a table is silently ignored. Dev/test tooling lives in the root pyproject.toml under [dependency-groups] dev (pip install --group dev).

docs.title: Markers and what CI runs
docs.text:
Three independent things can make a test unrunnable in the fast job, so they are three markers. A test may carry more than one.

Marker Means Provided by integration Needs external resources: the demo's SQLite databases - vendored Chinook and the generated support and webanalytics, read from the installed package (nl2sql.testing.config.make_demo_config) - or the downloaded ONNX embedding model. The package; tests/e2e writes its own project with nl2sql init --demo llm Needs a real OPENAI_API_KEY. Costs money per run. Nothing in CI - never selected. realdb Needs a real PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQL Server: the test bed. testbed/docker-compose.yml, in the realdb workflow

Everything under packages/nl2sql/tests/integration/ is marked integration automatically by packages/nl2sql/tests/conftest.py, and everything under packages/nl2sql/tests/realdb/ is marked realdb the same way. The llm marker is declared per module, next to a comment saying which call needs the key. Only four modules carry it - test_ast_planner_real_data.py, test_decomposer_real_data.py, test_logical_validator_real_data.py and test_answer_synthesizer_real_data.py - all of them nodes that call a chat model directly. Nothing else in the directory needs a key: indexing calls no model, so tests that index real data run key-free.

.github/workflows/test.yml has three test jobs over the source tree:

  • test runs pytest -m "not integration and not realdb" across Python 3.12 and 3.13. This is the fast job and must stay fast.
  • integration runs pytest -m "integration and not llm" on one Python version, after writing and indexing a demo project (nl2sql init --demo demo-ci and nl2sql --config demo-ci/nl2sql.yaml index), key-free with the local embedder. The ONNX model is cached across runs. That subset covers schema indexing, datasource resolution, schema retrieval, aggregation and the local embedder against the real Chinook database; run it with --collect-only -q for the current list.
  • eval-gates runs in parallel with integration: the same demo project and model cache, then the three key-free eval gates (plans, retrieval, routing; see Evals) and the upload of their reports.

integration and eval-gates are skipped, and count as passing, on a pull request that changes only documentation (docs/** or Markdown files); the code-changes job decides.

A separate workflow, .github/workflows/realdb.yml, runs pytest -m realdb against the test bed on GitHub's runners: on pull requests that change database-facing code, nightly on main, and on demand before a release. Its realdb-gate job always runs and is the required check.

Three more jobs test the package rather than the source tree:

  • api-image builds the root Dockerfile (the web app's Node stage, then the API), the image the release pushes to GHCR, without pushing it. It imports nl2sql_api.main inside it, checks that pyodbc.drivers() lists the SQL Server driver, records the image size in the job summary and checks that GET / answers the built page. tests/unit/test_docker_images.py separately checks that every Dockerfile's FROM python:X.Y satisfies every package's requires-python.

  • build builds the web app first, then the three wheels and sdists (the nl2sql-api wheel must carry static/index.html), installs them into a clean virtualenv and runs import nl2sql and nl2sql --help.

  • fresh-install takes those wheels and installs them the way a user does, pip install "nl2sql-cli[web]", into an empty virtualenv outside the checkout. It then boots nl2sql-api serve --demo --hosted (the command the Hugging Face Space runs) with no API key, and passes only when the web app page, /api/v1/meta, each datasource's schema, /api/v1/index, the recorded guided questions and their scripted follow-up all answer from that install. It is what catches a wheel that imports but ships without the built web app, the sample databases or a dependency the demo extra forgot. scripts/fresh_install_check.py is the whole check, so it runs the same on a laptop:

    pip install build
python scripts/fresh_install_check.py --build   # builds into dist/ first

Any *_API_KEY in your environment is dropped for the run, so a key you exported cannot make it pass where CI would fail. The decisions it makes are unit-tested in tests/unit/test_fresh_install_check.py. After a release the same script runs twice more, from publish_pypi.yaml: with --pypi X.Y.Z to install the published version from PyPI itself, and with --url https://nadeem4nk-nl2sql-demo.hf.space --expect-version X.Y.Z to wait for the live Space to serve it, then once more with its custom domain as --url (see Releasing).

Nothing selects llm. Those tests are run by hand with a key:

OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... pytest -m integration

Collection is not enough to keep these honest. Every test in the directory imports cleanly even when it calls a method that no longer exists, so rot shows up only at call time - which is the point of running the key-free subset in CI rather than gating on --collect-only. The subset is worth keeping wide: every test that can run without a key should, because the ones that cannot are never run by CI at all.

tests/e2e builds one demo project per session (demo_project), indexes it, then moves its .nl2sql aside and leaves a file of that name, so no test can open the shared index or state store. Each test runs on its own copy: private_storage(demo_project, tmp_path / "store") as project_config's storage, or copy_demo(demo_project, tmp_path / "demo") for a whole project. When tests shared the one state.db, engines left open by one test, copies taken while it was open and CLI runs writing it all met in the same file, and CI failed with disk I/O error in whichever test pytest-randomly ran next.

docs.title: Randomised test order
docs.text: pytest-randomly shuffles the order of tests on every run, which turns order-dependent tests - shared class-level caches, leaked globals, fixtures that do not unwind - into loud local failures rather than intermittent CI ones. Each run prints the seed it used; reproduce a failure with pytest -p randomly --randomly-seed=<seed>.

docs.title: Settings in tests
docs.text:
The engine reads its settings from its runtime, not from a process global, so a test sets them on the runtime it builds:

  • One node or service: nl2sql.testing.runtime.fake_runtime(settings=..., policies=..., traces_dir=..., **attrs) builds a stand-in runtime with a real config, a local results store and a files trace store on traces_dir (pass traces= for another trace store). Settings are written as in YAML: settings={"traces": {"mode": "always"}}.
  • A whole engine: Runtime.from_config(make_config(tmp_path, ...)). An Embeddings(instance=FakeEmbeddings(size=8)) keeps it free of any model.
  • One run with different settings: ctx.derive({"settings.pipeline.plan_cache": True}) returns a run-scoped runtime with a derived config, its own curated answers and its own LLMSet, sharing the stores and the engine's LLM client cache. Evaluation and trace replay use it the same way; the runtime it came from never changes. tests/unit/test_run_scoped_runtime.py pins that down.

There is no process-global settings object to monkeypatch, and no module writes os.environ: a test sets what it needs in the config it builds. The architecture tests keep it that way (An Engine Owns Its Config).

flowchart TD
    Unit[Unit Tests] --> Core[Core Components]
    Integration[Integration Tests] --> Pipeline[Pipeline Nodes]
    E2E[End-to-end Tests] --> Orchestration[Full Orchestration]

docs.title: Runtime coverage targets
docs.text:
• Pipeline nodes (test_node_*.py)
  • Subgraph orchestration (test_sql_agent_subgraph.py)
  • DAG layering (test_graph_layers.py)
  • Registry and store behavior (test_*_registry.py, test_state_store.py)
  • REST contract (packages/api/tests/) via FastAPI TestClient with the get_engine dependency overridden, so no datasource, LLM or network is needed

docs.title: Deterministic validation
docs.text:
Tests enforce deterministic behavior by:

  • using structured output schemas for planner/decomposer
  • validating stable IDs and DAG layering
  • running logical validator checks for expected schema alignment

docs.title: Adapter compliance testing
docs.text: The SDK includes testing utilities to validate schema introspection and result contracts for new adapters.

docs.title: Source references
docs.text:
• Test configuration: pytest.ini
  • Core tests: packages/nl2sql/tests/
  • API tests: packages/api/tests/

docs.title: Conversations
docs.text:
Release 0.9

start, ask, stream, retry, ask_only, tool, report, get, list and delete work, with the chat tools chart, diagram and report.

A conversation is a chat over the database. The model decides, step by step, whether to answer or to ask the database a question through the same typed plan and validator as run_query. It never writes SQL and never sees result rows.

conversation = engine.conversations.start(user_context=me)
turn = engine.conversations.ask(conversation.id, "How many customers are there?", user_context=me)
print(turn.reply)                       # the model's closing message
print(turn.steps[0].result.sub_queries[0].sql)   # what ran; the rows are not stored
follow_up = engine.conversations.ask(conversation.id, "and by country?", user_context=me)

Every method takes the caller (user_context, keyword-only and required). The methods are listed in Conversations API.

docs.title: A turn
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  IN["ask(text) or ask(choice=...)"] --> K{"choice?"}
  K -->|yes| RE["ask step: the pending question, with the choice"]
  K -->|no| M["model call: reply or tool call"]
  M -->|reply| ST["store the turn"]
  M -->|"ask"| RUN["run_query: typed plan, validator, cost rule"]
  M -->|"chat tool"| TOOL["registry tool: no model call"]
  RUN -->|"clarification, approval or stop"| ST
  RUN -->|"ok or error"| M
  TOOL --> M
  M -->|"bound reached"| LAST["one last call, tools off"]
  LAST --> ST
  RE --> ST
  • The model chooses. Each step is one structured call (ModelStep): a reply, or one call of the ask tool with a question that stands alone, or of an enabled chat tool (a chart, a report). A reply may carry offers: tools it suggests, which run only when a client calls tool. The model sees the last context_turns turns as one JSON object (the questions that ran, each answer's summary, the columns, the datasources and tables read), never rows. Everything earlier said, the new message included, reaches it as a JSON string value: text in the history cannot pass for an instruction or a section marker.
  • The bound. At most max_tool_calls tool calls per turn, then one more model call with the tools off. A turn makes at most max_tool_calls + 1 model calls. They count against settings.pipeline.max_llm_calls and max_cost_usd; a refusal ends the turn stopped.
  • A step the model got wrong (an unknown tool, a bad argument, an option id that is not pending) is sent back with what was wrong. After the parse retries the turn ends error with MODEL_STEP_INVALID (Turn.error) and the reply "I could not tell what to do with that. Please ask it as a full question."
  • Each ask step is a run of its own, with its own trace_id, events and result pages, and the cost rule, scope and hooks of any run. A hook at run.before sees conversation_id.

docs.title: Clarifications and approvals
docs.text:
• A run that ends needs_clarification ends the turn and sets Conversation.pending. The next turn can pass choice="b" (an option id; the turn is of kind choice, its text the option's label, and no model is called) or text the model maps to an option by calling ask with choice. Either way the pending request's own question is re-asked with the choice. Any next turn clears pending. A choice with nothing pending is a ValueError.
  • A run that ends needs_approval ends the turn. An approver acts on each ApprovalRequest in turn.steps[i].result.approvals_needed outside the conversation; the asker then calls retry(conversation_id, user_context=..., approvals=[...]), which re-runs the last ask step's question as a turn of kind retry, with no model call.
  • ask_only(conversation_id, question, user_context=..., choice=None, cancellation_token=None) runs just the ask tool (a turn of kind tool, no model call) and returns the full QueryResult with its rows. MCP's ask will use it.
  • A run that times out (pipeline.timeout_s) fails only its step, with error.code PIPELINE_TIMEOUT; the turn goes on and the model replies, for example by suggesting a narrower question. Each ask step runs on its own cancellation token, a child of the turn's, so the timeout never cancels the turn, while cancelling the turn (cancellation_token, or closing a stream) still stops the step in flight. Only a cancel ends a turn CANCELLED. After a timeout the old run may still finish its in-flight model call or SQL while the loop goes on, so the next ask step can overlap it.

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text: stream(...) takes the same arguments as ask and yields the caller-safe run events of each ask step (run.started to run.finished), conversation.step after each step and, last, conversation.turn whose data["stored"] is the stored Turn as JSON. Ownership and the arguments are checked at the call; a conversation that is already running a turn raises ConversationBusy from the first next. Closing the iterator early cancels the turn and stores nothing.

docs.title: Ownership and retention
docs.text: Rule Detail Owner start records the caller's tenant_id (else the engine's) and user_id. Any other caller gets ConversationNotFound, as for an id that does not exist. Roles Never stored. Each turn runs with the user_context passed to that call, so a role taken away applies at the next turn. No user_id Allowed, and owned by "no user": every caller without one in that tenant sees those conversations. Fine for a script, not for a server. One turn at a time A turn holds the state store's lock conversation:<id>; a second ask, retry or stream raises ConversationBusy. Limits conversations.max_turns (50): the next turn, whichever of ask, stream, retry or ask_only it is, is a ValueError naming CONVERSATION_TOO_LONG and the fix, "Start a new conversation." Results A stored step keeps its question, plan, SQL, explanation and summary, never the rows. Read them with engine.results.page(step.trace_id, ..., user_context=caller), as the conversation's caller, until they are purged. Retention engine.storage.purge() deletes conversations last updated more than conversations.max_age_days (30; null keeps them) ago and reports conversations in retention.purged.

docs.title: Events
docs.text: conversation.started (from start), conversation.step (after each step, in the turn's scope, with the tool, the status and the argument names, never values) and conversation.turn (once the turn is stored; it closes the turn's scope). The turn's trace_id carries the loop's own llm.calls, and Turn.usage holds their usage.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: conversations: in nl2sql.yaml (context_turns, max_tool_calls, max_turns, max_age_days) and the conversation agent in llm.yaml; see Configuration System and LLM.

docs.title: Chat tools
docs.text:
Release 0.9: the runner and the five tools are built

A chat tool turns something a conversation already has into something else, with no model call of its own. The five built-ins:

Tool Does chart Draws an answer's data as a line, bar, big number or table (Charts); args turn, step, result_id, kind diagram Draws the tables of an answer, or of a datasource, as Mermaid (Diagrams); args view (answer or schema), turn, step, datasource_id, tables report Writes the conversation's answered turns up as Markdown; args turns, title dashboard_edit Builds or changes a dashboard (Dashboards); args edits, dashboard_id, title, workspace_id dashboard_pin Saves the dashboard being built, whole; args dashboard_id, workspace_id, title

docs.title: Which tools are on
docs.text: chat_tools: in nl2sql.yaml lists registered names. Absent, the default tools are on: chart, diagram, report, dashboard_edit and dashboard_pin, those of them the registry has (an engine built on Registry.empty() has none). [] turns every registry tool off and leaves ask, the conversation's own tool, which is always on. A name you list that the registry does not know is a config error when the engine is built, and so is ask (it is not a registry tool). engine.chat_tools.list() returns the enabled tools (ChatToolInfo: name, description, JSON Schema of the arguments); it takes no caller, as it lists names.

docs.title: Three ways a tool runs
docs.text:
• The model calls it. In a turn the model may call an enabled tool after any result. Its arguments are checked against the tool's args_model before it runs, and a bad call goes back to the model with what was wrong. The tool sees the conversation including the steps already taken in this turn, so a chart of the answer just asked for works in one turn. The model gets the step back as a short description (a chart: its kind, why and its columns; a diagram: its text; a report or JSON: its title only) and never the data. max_tool_calls bounds ask and tools together.
  • The model offers it. A reply may carry offers, tools it suggests (Turn.offers). Nothing runs; a client shows a button and, on a click, calls conversations.tool.
  • A client calls it by name. engine.conversations.tool(cid, "chart", {"turn": 3}, user_context=me) runs one enabled tool as a turn of kind tool, with no model call. Arguments that do not validate raise ValueError and store nothing. A name that is not enabled is stored as a failed step.

docs.title: The dashboard tools
docs.text: dashboard_edit takes edits, the list of dashboard edits a person can make by hand plus add_tile, replace_plan, add_verified_tile and add_saved_tile, and applies them with engine.dashboards.edit, all or none. Its other arguments are dashboard_id (the conversation's dashboard when absent), and title and workspace_id for a new draft. The first call in a conversation makes a draft tied to it (Conversation.dashboard_id, Dashboard.conversation_id); later calls edit the same one, and a conversation started with start(dashboard_id=...) edits that dashboard. add_tile and replace_plan name an answer by from_step (turn, which defaults to the turn being answered, and which of that turn's ask calls with a result, counting from 1): the engine reads the whole plan from its own stored step, never from model text, and checks it with a run that executes nothing before saving, so a plan the validator rejects ends the step as TOOL_NOT_APPLICABLE with the validator's message and saves nothing. add_verified_tile (datasource_id, verified_id, params) and add_saved_tile (saved_id) name a reviewed query or one of the caller's own saved answers by id, with no question asked and no conversation step needed; they are checked the same way. A verified query the caller cannot see (engine.curated.list does not list it) is refused as "no verified query", exactly like an id that does not exist. A draft this call made is removed again, whatever the failure. If the conversation's dashboard was deleted, the next edit makes a new draft and the conversation is tied to that. dashboard_pin saves the whole draft (engine.dashboards.pin) and is called only when the user asks. A dashboard that is not the caller's is "not found". Neither tool calls a model or shows the model a row: it gets the step's kind, title and refs ({"dashboard_id": ...}), and the open dashboard in [CONVERSATION] as dashboard (id, title, status, and each chart's id, title, question, chart and last status, with the reason for a needs_fixing or denied one), re-read at every step so it shows this turn's edits.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A step that does not succeed has status error and ToolStep.error = {"code", "message"}; the model sees it and may go on.

Code When TOOL_FAILED The tool raised, or returned something that is not a ToolOutput. The message gives the exception type only, since its text can quote data; the full error is in the log. TOOL_NOT_APPLICABLE The tool raised ToolNotApplicable(message): it cannot apply to that turn (no answer to chart, rows expired). UNKNOWN_CHAT_TOOL The name is not enabled; the message names the enabled tools.

Every call, successful or not, publishes chat_tool.called (tool, conversation_id, turn, ok, seconds, error_code).

docs.title: The diagram
docs.text: diagram has two views. answer (the default) draws the tables the chosen answer read, from its stored plans, through nl2sql.diagram_for; turn picks the turn and step which of its answers (the latest turn with an answer, its first, by default). schema draws datasource_id through engine.datasources.diagram for the conversation's caller, so a table that caller may not read is not drawn; tables narrows it. No data is in either diagram, and a hidden table and a missing one give the same TOOL_NOT_APPLICABLE. See Diagrams.

docs.title: The report
docs.text: engine.conversations.report(cid, user_context=me, turns=None, title=None) returns Markdown assembled from the stored turns, with no model call: for each answered question its summary, the plain-English explanation, the first 20 rows, the takeaway of the chart the data is drawn as (unless it is a table), the SQL in a <details> block and the trace id. Rows are read back through engine.results; once they are purged the section says "Results expired." and keeps the text, the SQL and the trace. turns picks turn numbers (an unknown one is a ValueError); the default is every answered turn. A conversation with nothing answered is a ValueError. Every turn is considered, and a question counts when its ask step succeeded, even if a later tool step in that turn failed. The report tool is the same call, so it covers earlier turns, not the one it is called in. A stored tool output never holds row data: the report tool stores the report without its row tables and chart takeaways, and a stored chart output has its spec and columns but data.rows is empty. Ask conversations.report again for the full report, and engine.results.chart to draw a chart; both read the rows from the results while their retention keeps them.

docs.title: Writing one
docs.text:
A tool is a class with interface_version = 1, a one-line description the model reads, an args_model (a pydantic model that must forbid extra keys, or the engine refuses it when it is built; its JSON Schema is shown to the model) and __call__(ctx: ToolContext, args) -> ToolOutput. It is built with no arguments. It reaches the engine only through the public NL2SQL facade in ctx.engine, and may import only the top-level nl2sql and nl2sql.chat_tools. Register it under the nl2sql.chat_tools entry point group, or with registry.add_chat_tool(name, cls), and name it in chat_tools: in nl2sql.yaml. The name ask is taken.

from typing import ClassVar

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

from nl2sql.chat_tools import ToolContext, ToolNotApplicable, ToolOutput


class CountArgs(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")


class QuestionCount:
    interface_version: ClassVar[int] = 1
    description: ClassVar[str] = "Say how many questions this conversation has answered."
    args_model: ClassVar[type[BaseModel]] = CountArgs

    def __call__(self, ctx: ToolContext, args: BaseModel) -> ToolOutput:
        asked = sum(s.call.name == "ask" for t in ctx.conversation.turns for s in t.steps)
        if not asked:
            raise ToolNotApplicable("Nothing has been asked yet.")
        return ToolOutput(kind="markdown", title="Questions", body=f"{asked} questions so far.")


registry.add_chat_tool("question_count", QuestionCount)

ToolOutput.kind is chart (a ChartSpec as JSON), mermaid, markdown or json; refs carries ids a client needs ({"dashboard_id": ...}). A tool makes no model call. ctx.conversation is a copy, so a tool cannot change it.

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text:
Partly built (release 0.9)

Workspaces, the dashboard store, pin, move and the manual edits work, and so do open, refresh, stored results and schedules, and so do filters and filter_values, generate and suggest_questions, the starter dashboard, and building in chat.

A dashboard is a set of charts, each holding the typed plan that produced it, saved whole into a private workspace. Opening one serves stored results after the access check; refreshing re-runs the stored plans as the caller with no model call. The methods are in Dashboards API.

Part What it covers Store Workspaces, the dashboard store, pin, move and the manual edits Refresh open, refresh, stored results, schedules and nl2sql dashboards refresh Filters refresh(filters=...) and filter_values Starter The starter dashboard: generate and suggest_questions, with no model In chat Building and editing a dashboard in a conversation (dashboard_edit, dashboard_pin) and create_draft

docs.title: Workspaces
docs.text: A workspace is a named folder of your dashboards ("Sales", "Ops"). A dashboard lives in exactly one, and both are private to you: someone else's is "not found". engine.workspaces.create, rename, list and delete manage them; delete refuses a workspace that still holds a dashboard, draft or saved. The first time you pin with no workspace in mind, a workspace named "General" is made for you.

docs.title: Drafts and pinning
docs.text:
A dashboard built in chat is a draft tied to its conversation. It is listed only with list(status="draft") and is deleted by engine.storage.purge() once it has not changed for conversations.max_age_days (30). pin saves the whole dashboard (status saved), in the workspace you name, else the one it is already in, else "General". A chart is never pinned alone. A saved dashboard is never purged.

ws = engine.workspaces.create("Sales", user_context=me)
board = engine.dashboards.pin(draft.id, user_context=me, workspace_id=ws.id, title="Revenue")
engine.dashboards.move(board.id, other.id, user_context=me)

docs.title: Editing by hand
docs.text:
Every change a person can make is a typed edit, and no edit calls a model or takes a question or a plan:

Edit Method What it does rename rename(id, title) Renames the dashboard rename_tile rename_tile(id, tile_id, title) Renames one chart set_tile_chart set_tile_chart(id, tile_id, chart) auto, line, bar, big_number or table; a kind the last result cannot be drawn as is a ValueError naming the ones it can remove_tile remove_tile(id, tile_id) Removes a chart and its stored result arrange arrange(id, layouts) Moves or resizes charts on the 4-column grid; the others stay put set_filters set_filters(id, filters) Stores the filter definitions (their values are passed to refresh, see Filters) set_schedule set_schedule(id, every_minutes) Stores a schedule and a snapshot of your user, tenant and roles; None removes it. Below dashboards.min_refresh_minutes (15) is ScheduleTooFrequent move move(id, workspace_id) Moves it to another of your workspaces

edit(id, [RenameDashboard(...), RemoveTile(...)], user_context=me) applies a list in order and all or none: if one edit is refused, nothing is saved. A draft and a saved dashboard take the same edits. Stored chart results stay valid across a rename, a redraw, an arrange, a move and a schedule; removing a chart or changing the filters discards the results they invalidate. add_tile and replace_plan, which change what data a chart shows, are only for a conversation (add_verified_tile and add_saved_tile add a chart from a verified query or a saved answer without asking a model; the guided builder uses them) (see Building in chat and The guided builder).

Each change publishes dashboard.changed (the kinds, never the values), set_schedule also dashboard.schedule_set (it saves a role snapshot, so it is audited) and the workspace calls publish workspace.changed.

An edit, pin and delete take the dashboard's refresh lock (see Open, refresh and stored results), so a refresh that is running cannot store results after an edit has made them wrong. If the lock is held you get a ValueError (DashboardBusy) that says the dashboard is being refreshed; try again when it is done.

docs.title: Building in chat
docs.text:
In a conversation the model builds a dashboard the way a person would: one question per chart, then the dashboard_edit chat tool with an add_tile edit for each answer it wants, and further edits to the same draft.

chat = engine.conversations.start(user_context=me)
engine.conversations.ask(chat.id, "Build me a dashboard of orders by city and customers by country", user_context=me)
board = engine.dashboards.get(engine.conversations.get(chat.id, user_context=me).dashboard_id, user_context=me)
engine.conversations.tool(chat.id, "dashboard_pin", {"title": "Sales"}, user_context=me)   # only when asked
  • A draft on first use. The first dashboard_edit makes an empty draft (create_draft) in "General" or the workspace named, tied to the conversation. A conversation started with start(dashboard_id=...) edits that dashboard instead. It stays a draft until dashboard_pin (the model calls it only when the user asks) saves it whole.
  • add_tile takes a title and from_step (turn, which defaults to the turn being answered, and which of that turn's ask calls). The chart keeps the whole plan of that answer: its decomposition, the plan of every sub-query and the combine step, or the verified query that answered. The model never writes or sees a plan or SQL, and the engine reads the plan from its own stored step.
  • A chart is checked before it is saved. The plan goes through a run that executes nothing (the check open uses), as the caller. If the validator rejects it, or the caller may not read it, nothing in that dashboard_edit call is saved and the model is told why.
  • Fixing a chart. A chart that is needs_fixing is shown to the model in the open dashboard with the validator's reason. It asks the question again and calls replace_plan with the new answer: the chart keeps its id, title, chart type and place, takes the new question and plan, and its stored result is discarded. This is the only part of the dashboard that spends tokens.
  • The same edits as by hand. dashboard_edit takes every manual edit in the table above, so the model and the person change a dashboard in the same ways and with the same checks. The model sees the open dashboard (charts with their ids, questions and last status) at every step, never a row.
  • The facade. engine.dashboards.edit(id, edits, user_context=me, conversation=chat) takes the two chat-only edits when it is given a conversation of the caller's; without one they are a ValueError. The named methods take no question and no plan.

docs.title: Open, refresh and stored results
docs.text:
A chart is re-run from the plan it keeps, never by asking the question again, so refreshing costs no tokens. Each chart is one run_query(question, plan=SuppliedPlan(...), answer=False, user_context=...): the plan goes through the plan.after hooks, the validator and the generator under the caller's scope, is never cached and is never sent to the refiner, and no answer is written. A multi-query chart re-runs every stored query and its combine step; a verified chart re-runs its verified query with its stored values.

view = engine.dashboards.open(board.id, user_context=me)        # the stored results, after the access check
run = engine.dashboards.refresh(board.id, user_context=me)      # every chart, in layout order
run = engine.dashboards.refresh(board.id, tile_id="t3", user_context=me)   # one chart
Rule What it means Stored with a time The last result of each chart (its rows, at most charts.max_points, and the columns' kinds) is saved with an at time, replaced by each run and deleted with the dashboard. open serves it at once and refreshed_at is the oldest at. A run that fails (error, such as a database outage) does not replace it: the chart keeps its last good result and the refresh returns the error. Open checks access first Before any stored row is served, each stored plan is checked under the caller's current roles, and the check runs no query: a generated plan is validated and generated, a verified query is checked by the curated matcher (the caller's scope, its values, every table it reads) and by the execute.before hooks, its only hook point, leaving out the cost hook: a hook's Deny makes the chart denied, and a request for approval does not block the check, which runs nothing. Rows are served only when the check ends ok or empty, or needs_approval with nothing else wrong. A chart the caller can no longer read comes back denied (also when only one of its queries is refused, or a hook dropped one of them), one whose plan no longer validates needs_fixing, and a check that fails otherwise error, all without rows. Only charts this open checked, or refreshed itself, are served: a result another process stored meanwhile waits in due. Only what is old With refresh_due=True (the default) open then refreshes the charts older than the schedule's every_minutes (or never run), as the caller. A dashboard with no schedule has nothing due. An app that wants an instant open passes False and refreshes the ids in view.due. needs_fixing A stored plan that no longer validates (a column was dropped), or no longer parses, is not repaired by a model. The chart is needs_fixing with the validator's message and no rows, and the other charts keep working. Fixing it is a conversation turn: replace_plan. Cost guard A hook that wants a person's yes makes the chart needs_approval: it is not run, keeps its last result, and the request is in the run's approvals_needed. Pass an Approval for it to a manual refresh(approvals=[...]). open and a schedule never approve. Caps A chart stopped at a cap (stopped) ends the refresh; the rest are stopped too and keep their last result. No double runs A refresh holds the state store's lock dashboard-refresh:<id>. A second refresh on the same dashboard raises DashboardBusy; open leaves the charts due; a schedule skips it.

Each refresh publishes dashboard.refreshed (the counts per status and the ids of the filters applied; the trigger is open, manual or schedule). Each chart is a run, with its own run.started and run.finished.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
A dashboard's filters are definitions (set_filters): an id, a label, a column datasource.schema.table.column, its kind and an operator (in for the values of a dimension, between for a range of a number or a date). A viewer's values are passed to refresh:

engine.dashboards.set_filters(board.id, [DashboardFilter(id="country", label="Country", kind="text", op="in",
                                                          column="shop.main.customers.country")], user_context=me)
engine.dashboards.filter_values(board.id, "country", user_context=me)   # ["Brazil", "Canada", ...]
run = engine.dashboards.refresh(board.id, filters={"country": ["Brazil"]}, user_context=me)
Rule What it means A predicate, not text Each value becomes a typed literal in a predicate added to the stored plan before it goes to run_query, so the hooks, the validator and the generator all see it. between [a, b] is col >= a AND col <= b, except that a date-only b ends with that whole day (col >= a AND col < the next day); in is col = v1 OR col = v2 .... Nothing is added to the question or to SQL text, and the generator escapes the values like any literal. A filter only adds a condition and runs as the caller, so it never widens what the caller may read. It can still change what a chart shows: a HAVING threshold or a step after the combine sees the filtered rows and may keep different groups, a LEFT JOIN from or to the filtered table behaves as an inner join (rows with no match are dropped), and when a table is joined to itself every alias of it is filtered. Checked first Before anything runs, each value is checked against the filter's kind: a number takes numbers, a date YYYY-MM-DD or a timestamp YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM[:SS[.ffffff]] with an optional Z or +HH:MM offset (so 2024-01-31 and 2024-01-31T12:00:00Z, not 20240131), a boolean true or false, text a string; in takes 1 to 100 values, between exactly two. A wrong value, or an id the dashboard does not have, is a ValueError naming the filter, and nothing runs. Where it applies To every stored query whose plan reads the filter's table, by schema and name (on the filter's datasource). A query that does not read it, a plan table that names no schema (it might be another table of the same name), and a verified query (it has no plan) run unfiltered. TileRun.filtered is true only when every query of the chart got a filter and every active filter reached the chart, so a page can say which charts were not filtered throughout. Not stored A filtered refresh is returned (DashboardRun.filters holds the values) and not stored: the stored results, which open serves and a schedule replaces, stay the dashboard's own and unfiltered. Because it stores nothing it takes no refresh lock, so changing a filter never makes a schedule skip or raises DashboardBusy; an unfiltered refresh keeps the lock. filter_values The distinct values of an in filter's column (up to limit, in order), or [min, max] of a between one, from a plan built in code and run as the caller through run_query: the caller's scope and policies apply, a column they cannot read is a ValueError, and no model is called. Dates come back as ISO text.

docs.title: One access rule
docs.text: A datasource's stored connection sets the most anyone can see through it, and a person's roles and policies narrow that. Every way to data uses the same path and the same checks: a question, a refresh, an open and a schedule all go through run_query with the caller's UserContext (a schedule's is its owner's saved snapshot). So losing access to a table removes its rows from every dashboard at the next open, and stored results are never served before the check passes.

docs.title: Schedules
docs.text:
set_schedule(id, every_minutes) re-runs a dashboard by itself. It runs only inside a long-running process: nl2sql-api starts a runner in its lifespan that calls engine.dashboards.run_scheduled() every minute (a local app does the same, or cron runs nl2sql dashboards refresh --due). With nothing running, nothing refreshes.

  • As its owner, as saved. set_schedule saves your user, tenant and roles on the schedule. Each run resolves that snapshot against the current policies, so it can only narrow what you can read, never widen.
  • It stops, visibly. The schedule becomes stopped, with a code and message in schedule.error (shown on the dashboard that open and get return), and dashboard.schedule_stopped is published (audited) when the saved identity is older than dashboards.schedule_identity_max_age_days (30, SCHEDULE_IDENTITY_EXPIRED), a role in it is gone from the policies (SCHEDULE_ROLE_REMOVED), a chart can no longer be read by its owner (SCHEDULE_ACCESS_DENIED) or a hook denied a chart (SCHEDULE_HOOK_DENIED, with the hook's reason). Nothing retries it. Setting the schedule again saves a fresh snapshot and starts it again.
  • A failure is not a stop. A chart whose run fails (error) keeps its last good result and the schedule goes on.
  • It never approves. A chart that needs a person's yes is skipped and keeps its last result; the schedule goes on.
  • One run at a time. A dashboard another process is refreshing is skipped, so two runners (or a runner and cron) do not double up.
nl2sql dashboards refresh --dashboard sales --as analyst --user ana --tenant acme   # one dashboard, as that caller
nl2sql dashboards refresh --due                                                      # every schedule that is due

--user and --tenant act as that owner: the command is for the operator, who holds the config and the credentials. --dashboard needs --user, since a dashboard belongs to a user. --due runs each schedule as its saved owner, so it refuses --as, --user and --tenant.

docs.title: The guided builder
docs.text:
The guided builder makes a dashboard from questions a person picks, without chat. Three facade calls, each with the caller's user_context:

opts = engine.dashboards.builder_options("sales", user_context=me)     # what it offers; no model, nothing run
tiles = engine.dashboards.propose_tiles("sales", user_context=me, sources=["curated", "asked"],
                                        curated_ids=[...], metrics=[...], dimensions=[...])   # TileProposal list
board = engine.dashboards.build("sales", tiles, user_context=me, title="Sales")   # answers each ticked tile

builder_options lists the verified queries the caller's scope reaches, their saved answers, and the glossary metrics, breakdowns, periods and date columns. propose_tiles turns the chosen sources into tiles to tick, untick or reword; only the asked source uses a model (at most 3 new questions) and so needs a key. build adds each ticked tile (a verified or saved one without asking a model) and reports the questions it could not answer. Over REST these are GET /dashboard-builder/options, POST /dashboard-builder/proposals and the job POST /jobs/dashboard-build.

The web app's Build a dashboard panel (beside Generate) walks four steps: sources (curated, your saved answers, "tell us what matters"), the chips builder_options offers, a review of the proposed charts, and the build. In the review, a new question can be reworded and any chart can be set to auto, line, bar, big number or table; a curated or saved chart keeps its stored query, so its question is shown as text. If the build fails or is cancelled, Back to review keeps the ticked list. See the web app.

docs.title: The starter dashboard
docs.text:
generate makes a first dashboard from a datasource's schema, with no model and no profile run: it needs an index.

board, run = engine.dashboards.generate("sales", user_context=me)          # saved in your "General" workspace
engine.dashboards.suggest_questions("sales", user_context=me, n=5)         # the first five questions, nothing run

What it reads. Each column gets a role from the indexed snapshot alone (no query): what the schema proves (a key is an identifier, a date type a date), then name and statistics rules (money, quantity, enum, a date held as text), and a role in glossary.yaml for that column wins over both. The dashboard reads them as a measure (money, quantity, on a number column), a time (date), a dimension (enum, or a text column with 2 to charts.max_categories (20) distinct values) or an identifier, which is never charted. A rule's guess only picks a chart; it is never sent to a model. Only the tables you can read are looked at: a table your roles deny is never charted or run.

What it builds. Four templates fill typed plans in code (the questions use the columns' names, humanised):

Group Question Chart At most Key totals "How many rows are in orders?"; "What is the total revenue?" big number 4 Trends "What is the total revenue by month over the last 12 months of data?" line 2 Top N "Which 10 customers have the highest total revenue?" bar 2 Distributions "How many orders rows are there per status?" (at most 12 values) bar 2

Tables rank by row count, then by how many measures they have; measures by their non-null share; dimensions by distinct count (fewer first); ties break by name. So the same snapshot and glossary always give the same dashboard. With no measure there are only row counts and distributions. The size is max_tiles (else dashboards.max_tiles, 10).

What it keeps. Each chart is run as you, through the same path as any question (the plan.after hooks, the validator, the generator, the execute.before hooks such as the cost guard), with no model call. The ones whose first run is ok are kept; the rest are listed in run.skipped with their status and the reason, and leave no stored result. If none answered, NoTiles says why and nothing is saved. A datasource that was never indexed raises NotIndexed ("Index it first: nl2sql index --datasource sales"), and so does one you cannot reach (the same error, so it tells you nothing about it); a caller who reaches the datasource but no table gets NoTiles. If no chart is kept, a "General" workspace this call made is removed again. suggest_questions needs n of at least 1.

Where it lands. The dashboard is saved, owned by you, in workspace_id or your "General" workspace (made on first use), titled "<datasource> overview" unless you pass title. It has a between filter on the time column the trends use and an in filter on each dimension the distributions use (their values are applied by refresh). Layout follows the charts that were drawn: big numbers first, one column wide on one row; then lines (the first four wide); then bars (two wide); tables last. It is an ordinary dashboard: rename, rearrange, remove, set a schedule, refresh, all by hand, exactly as for one built in chat.

Each call publishes dashboard.generated (the counts, no titles) and the first run publishes dashboard.refreshed with the trigger generate.

docs.title: Over REST
docs.text: nl2sql-api serves each method above as a route, with the caller taken from the request: see Dashboards and workspaces API.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: dashboards: in nl2sql.yaml (max_tiles, min_refresh_minutes, schedule_identity_max_age_days) is accepted; max_tiles is read by generate and suggest_questions, min_refresh_minutes by set_schedule and schedule_identity_max_age_days by the scheduler.

docs.title: Deployment Architecture
docs.text: NL2SQL is a Python engine that you embed in a service of your choice, or run as nl2sql-api. The runtime is a single process that builds one engine from one config, nl2sql.yaml, checks it, and invokes the pipeline per request.

docs.title: Runtime process layout
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Config[nl2sql.yaml and its files] --> App[Service Process]
    App --> Engine[NL2SQL engine]
    Engine --> Registries[Registries + Stores]
    Engine --> Graph[LangGraph Pipeline]
    Graph --> Exec[Executor Services]
    Exec --> DB[(Datasource)]

docs.title: Deployment inputs
docs.text:
• The config: nl2sql.yaml and the files it includes (nl2sql init writes them). The entry point finds it through NL2SQL_CONFIG, else ./nl2sql.yaml; the CLI also takes --config. See Configuration.
  • The environment: provider keys (OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY) and any variable the config names as ${env:VAR}. The CLI, nl2sql-api and the demo load the .env next to nl2sql.yaml at startup, never overriding a variable that is already set.
  • Adapter packages installed in the runtime environment.
  • A volume for storage.path: the vector index (index/), the state store (state.db: schema snapshots, the plan cache, feedback), run traces (traces/) and result files (results/).

docs.title: Startup
docs.text: Building the engine never connects. The entry points then call engine.check(): each datasource connects or is reported as failed and left out of routing, and each agent's key is checked without a model call. A datasource with required: true that cannot connect makes check() raise EngineNotReady, and the entry point refuses to start: nl2sql-api before it accepts a request, the CLI before it runs a command, nl2sql demo before it serves the playground.

docs.title: Runtime modes
docs.text:
• Local dev: nl2sql init, local embeddings, storage.path: .nl2sql.
  • Production: a mounted config, storage.path on a persistent volume, secrets from a secret provider, required: true on the datasources the service cannot run without, an observability exporter enabled.
  • Self-hosted: the nl2sql-api image with the web app, run by Docker Compose: one service, one data volume, API keys on.
  • Hosted demo: the playground on the shipped sample databases, holding no API key of its own; each visitor brings theirs. See Hosted demo.

docs.title: Scaling and isolation
docs.text:
• Orchestration runs in-process and can scale horizontally with your service.
  • There is no process-level sandbox. The graph runs on a one-worker thread pool inside your service process, so a driver-level crash takes the process down. If you need blast-radius containment, isolate at the deployment boundary — a replica or container you are willing to lose — and let your supervisor restart it. See ../execution/isolation.md.

docs.title: Source references
docs.text:
• The engine and its lifecycle: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/public_api.py
  • Building the runtime from the config: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/runtime.py
  • The config models and load_config: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/config/

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
Self-host NL2SQL with the web app: one api service, one data volume, API keys on. The files are in deploy/compose/:

deploy/compose/
  docker-compose.yml    one service, one volume, a /ready healthcheck
  config/nl2sql.yaml    the example config: the Chinook sample, api.auth: api_keys
  README.md             the three commands
  .env.example          the provider key and NL2SQL_MODE

The image is built from the Dockerfile at the repository root: a Node stage builds the web app, and the API stage carries all five adapters, Microsoft's ODBC driver for SQL Server, the sample databases and the local embedding model. See Docker for the image on its own.

docs.title: Up
docs.text:
cd deploy/compose
cp .env.example .env          # set OPENAI_API_KEY (or the key your provider needs); .env is git-ignored
docker compose up -d --build

The service starts but is not ready until an index exists: GET /api/v1/ready answers 503, and an admin gets the reason. Nothing indexes on up.

docs.title: Index
docs.text:
docker compose run --rm api nl2sql index

Run it once, and again when the schema changes (or POST /api/v1/jobs/index as an admin). The index lives in the nl2sql-data volume.

docs.title: The first key
docs.text:
api.auth: api_keys means every request carries a key. Create the first admin key; it is printed once:

docker compose run --rm api nl2sql keys create --as admin --user admin --role admin

Open http://localhost:8000, paste the key where the app asks, and ask a question. From code, send Authorization: Bearer <key> to /api/v1.

docs.title: Connect your database
docs.text:
Edit config/nl2sql.yaml: replace the chinook datasource and the roles' allow lists, for example

datasources:
  - id: sales
    type: postgres
    connection:
      host: db.internal
      database: sales
      user: nl2sql_reader
      password: "${env:SALES_PASSWORD}"

add SALES_PASSWORD to .env, then docker compose up -d and index again. Keep api.auth: api_keys: the server refuses to listen beyond loopback with auth: none.

docs.title: Demo or your data
docs.text: mode: in nl2sql.yaml and NL2SQL_MODE in .env choose between demo and your_data; the variable wins. The example uses your_data. The public demo is a different deployment: see Hosted demo (hosted drops api_keys for anonymous sessions and refuses to start with a provider key set).

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
Put a reverse proxy in front. With Caddy:

nl2sql.example.com {
    reverse_proxy api:8000
}

docs.title: Backups and upgrades
docs.text:
Everything the service writes is in the nl2sql-data volume (index, state store, traces, results, audit log). Back it up with a throwaway container:

docker run --rm -v nl2sql_nl2sql-data:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine tar czf /backup/nl2sql-data.tgz -C /data .

To upgrade, pull the new source, docker compose up -d --build, and re-index if the release notes say the index format changed.

docs.title: Docker Deployment
docs.text:
NL2SQL can be deployed as a standalone HTTP service using the nl2sql-api package and Docker. You can also embed the core library in your own service.

For a ready-made stack (one service, one volume, API keys on), see Docker Compose.

For the playground served as a public demo of the sample databases, where each visitor brings their own API key, see Hosted demo.

docs.title: Container requirements
docs.text:
• Install nl2sql-engine and add adapters via extras (e.g. nl2sql-engine[postgres]). The repository's Dockerfile also installs nl2sql-cli, so docker compose run --rm api nl2sql index works in the image.
  • Provide the config: nl2sql.yaml and the files it includes, at the path NL2SQL_CONFIG names. The Dockerfile at the repository root sets NL2SQL_CONFIG=/etc/nl2sql/nl2sql.yaml, so mount a config folder there.
  • Provide the provider keys and any variable the config reads as ${env:VAR}, in the environment or in a .env next to nl2sql.yaml (loaded by nl2sql-api serve, the image's command, never overriding a variable already set, and never when hosted; plain uvicorn does not load it).

docs.title: Persistence mounts
docs.text:
Everything the engine writes lives under storage.path: the vector index (index/), the state store (state.db: schema snapshots, the plan cache and feedback), run traces (traces/) and result files (results/). Mount one volume and point storage.path at it, typically from the environment:

# storage.yaml
path: "${env:NL2SQL_DATA_DIR}"

docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 \
  -v "$PWD/config:/etc/nl2sql:ro" \
  -v nl2sql-data:/data -e NL2SQL_DATA_DIR=/data \
  -e OPENAI_API_KEY \
  nl2sql-api

See Storage.

docs.title: Startup
docs.text: The API builds the engine from the config and calls engine.check() before it accepts a request. A datasource with required: true that cannot connect stops the container (EngineNotReady in the log); any other one that fails is logged and left out of routing. Mark the datasources the service cannot run without required: true, so the orchestrator restarts a container that started broken.

docs.title: API roles
docs.text:
nl2sql-api identifies callers from api.auth (api_keys, proxy, static or none), and policies.admin_roles (default [admin]) says which roles may change datasources, LLMs and the index. The image binds 0.0.0.0, and serve refuses to start under the default none, so set api.auth for a container, for example api_keys:

api:
  auth: api_keys

Create keys with nl2sql keys create. See API settings, Identity and Admin routes.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Schema indexing is not automatic; you must run indexing in your operational flow: nl2sql --config /etc/nl2sql/nl2sql.yaml index against the same storage, or POST /api/v1/jobs/index (admin role).
  • Observability exporters require network access. They are observers in the config's observers section: an otel observer with its endpoint (the API image installs the otel extra; see Observers). NL2SQL_LOG_FORMAT=json gives JSON log lines. The audit observer writes under storage.path, so mount that volume to keep the audit log.

docs.title: Reference configuration
docs.text: See Configuration for the whole config and the environment variables it reads.

docs.title: Hosted demo
docs.text:
nl2sql-api serve --demo --hosted serves the web app as a public demo of the sample databases, where the server holds no API key and every visitor brings their own.

It is a third state, not a loosened local server. Locally, nl2sql demo (the launcher for nl2sql-api serve --demo) saves your key to the demo project's .env and spends it on your questions; that is right on your own machine and wrong on a shared address. Hosted mode removes the key from the server entirely instead of relaxing the gate that protects it.

local (nl2sql demo) hosted (nl2sql-api serve --demo --hosted) the API keys saved to the project's .env, used by the process one per provider, held by the browser tab, sent per request, used in memory, dropped a model per step written to the project's llm.yaml chosen in the browser tab, sent per request, saved nowhere Settings writes .env and llm.yaml writes nothing; the page keeps the keys and the choices Rebuild on for an admin refused Answer ratings on off Retrieval inspector on on, read only, at the hosted rate Pipeline page on on, read only: it names the steps and their models, never a key recording answers scripts/record_demo_answers.py (a maintainer's script) not offered a visitor with no key replay mode, if no key is configured the guided questions replay recorded runs; anything else asks for a key the sample databases read-only read-only limits none a rate limit per visitor and a cap per session 
nl2sql-api serve --demo --hosted --host 0.0.0.0 --port 7860 --questions-per-minute 6 --questions-per-session 30

There is no environment variable for it: hosted mode and its limits are flags on the command, and the container's CMD passes them.

docs.title: Recorded answers without a key
docs.text:
A visitor does not need a key to see the demo work. The guided questions are answered from recordings of real runs: every model step's actual reply to each guided question, captured once from a Claude model and shipped in the wheel at nl2sql/datasets/recordings/chinook.json (none ship until the first recording run below has been made and merged). At start-up the hosted server loads them into a replay server on loopback (the same FakeLLMServer local replay mode uses) and, for a question that carries no key:
