  • a guided question with a recording runs the whole pipeline -- retrieval, the checks, SQL generation and the query against the sample database are all real and run now -- with each model step answered from the recording. The response carries "recorded": true, and the page puts a Recorded run badge beside the question, so nobody mistakes it for a live run. It is paced by the per-minute limit but not counted against the session cap, since it spends nothing.
  • anything else never runs. It answers 200 with "replay_miss": true and the sentence "No recorded answer for this question. Add an API key to ask it live."; the page shows that with an Add a key in Settings button.

With a key, every question -- guided or not -- runs live on that key, exactly as before. /api/meta lists the questions that replay as recorded, and the page marks those chips with a dot.

The model a replayed run names is the one that recorded it. The recordings file says which provider and model answered ({"provider": "anthropic", "model": "claude-opus-5", "recordings": [...]}; a bare list, the older format, still loads and names none). The hosted server's own config falls back to an OpenAI default, so without this a keyless visitor would be told a model produced the answer that did not. Instead, a keyless replay asks the replay server for the recorded model, which echoes it, so every call in the run's usage ledger -- and the Debug pane and the trace with it -- names claude-opus-5. /api/meta and /api/pipeline report the same recorded_with, and the Pipeline page shows that model on each model step, tagged recorded, until the visitor adds a key; then it shows the models their run will use, as before. Local replay mode (nl2sql demo with no key) does the same.

Verified answers replay too. The image's demo project has the six verified queries of its curated.yaml indexed (see Curated answers), so every question first asks the curated matcher's model call, VerifiedQueryChoice. The shipped recordings hold that call for every guided question, so a guided question a verified query answers replays with the Verified badge, and the rest replay the model's none_of_these and their generated answer. If a recording ever lacks the call, the matcher falls back (model_failed) and the run goes on to the recorded generated answer.

If no recordings ship (the file is missing or covers no guided question), the keyless path still works: the chips and the question box stay open and every question answers with the key prompt. The console line at start-up says which: "N guided questions answer from recordings without a key", or "No recordings ship with this install".

docs.title: Making the recordings
docs.text:
The recordings are made with a real Claude model, which costs money, so it is a deliberate act, never part of CI. Either:

  • Locally, from the repository root:
python scripts/record_demo_answers.py

It reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment or, failing that, from the repository root's .env (read with python-dotenv, never loaded into the environment; nothing prints the key), builds a fresh demo project, and runs the recorder with that key passed explicitly, so an exported OpenAI or OpenRouter key never wins. The script writes nothing to the environment. The demo records through the recording proxy on Anthropic's own wire with the Anthropic preset's default model, and writes packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/datasets/recordings/chinook.json, stamped with the provider and the model the proxy saw requested. A question is recorded only when its run succeeded -- rows, an answer, no error. A failed run's recordings are dropped, because every model call is recorded as it passes through the proxy and a run that failed in the aggregator would otherwise still count (a real run once said "Recorded 20 of 20" with ten failed). The file is written with the runs that succeeded, and every question that was not recorded is listed with its error. It exits 0 when every guided question was recorded, 1 when some were not or when the demo stopped before recording (its indexing failed: the recorder refuses to record answers given against no index, and nothing is written), 2 with no key or without langchain-anthropic (pip install "nl2sql-engine[anthropic]"). Its output is safe to redirect to a file on Windows: it makes stdout and stderr UTF-8 before the demo prints anything. Review the diff and commit it. - In CI, Actions → Record demo answers → Run workflow (.github/workflows/record_demo.yml). It runs the same script with the repository secret ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and opens a pull request with the new recordings. It only ever runs by hand. The same workflow with record: clips re-records the playground home page's clips, which needs no key: Ask's clip is made from these recordings, so record the answers first.

The recordings ship inside the nl2sql-engine wheel, and the public Space runs released versions only, so merged recordings reach the Space with the next release (see Deployed by the release), not when their pull request merges.

tests/e2e/test_record_demo_answers_fake_llm.py runs the whole chain -- the script, the proxy on the Anthropic wire, a keyless hosted visitor replaying the result -- against a stand-in provider, so it is tested with no key and nothing spent.

docs.title: What the visitor's key does, and does not do
docs.text:
A visitor without a key is told what they can do before they ask. The Ask page opens with the pitch and, when recordings ship, the guided questions straight under it, the recorded ones marked; the key form (a provider choice, the key and Use this key, under three facts -- Stored in this browser tab only, Sent with each question in a request header, Never written to disk, logs or traces) is folded under Use your own key, and open from the start when nothing is recorded. Nothing is disabled: a question nobody recorded comes back with the way to add a key. The moment a key is saved the block clears, with no reload. The status pill in the top bar reads Hosted demo · Recorded runs (or Hosted demo · No key yet with nothing recorded), and once there is a key it names whose key answers (Hosted demo · OpenAI key in this tab), with the limits in its tooltip. None of this appears in local mode.

The visitor pastes a key on the Settings page, one per provider. From there:

  1. The browser keeps it, in that tab's sessionStorage, under that provider's own name. Closing the tab clears it. Nothing else in the page reads it.
  2. It travels as a request header of its own, X-NL2SQL-Api-Key-<provider> (X-NL2SQL-Api-Key-anthropic), on POST /api/ask (or its streamed twin, POST /api/ask/stream, which applies the same rules) and nowhere else. A header rather than the body, because a body is what request logs and validation errors quote back; one header per provider, so a key never shares a header with anything else and nothing that parses or quotes a header can expose two at once. With exactly one key the older X-NL2SQL-Api-Key is sent as well, and on its own it still means what it always did. The playground is served over plain HTTP locally and over the host's TLS when it is published, so deploy it behind HTTPS.
  3. The server uses it for that one request. It is bound to the request with nl2sql.llm.request_key and the LLM registry builds each step's client from it while the pipeline graph is constructed. The client is cached nowhere, so no later request and no other visitor can be handed it.
  4. Then it is gone. It is never written to a file, never put in an environment variable, never held in a module-level cache, and never included in a response.

A key sent without naming a provider has its provider read from its shape, by the engine's own rule: sk-ant- is Anthropic, sk-or- is OpenRouter, anything else is OpenAI. Such a key also moves the model to that provider's default when it differs from the server's configured one, since a gpt- model means nothing to Anthropic.

docs.title: A model for each step
docs.text:
Choosing a model asks the server to remember nothing, so hosted mode keeps it. Under Model for each step on the Settings page (open beside the key card on a wide window, collapsed on a narrow one), the visitor can put each of the seven model-using steps on a provider and model of their own. The choice lives in the same tab's sessionStorage and travels with each question in one more header:

X-NL2SQL-Models: {"astplanner":"anthropic:claude-opus-5"}

A compact JSON object, agent name to provider:model, and nothing else; it carries no secret, which is why it is the one header the server parses and the one thing a refusal repeats. A step with no entry runs on the configured default, so the simple path stays one key, the defaults, and a question.

The server checks every name against what the engine knows -- the pipeline's own steps, and the verified model lists in nl2sql/llm/providers.py -- before anything reaches a client. Each step is then built from the key for the provider it names: the planner can be on Claude while the answer writer stays on OpenAI, each calling its own endpoint with its own key.

A step whose chosen provider has no key is refused before the question runs, with 400 and a sentence naming both, for example "The Query planner step is set to run on Anthropic, but no Anthropic key was supplied. Add one under Settings, or put that step back on a provider you have a key for." Nothing is spent on the keys that were supplied. A step nobody chose a provider for is never refused this way: it takes the key for the provider it is configured on, or, failing that, the first key the request brought, exactly as a single key has always worked.

What it does not do:

  • It is not stored, so it cannot be reused for anyone else's question, and there is nothing to leak if the container is compromised later.
  • It does not reach a trace. Run traces are written as usual (that is what the playground's Debug drill-down reads), and the trace redactor is told about the request's key along with every other credential, so it is masked if it ever reaches a prompt or an error. The demo project's settings.yaml sets traces: { mode: always }, so every question leaves a file on the container's own disk; mode: on_failure keeps only the runs that went wrong.
  • It does not reach the log. Nothing logs the header, and errors about a key report its type, never its value.
  • It does not reach your data. The hosted demo answers only from the three sample databases shipped with the engine.

A question with no key at all is never a 401: it replays, or it is a replay miss that asks for a key (see above). A malformed key answers 400 without quoting what was sent, and no refusal ever repeats something shaped like a key, not even when one was pasted into the model header by hand.

docs.title: Serving it with nl2sql-api
docs.text:
The same demo is served by the API server, which also serves the web app:

nl2sql-api serve --demo --hosted --host 0.0.0.0 --port 7860 --questions-per-minute 6 --questions-per-session 30

--demo prepares the demo project in --dir (default nl2sql-demo) and serves it; with --hosted the project is prepared on the replay provider, and the server refuses to start while a model key is in its environment (the message names the provider, never the key) or when the visitor role (policies.default_role, else viewer) is an admin role. NL2SQL_MODE (demo, your_data or hosted) sets the mode when no flag does, and beats the mode: key of nl2sql.yaml; GET /api/v1/meta reports it.

In hosted mode every browser is an anonymous session: a random nl2sql_demo_session cookie (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax) finds it. The cookie is a secret and is never sent back: the server turns it into a one-way visitor id (visitor- and 32 hex characters of its SHA-256), and that id is the user_id of everything the visitor owns (conversations, dashboards, jobs, approvals), the key of the limits below, and what GET /meta shows as caller.user_id. The visitor holds the one visitor role and is never an admin, so the admin routes answer 403. Only a token this server signed is accepted as the cookie (64 hex characters: a random nonce and its HMAC-SHA256; nothing is stored per visitor, so no number of requests can push a visitor out). A cookie it did not sign, such as one a visitor chose or changed, gets a new session, so no one can fix the token another browser will use, and the cookie is Secure when the request came over HTTPS (directly, or as X-Forwarded-Proto). Each session may have one job (a start reserves the slot at once, so parallel starts cannot pass it) and two open streams at a time, besides the limits below; going over any of them is 429 LIMIT_REACHED with a Retry-After header. GET /api/v1/meta tells a visitor the limits and how many questions the session has asked (limits). nl2sql demo is only a launcher for nl2sql-api serve --demo and takes --dir, --host, --port and --no-browser; the public variant, with its limits, is nl2sql-api serve --demo --hosted.

nl2sql-api serve loads the .env beside the config (before it looks at the environment for a model key), except for a hosted server, which never loads one: it holds no model key, and a .env with one beside a hosted config is left alone. uvicorn nl2sql_api.main:app loads no .env at all, so export what it needs first, and it refuses to start over a config that says mode: hosted: the sessions and limits belong to nl2sql-api serve.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Both live in this one process's memory. There are no accounts, no analytics and no storage.

Limit Default Set by Keyed by Questions per minute 6 --questions-per-minute client address (a token bucket) Questions per session 30 --questions-per-session the visitor id (from the session cookie) Query timeout 300s settings.pipeline.timeout_s in the demo's settings.yaml the run Rows returned 10,000 the demo datasources' limits.row_limit, bounded by settings.results.row_limit the query

Hitting one is a 429 with a sentence, never a stack trace: the rate limit says to wait a moment, the session cap says to run the demo locally for no limit at all. The retrieval inspector spends from the same rate bucket (it costs no tokens, but it does embed text) and does not count against the session's questions.

These limits hold an honest browser to its share; they do not stop a script. The session cap counts a cookie the client keeps or drops, and the rate bucket is keyed by the first hop of X-Forwarded-For, which the client writes (the proxy appends to the right of it), so a script that sends no cookie and a made-up address is not limited by either. They never spend a model key (the server holds none), but they do not protect the shared job worker or the sample databases from one.

Builder proposals (POST /dashboard-builder/proposals) spend a question like a query, because they may ask the model; so does the start of the dashboard build job. A refused or invalid request still spends a question (the charge comes before the route runs, so a 403 or a 422 costs one). Writes that start no model work spend none and are uncapped: workspaces, conversations, knowledge choices, corrections, example proposals, a dashboard refresh and the retrieval inspector (it spends from the rate bucket only); the disk is ephemeral.

A question is charged when it arrives, before it runs, so one the visitor stops still counts toward both limits. Stopping does end the work: the page aborts its request, the server sees the connection close and cancels the run before its next step or model call (the call already in flight finishes).

The session cookie is a random token this server signed. It carries no key and names no one; it is the visitor's only credential, so it appears in no response body, stored record or log line (only the id derived from it does). A visitor who clears their cookies starts a new session; the rate limit, keyed by the address the client reports, is what holds an honest browser's pace down in the meantime.

Restarts and workers. The signing key is made once, as hosted_session.key (32 random bytes, mode 0600 where the OS supports it), in the storage directory (storage.path), beside the state store whose conversations, dashboards and approvals also survive a restart. So a restart or a redeploy on the same volume keeps every visitor's cookie, and with it their work. Jobs and the limits' counters are in memory and start again. Several workers sharing that directory share the key, so a cookie one signed is valid at all of them (the limits and job slots are still counted per worker). On a volume that is wiped, the key is made again and every visitor starts a new session. A key file that is not exactly 32 bytes stops the start with a message; delete it to make a new one. The key is never read from the environment and is not part of any response or log.

docs.title: What is off, and what is on
docs.text:
Off: Settings persistence (choosing a model is on; it is only the saving that is off), Rebuild, and answer ratings. A server-side key is refused: it is the one thing hosted mode is built to avoid, and any provider key exported into the process is cleared at start-up so nothing can fall back to it.

Rebuild being off is said on the page rather than left as a gap: the index panel reports that the index was built before the demo started and which databases it covers, and where the button would be it prints the server's own reason -- rebuilding writes to disk and the sample data never changes.

On: the guided questions without a key, from recorded runs; asking them or any other question live with a key; a key per provider and a model per step (both kept by the browser), the schema view of any of the three databases (the rail's Showing switcher), which database answered a run, the per-node Debug drill-down with its traces, and the retrieval inspector read-only.

docs.title: Read-only sample data
docs.text: The SQLite adapter opens every database file through SQLite's own URI form with mode=ro, so the demo's three databases are read-only with no setting. The driver refuses a write before any SQL is parsed, under the RBAC policy and the validator rather than instead of them. This is not specific to hosted mode: nothing in the engine writes to a demo database, so they are opened read-only everywhere.

docs.title: The container
docs.text:
deploy/huggingface/Dockerfile builds the playground as a hosted demo. It is a Space root rather than a repository build: it needs no build context, so the whole deploy is that one folder, copied to the Space's root.

It installs whatever the build arguments NL2SQL_SPEC (the command line app and, through its web extra, the web app), NL2SQL_ENGINE_SPEC and NL2SQL_API_SPEC name. On the Space that is always a released version from PyPI, nl2sql-cli[web]==X.Y.Z beside nl2sql-engine==X.Y.Z and nl2sql-api==X.Y.Z, written into the copy of the Dockerfile the release pushes. The checked-in default is a GitHub archive of the tip of main, which is only what a local docker build gets; pass --build-arg NL2SQL_SPEC="nl2sql-cli[web]==X.Y.Z" --build-arg NL2SQL_ENGINE_SPEC="nl2sql-engine==X.Y.Z" --build-arg NL2SQL_API_SPEC="nl2sql-api==X.Y.Z" to build a release locally. Then it runs nl2sql init --demo /home/demo/demo and nl2sql index at build time, with NL2SQL_CONFIG=/home/demo/demo/nl2sql.yaml set in the image so every command and the server read that config. That bakes three things into the image so the container reaches nothing but the model at run time and the first question is answered at once:

  • the three sample databases and their config,
  • their vector index, built with the local embedder,
  • the local embedding model itself, roughly 79 MB of ONNX all-MiniLM-L6-v2 that chromadb would otherwise download on the first question. The 83 MB archive it was extracted from is deleted; chroma reaches for it only when the extracted files are missing.

The container runs as uid 1000 (not root), listens on $PORT (7860 by default, which is what a Space routes to), and carries a healthcheck that polls /api/v1/health. That route reads nothing but process state and answers {"status": "ok", "version": {"engine": "X.Y.Z", "api": "X.Y.Z"}}, the installed nl2sql-engine and nl2sql-api versions, in every mode; the release pipeline polls it on the live Space to know the new version is the one being served. Its CMD runs nl2sql-api serve --demo --hosted --questions-per-minute 6 --questions-per-session 30; a public demo must never be started without --hosted.

cd deploy/huggingface
docker build -t nl2sql-demo .
docker run --rm -p 7860:7860 nl2sql-demo

docker compose up --build in the same folder does it through docker-compose.yml, which builds the same image with the same settings.

Measured on a build of this Dockerfile: 1175 MB on the container's own filesystem (docker image ls reports 1.65 GB, which includes the build attestations). Most of it is chromadb's transitive dependencies (polars, pyarrow, kubernetes, onnxruntime), which the vector store needs. Boot is about 5 seconds from docker run to the first answered request, and a guided question through a stand-in provider answered in 1.2 seconds.

docs.title: Deploying it as a Hugging Face Space
docs.text:
The Space is nadeem4nk/nl2sql-demo: public, Docker SDK, CPU basic. The full steps, and what each Space setting does, are in deploy/huggingface/README.md -- that file is also the Space's own front page, since a Docker Space reads its configuration from the front-matter of the README.md at its root.

The Space's public address is https://nl2sql.codewithnk.com, its custom domain; https://nadeem4nk-nl2sql-demo.hf.space serves the same app too. Both hosts serve every path, so deep links and API calls work on either:

curl https://nl2sql.codewithnk.com/api/health

The custom domain is set up in two places, and redoing it is the same two steps:

  1. On the Space: Settings -> Custom domain, enter nl2sql.codewithnk.com.
  2. At the DNS host for codewithnk.com: a CNAME record from nl2sql to hf.space.

Hugging Face checks the record and issues the TLS certificate itself; there is nothing to upload. Until it has, the domain fails with a certificate error and the hf.space address keeps working.

Never give the Space an API key, as a secret or otherwise. Hosted mode refuses to start when a provider key variable (OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY) is set, because a key there would be spent by every visitor.

docs.title: Deployed by the release
docs.text:
The public Space runs released versions only, and a release deploys it with nothing to do by hand. Merging the release pull request tags vX.Y.Z, and publish_pypi.yaml then runs, in order:

flowchart LR
    PY[pypi: the four packages<br/>reach PyPI] --> PS[pypi-smoke: install X.Y.Z<br/>from PyPI, boot the demo]
    PS --> SP[space: publish_space.yml<br/>pins and pushes the Space]
    SP --> SS[space-smoke: the live URL<br/>reports X.Y.Z]
  1. pypi-smoke installs nl2sql-cli[web]==X.Y.Z from PyPI into an empty virtualenv on a fresh runner, boots this same nl2sql-api serve --demo --hosted with no key, asks every recorded guided question and its scripted follow-up, and checks it serves. The Space is never built on a version that does not install from PyPI.
  2. space calls publish_space.yml with the tag. It mirrors deploy/huggingface/ onto the Space's root, pins the image to the release, pushes, and waits for the Hub to build it. Before pushing it waits until PyPI's simple index lists X.Y.Z, and the Dockerfile retries its install (10 attempts, 30 seconds apart): the index the Hub's builder sees can lag a fresh upload, which is what failed v0.2.0's first Space build.
  3. space-smoke polls https://nadeem4nk-nl2sql-demo.hf.space/api/health until it reports X.Y.Z, then checks the page and /api/meta. A Space goes on serving its previous image while the new one builds, so a build that finished is not yet proof that visitors see it. It then runs the same check against the custom domain, SPACE_CUSTOM_DOMAIN at the top of publish_pypi.yaml, which proves the DNS record and certificate still reach the release; a fork sets its own domain there, or empties it to skip the check.

The whole release flow is in Releasing.

A push to main does not deploy the Space. It used to: every merge that touched the engine, the playground or this folder rebuilt the public demo from that commit, so the demo ran code no release contained, and a broken merge reached visitors before anyone had decided to ship it. Now a merge reaches the Space with the next release. Nothing is lost by waiting: the fresh-install job on every pull request builds the wheels, installs them as a user would and boots this exact command, so a change that would break the Space fails its PR. To see a change running on a Space before it is released, deploy it to a scratch Space of your own (below), never to the public one.

What a deploy puts at the Space root. The four files of deploy/huggingface/ -- Dockerfile, README.md (the Space's configuration and front page), docker-compose.yml, and SOURCE_SHA -- with two of them rewritten:

At the Space root What the deploy writes Dockerfile its ARG NL2SQL_SPEC= line (and NL2SQL_ENGINE_SPEC, NL2SQL_API_SPEC): nl2sql-cli[web]==X.Y.Z for a release, or a GitHub archive of the commit for a tagless run by hand SOURCE_SHA the full sha of the repository commit the deploy came from -- the tagged commit, on a release

The Dockerfile rewrite is what makes the Space run the release: the same bytes a user gets from pip install, not whatever main was at build time. Because the text of the ARG line changes with every release, the Hub always has a new commit to rebuild on and the layer cache below it is busted, so the engine is genuinely reinstalled. The workflow rewrites the default rather than passing --build-arg, because a Space build takes no build arguments from us; a grep right after the rewrite fails the deploy if that line is ever renamed, instead of quietly shipping a Space that builds something else.

The one secret. A Hugging Face access token with write permission (https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens), added as the repository secret HF_TOKEN at https://github.com/nadeem4/nl2sql/settings/secrets/actions. That is the only credential the workflow uses. release_please.yml and publish_pypi.yaml hand it down with secrets: inherit, since a called workflow sees no secret it is not given. Without it -- on a fork, or before it is added -- the deploy logs a line saying so and finishes green, space-smoke is skipped, and the rest of the release is unaffected; it never fails for a missing secret.

The token is read into the job's environment and used in exactly two places: by huggingface_hub, which picks HF_TOKEN up from the environment on its own, and as the password in the git push URL. It is never echoed, never traced (no set -x), and never written to a file: the Space remote is passed to each git command rather than saved into .git/config.

What it reports. The job never calls a build that did not happen a success. If the push produced a commit, the workflow checks the Space's head is that commit, then waits for a build to actually start and finish; a Space that never starts one within five minutes fails the job rather than reporting the previous build's RUNNING. If there was nothing to push -- the same release deployed twice -- the Hub starts no build on its own, so the workflow asks it for a factory rebuild (restart_space(..., factory_reboot=True)) whenever the Space is not running, and on every run by hand unless factory_rebuild is unticked, then waits for that build the same way; the summary reads "Factory rebuild". Only a release re-run against a Space already running that deploy skips the rebuild, and its summary reads "No rebuild". The job succeeds only when the Space ends RUNNING: a redeploy of v0.2.0 once found the Space in BUILD_ERROR, pushed nothing and still went green, which is what this closes. One deploy runs at a time; a run overtaken by a newer one is cancelled.

By hand. Actions → Publish Space → Run workflow, or:

$ gh workflow run publish_space.yml -f tag=v0.2.0

Four optional inputs: tag, the release to deploy; space_id, which defaults to nadeem4nk/nl2sql-demo; token_secret, the name of the secret holding the token, which defaults to HF_TOKEN; and factory_rebuild, on by default, which rebuilds the Space from scratch when there is nothing new to push. With a tag it does exactly what a release does. With no tag it deploys the commit of the branch it was run from, installed from a GitHub archive of that commit -- which is how to try an unreleased change on a Space: point space_id at a scratch Space of your own. Do not run it tagless against the public demo; that is the "unreleased code in public" this design exists to prevent.

What the first run does. The Space does not have to exist. The workflow calls create_repo(repo_type="space", space_sdk="docker", private=False, exist_ok=True), which makes a public Docker Space on CPU basic, then pushes the folder into it. On every later run exist_ok makes that call a no-op: the Hub ignores visibility, SDK and hardware for a Space that already exists, so a hardware upgrade or a visibility change made in the Space's own settings survives a deploy.

Rolling back. Run it by hand with the earlier tag, gh workflow run publish_space.yml -f tag=v0.1.9. It checks that tag out, pins the image to that version on PyPI and rebuilds, so the engine and the playground both go back. PyPI keeps every version, so any earlier release can be redeployed this way.

The workflow adds a commit on top of whatever the Space's main already is, so the Space's history is never rewritten and never lost -- including commits made in the Hub's own web editor. If a concurrent push lands between the workflow's fetch and its push, the push is refused and the job fails; re-running it picks up the new head and reapplies the folder. Nothing in the workflow force-pushes.

docs.title: By hand, as a fallback
docs.text:
If the workflow is unavailable, the owner can do the same thing from a clone:

  1. Create the Space at https://huggingface.co/new-space under nadeem4nk, named nl2sql-demo, SDK Docker (blank), CPU basic, public.
  2. Add it as a git remote: git remote add space https://huggingface.co/spaces/nadeem4nk/nl2sql-demo (pushing needs a write token from https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens).
  3. Push the folder as the Space root: git subtree push --prefix deploy/huggingface space main.

If step 3 is refused because the Space has commits of its own, git push space $(git subtree split --prefix deploy/huggingface main):main --force replaces the Space's history with this folder's. The workflow above never needs that, which is why it exists.

docs.title: The link preview
docs.text:
Two different links go around, and each unfurls from a different place:

Pasted link The card comes from https://nl2sql.codewithnk.com or https://nadeem4nk-nl2sql-demo.hf.space the Open Graph and Twitter tags in the page the app serves https://huggingface.co/spaces/nadeem4nk/nl2sql-demo short_description and thumbnail in deploy/huggingface/README.md's front-matter

Both show the same 1200x630 card:

The app's tags are added to the built page's <head> by preview.py as each request goes out, not baked into the bundle. A crawler runs no JavaScript, so a tag React adds on mount is a tag nobody sees; and og:image and og:url have to be absolute, while the same page is the Space, a container and http://127.0.0.1:8000. So the host comes off the request: X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Host when a proxy set them (which is what the Space does), the Host header otherwise, and the URL the app itself saw if neither is a host. On the public Space, reached on either host, og:url, og:image and twitter:image all name https://nl2sql.codewithnk.com instead, so a shared link carries the short address. The card is served by the app at /social-card.png and ships in the wheel, so a pip install serves it too.

The Space's card reads thumbnail over raw GitHub rather than from the Space, so it works before the Space has built and while it is asleep.

docs.title: Regenerating the card
docs.text:
The card is rendered from scripts/social_card.html, which uses the web app's own colours and both of its typefaces. Edit that file, then:

cd nl2sql-ui && npm ci && cd ..   # the fonts the card borrows
python scripts/render_social_card.py

Headless Chrome shoots it at 1200x630 and the script writes the same bytes to both places that need them: docs/assets/social-card.png, which the Space's thumbnail reads, and packages/api/src/nl2sql_api/web/assets/social-card.png, which the app serves. A test holds the two byte-identical, so regenerating into only one of them fails rather than going out half-changed.

A card validator needs a public URL, so the check that the card really unfurls can only be run against the deployed Space, with X's card validator or https://opengraph.dev. What the tests check is everything up to that: the tags are in the served HTML, their URLs are absolute, and the image is served as image/png.

docs.title: The mark
docs.text: The wordmark's icon on the card is the playground's favicon, the plan spine: a root bar and stem with two indented steps, the typed plan the model writes, in outline. Its one copy is docs/assets/favicon.svg; the playground inlines it, this site uses it as its favicon, and the card redraws it in the light colours. See the playground README for where each copy lives.

docs.title: Running it locally instead
docs.text:
Hosted mode exists to show the engine on our sample data. To ask questions of your own data, with no limits and a key that never leaves your machine:

pip install "nl2sql-cli[web]"
nl2sql demo

See Demo.

The hosted server always answers on the replay provider, whatever its project file names: nl2sql-api serve --demo --hosted replaces the llm section at start, and the Space image is built with nl2sql init --demo --provider replay. A keyed provider with no key ends a turn with a MISSING_LLM error, never a 500.

docs.title: Kubernetes Deployment
docs.text: Kubernetes deployment depends on the service you build around the engine, or on nl2sql-api. The engine expects one config, nl2sql.yaml, and the variables it names to be available to the runtime container.

docs.title: Configuration and secrets
docs.text:
Mount the config folder (a ConfigMap of nl2sql.yaml and the files it includes) and inject secrets so that:

  • NL2SQL_CONFIG names the mounted nl2sql.yaml (the API image defaults to /etc/nl2sql/nl2sql.yaml);
  • provider keys (e.g., OPENAI_API_KEY) and every variable the config reads as ${env:VAR} (database passwords, NL2SQL_DATA_DIR) are injected into env, or a secret provider in the secrets section reaches them.

Keys never go in the ConfigMap: the config holds references (password: "${env:SALES_DB_PASSWORD}"), not values.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text: Everything the engine writes lives under storage.path: the vector index (index/), the state store (state.db), run traces (traces/) and result files (results/). Mount one persistent volume and point storage.path at it (path: "${env:NL2SQL_DATA_DIR}"). See Storage.

docs.title: Operational considerations
docs.text:
• Run schema indexing as a separate job or init container: nl2sql --config /etc/nl2sql/nl2sql.yaml index, on the same volume.
  • The API calls engine.check() before it serves. A datasource with required: true that cannot connect stops the pod, so a readiness gate on the process is enough; any other datasource that fails is logged and left out.
  • If you run nl2sql-api, set api.auth (proxy behind an authenticating ingress with api.proxy.trusted_from the ingress's CIDR, or api_keys) and the admin roles (policies.admin_roles, default [admin]): pod traffic is not the local operator, so under the default none every route answers HTTP 403. See Admin routes.
  • Configure observability exporters as observers in the observers section (an otel observer with its endpoint, with nl2sql-engine[otel] installed; see Observers), and set NL2SQL_LOG_FORMAT=json for JSON log lines. The audit log is under storage.path/audit/, on the same volume as the engine's other data.

docs.title: Reference configuration
docs.text: See Configuration for the whole config and the environment variables it reads.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
• engine.evals: suites of cases in evals.yaml, scored by registered scorers (result_match, outcome, retrieval_recall, faithfulness, routing), in three modes.
  • The Chinook suite: 47 cases (43 answerable, 4 deliberately not) with expected results per role, including refusals. A case may carry reviewed alt_sql alternatives, so a second correct way to answer it scores as correct; gold data is never edited to make a run pass.
  • Mode plans (no key, runs in CI): the hand-written plans through the validator, generator and executor with a fake LLM, so a failure is a bug in code, not the model.
  • Mode full (real model, costs money): end to end per config, with accuracy, answerability precision and recall, cost, latency, determinism and answer faithfulness (a deterministic check, no second model, that every number and name in the written answer comes from the rows). Accuracy is scored twice: strict, where the rows must match the gold answer exactly, and lenient, which allows extra and reordered columns and date labels. Each is published with a 95% Wilson interval, because 47 questions cannot separate small differences. Stops before spend could pass max_cost_usd. With curated answers on, a case a verified query answered also runs on the generated path, so accuracy_generated measures the model alone.
  • Mode retrieval (no key): the share of each case's needed tables and columns that schema retrieval sends the planner, and where routing sends it.
  • Feedback: playground ratings and guardrail rates via nl2sql feedback stats; feedback export --good drafts new eval cases for review.

Recorded runs are published with nl2sql eval publish to the README and Benchmarks. Details: the Chinook suite, Feedback and Signals.

engine.evals measures how well the engine answers your questions. You write cases (a question, what each role should get, and the SQL a person reviewed) in suite files. A run asks every case once per role and scores it with registered scorers, and the result is an EvalReport.

The package ships one answer suite for the demo, Chinook's 47 gold cases, and nl2sql init --demo copies it next to the demo's nl2sql.yaml. (It also ships routing and clarify suites, and a Pagila suite for table recall on the test bed: Cases and suites.) The format is in Cases and suites, and what makes a case pass is in Scorers. To build a suite for your own database, seed draft cases from its schema and review them (Benchmark your own database).

docs.title: Configuring it
docs.text:
evals.yaml is a config section, like curated.yaml. Its keys are strict and it is loaded with the config:

# nl2sql.yaml
evals: { file: evals.yaml }

# evals.yaml
suites: [evals/chinook.yaml]       # relative to nl2sql.yaml
scorers: [result_match, outcome, faithfulness, retrieval_recall, routing]   # the default: all five
curated: true                      # mode full: curated answers on (the default)
max_cost_usd: 5.00                 # mode full's dollar cap over a whole run; it needs one
gate: { max_regressions: 2, alpha: 0.05, max_cost_increase: 0.20 }

A suite file is data. It is read when a run asks for it, never when the engine starts, so a large suite does not slow down engine start. gate configures the regression gate, which compares a run with a baseline.

docs.title: The facade
docs.text:
from nl2sql import NL2SQL, load_config

engine = NL2SQL(load_config("nl2sql.yaml"))
report = engine.evals.run(mode="plans")          # no key, no cost
print(report.accuracy, report.accuracy_generated)
Method What it does engine.evals.load(path=None) The suites evals.yaml names, or the one file at path, as EvalSuites engine.evals.run(suites=None, *, mode="full", llm=None, cases=None, roles=None, scorers=None, curated=None, passes=1, max_cost_usd=None, on_case=None, clarify=False, cancellation_token=None) Runs every approved case once per role in its outcome map, passes times, and returns an EvalReport. Cancelling cancellation_token stops before the next case and the report says stopped: "cancelled" engine.evals.gate(report, baseline) The regression gate: report against a baseline report, record or benchmarks/ folder, with evals.yaml's gate settings. Returns a GateResult (The gate) engine.evals.regenerate(path, *, allow_packaged=False) Runs each approved case's sql and alt_sql through its datasource's adapter and writes rows and alt_rows (Regenerating rows). A suite the package ships is refused unless allow_packaged engine.evals.seed(datasource_id, *, count=20, out, user_context, max_cost_usd=None) Drafts up to count cases from the datasource's schema, as user_context sees it, and appends them to out as status: draft. Returns a SeedReport (Benchmark your own database) engine.evals.scorers() The registered scorer names: the five built-ins and any plugin's

The run arguments:

  • cases narrows the run by case id or tag. A selector that matches nothing is an error.
  • roles narrows it by role.
  • An argument left as None takes its value from evals.yaml.

on_case(config, record, spent) is called after each case. It gets the config's name, the case's record and the dollars spent so far.

docs.title: The modes
docs.text:
Mode What runs Model calls Curated answers Plan cache full The whole pipeline, on the configured LLM or on each named config yes; needs max_cost_usd as curated says (on by default) off plans Each case's hand-written plan through the validator, generator and executor, on the gold-plan fake LLM none off as configured retrieval Datasource routing and schema retrieval only none (the configured embedder) off not used

Every mode runs on a runtime derived from the engine's (ctx.derive), so the engine serving traffic never changes. In each mode:

  • Refusals are generic. A refusal message never names a table (policies.refusal_names_tables is off for the run). The outcome scorer checks for the generic message.
  • Mode full turns the plan cache off. A second pass asks the planner again instead of replaying the first pass's plans.
  • Modes plans and retrieval turn curated answers off. The curated matcher makes a model call the gold-plan fake cannot answer, and a verified hit would skip the plan or the retrieval being measured.
  • Mode retrieval always runs the vector search, and never a model. Its runtime sets settings.retrieval.full_snapshot_max_tables to 0, because Chinook's 11 tables are under the limit that would otherwise skip the search, and settings.retrieval.table_selector to false, because the table selector is a model call. The run covers the vector search, the glossary's tables and the join-path fill, and so records the floor without the model; the report's settings.retrieval says so. Mode full runs the selector.

docs.title: Mode full: the configured model, priced and capped
docs.text:
llm takes one of three values:

  • None: the engine's own llm section, reported as default.
  • One LLM.
  • A mapping of names to LLM sections. Each one runs on its own derived runtime over the same cases, and the report compares them.

The named configs in nl2sql/evaluation/presets/ are llm sections too: load_llm_file(path) and model_config("gpt-5.4") in nl2sql.evaluation.presets build one.

Every call costs money, so mode full checks prices before it starts and checks the cap before every case:

  • Every model must have a price. Before any call, every model that any node of any config would use must have a price, in llm.prices or the engine's dated table (Prices). A missing price is an UnknownPriceError naming the config, the node and the model.
  • The run stops before it could pass the cap. Before each case, the run adds the most expensive case so far to its running total. If that could pass max_cost_usd, the run stops and the report says stopped: "max_cost".
  • The first case always runs. So a run can pass the cap by at most one case's cost.
  • An unknown cost is not counted as zero. A call that reported no token counts (a failed call) cannot be priced. The run goes on, leaves it out of spent (so spent is a lower bound), counts it in the report's unknown_cost_calls, and logs one warning.

Each call is priced by the model its node is configured with, and the dollars are in report.spent and each record's cost.

docs.title: Curated answers in mode full
docs.text:
curated: true is the default. Each case record says where its answer came from in source (verified or generated).

A case that a verified query answered is run a second time with curated answers off, and that second run is scored as the case's generated answer (in the record's generated). Only the cases a verified query answered pay for the second run.

The report gives two accuracies:

Accuracy What it measures accuracy What users see accuracy_generated Every case on the generated path: the model's own skill, comparable across configs

Both are also split by source.

docs.title: Clarification
docs.text: A case may expect the engine to ask the caller to narrow the question (outcome clarify). Evals run with clarify=False, the default, so every other case measures the most likely reading: the clarify role runs are left out and counted in report.skipped. With clarify=True they run, and the outcome scorer passes them when the run's status is needs_clarification. The clarify suite holds such cases.

docs.title: The report
docs.text:
EvalReport has:

  • mode and suites (each suite's name, path and SHA-256 digest).
  • roles, passes, curated, clarify, max_cost_usd, spent, stopped, skipped and settings (mode retrieval's retrieval settings).
  • database: the datasource, engine and schema fingerprint of the datasources the suites name.
  • configs: one board per LLM config. Mode plans reports one board named plans, and mode retrieval one named retrieval.
  • comparison, when there are several configs.

report.accuracy and report.accuracy_generated read the first config's board.

Two accuracies, on purpose. accuracy.overall counts a case as passed only when every scorer that applies passes. In mode full with the default scorers, that includes faithfulness, retrieval_recall at 1.0 and routing. So it is stricter than the accuracy 0.6's tier 2 published. accuracy.execution is that older measure alone: result_match and outcome passed, no other scorer counted. Compare it, not overall, with the runs published before 0.7 (docs/benchmarks.md).

A board holds:

Field What it is accuracy overall (what users see), lenient, generated and execution, each with a 95% Wilson interval; pass_k over several passes; and the rates by_tag, by_difficulty, by_source and generated_by_source summary pass, fail, error and skip counts per role and in total scores Per scorer: how many cases it applied to, passed, failed and errored on, and its mean value retrieval The mean table and column recall over the cases retrieval_recall scored, how many were perfect, and how much was sent answerability, faithfulness, tokens_by_node, cost, latency, retries, errors_by_code, determinism As for a single run, summed or averaged over the cases models, planned_cases, completed_cases The config's model per node, and the cases the run would make and made results One record per case run: its status and reason, every scorer's score, the SQL (sql is the first sub-query's; for a split question that is one scan, not the combined result, and sql_by_sub_query has every sub-query's), the answer, the plans, source and generated

Accuracy over 47 cases has an interval about 14 points wide, so two runs are compared case by case, not headline to headline. The statistics are in the Chinook suite.

docs.title: Events
docs.text: Each case runs under its own run scope (QueryAPI.open_scope and close_scope), so it publishes run.started and run.finished like any question. This includes mode retrieval, where no graph runs: its scope closes with an empty result. Every finished case also publishes eval.case on the engine's bus, with the suite, case, role, whether it passed, the answer's source, each scorer's verdict and its cost. The end of the run publishes eval.finished, with the suites, the number of cases, both accuracies and the dollars spent.

docs.title: The regression gate
docs.text:
engine.evals.gate(report, baseline) compares a run with a baseline and returns a GateResult:

Field What it is ok True only when the runs were compared and nothing regressed regressions One line per problem: too many cases flipped to fail, a significant drop, or a cost rise series_break Why nothing was compared: another suite digest, another mode, or no config in common compared Per config and measure: the cases that flipped each way, McNemar's p-value, both accuracies and both costs per case

The baseline is an EvalReport (or the JSON nl2sql eval run writes), a record from benchmarks/, or a path to either. A path to a benchmarks/ folder means its newest record of the run's mode, database and config.

Only the same suite and mode compare. Two runs are compared only when the suites' digests match and the mode is the same. Anything else is a series break: ok is false and nothing is compared.

The gate reads execution accuracy. A case passes when result_match and outcome pass; no other scorer counts. That is accuracy.execution, the measure 0.6's tier 2 published, so a run compares with the history published before 0.7 and a faithfulness verdict alone is never a regression. A kind: routing case has no rows to check and is left out of it. With curated answers on, it is checked twice: as users see it, and on the generated path. Mode retrieval has no execution, so its cases are read by their status.

For each config both runs have, the gate fails when:

  • more cases passed in the baseline and fail now than are allowed. Mode full allows max_regressions (2 by default), because the model is noisy. Modes plans and retrieval run no model, so they allow none: any flip is a real break;
  • in mode full, more cases were lost than gained and McNemar's exact two-sided p-value on the flips is under alpha; or
  • cost per case rose by more than max_cost_increase.

Comparable means what the history page means by it (records.series_key): the same mode, suite digest and schema fingerprint and, in mode full, the same roles and curated answers. Both runs must also have run the same roles, so a role left out cannot quietly shrink the comparison.

The statistics are in the Chinook suite.

docs.title: The CLI
docs.text:
Command What it does nl2sql eval run [--suite PATH ...] [--mode full\|plans\|retrieval] [--llm SPEC ...] [--cases ID/TAG ...] [--passes N] [--max-cost USD] [--baseline PATH] [--out FILE] engine.evals.run, then engine.evals.gate with --baseline nl2sql eval regenerate PATH engine.evals.regenerate; exits 1 when a case's SQL failed nl2sql eval seed --datasource ID --out PATH [--count N] [--role R] [--max-cost USD] engine.evals.seed, as --role (else policies.default_role); exits 2 on a refusal, 3 at the cost cap or the call limit, and refuses to run when CI is set (Benchmark your own database) nl2sql eval publish [REPORT ...] [--note TEXT] [--from DIR ...] Records each report under benchmarks/, then rebuilds the results page and the README block. Run from the repo root

--llm names an LLM config to compare in mode full, and repeats:

  • gpt-5.4, mini-helpers or claude-planner: a preset from nl2sql/evaluation/presets/, named by itself;
  • mine.yaml: a file holding an llm section, named by its stem;
  • NAME=PRESET or NAME=FILE: either, under a name you choose.

Without it, the config's own llm section runs as default.

nl2sql eval run writes the report to --out, by default eval_<mode>.json next to nl2sql.yaml, with a run stamp: when it ran, and the engine version and commit. nl2sql eval publish records that stamp, not the time it publishes.

Exit code When 0 The run finished, and nothing regressed against --baseline 1 A regression against --baseline 2 A usage error: a bad --llm, a run the engine refuses (no cost cap, an unpriced model), mode full with CI set (whatever its value, CI=false included), a missing or unreadable baseline, or one that cannot be compared 3 The cost cap stopped mode full early: the report is partial 
# From a demo folder: the key-free gate CI runs, against the repo's records
nl2sql eval run --mode plans --baseline ../benchmarks
# A paid run comparing two configs, under a $10 cap
nl2sql eval run --mode full --llm gpt-5.4 --llm mini=mini-helpers --max-cost 10
# From the repo root: record it and rebuild the results page
nl2sql eval publish demo/eval_full.json --note "slim prompts"

docs.title: In CI
docs.text:
The key-free eval-gates job (parallel to the integration tests) runs the eval gate on the demo's Chinook suite and on the routing suite, after indexing them:

nl2sql --config demo-ci/nl2sql.yaml eval run --mode plans --baseline benchmarks
nl2sql --config demo-ci/nl2sql.yaml eval run --mode retrieval --baseline benchmarks
nl2sql --config demo-ci/nl2sql.yaml eval run --mode retrieval --suite evals/routing.yaml \
  --baseline benchmarks --out demo-ci/eval_routing.json

Each run is gated against the newest record of its mode and database in benchmarks/ (plans/chinook/, retrieval/chinook/ and retrieval/chinook-support-webanalytics/). The three reports are uploaded as the eval-reports artifact whether the gate passed or not. On the routing suite, a case that loses its routing top-1 or a shortlisted datasource is a flip, and mode retrieval allows none. A changed suite or schema starts a new series, so the gate exits 2 until the baselines are recorded again. The integration job also runs tests/e2e/test_evals_plans.py, where every case must pass for every role.

docs.title: Re-recording CI's baselines
docs.text:
CI's plans and retrieval baselines are recorded on CI's own runner (ubuntu-latest, Python 3.12), never on a laptop: retrieval recall passes a case only at 100% column recall, which near-tie rankings of the local ONNX embedder can move between platforms.

  1. Push the change. The eval-gates job's "Eval gate" steps run the three gates and upload eval_plans.json, eval_retrieval.json and eval_routing.json as the eval-reports artifact, pass or fail.
  2. Download them: gh run download <run id> -n eval-reports -D eval-reports.
  3. From the repo root, record the ones the change moved, naming where they came from: nl2sql eval publish eval-reports/eval_retrieval.json eval-reports/eval_routing.json --note "CI baseline: ubuntu-latest, Python 3.12, https://github.com/nadeem4/nl2sql/actions/runs/<run id>".
  4. Commit the records and the regenerated pages in the same PR, and push. The next run gates against them.

Never edit a record by hand, engine_version included. A change that moves the gate on purpose (a suite change, routing or retrieval work) re-records the baselines it moves this way, in the PR that makes the change.

Mode full spends a key: nl2sql eval run --mode full refuses to start when CI is set. The owner runs it before a release (Releasing).

docs.title: Cases and suites
docs.text:
A suite is a YAML file of cases. Each case is a question and what each role should get. An answerable case also has the SQL a person reviewed and the rows that SQL returns. nl2sql.evaluation.suite holds the model (EvalCase, EvalSuite), the loader and the writer.

version: 1
cases:

- id: chinook_001
  question: How many customers do we have, by country?
  datasources: [chinook]
  status: approved                  # draft | approved | retired; only approved cases run
  origin: hand                      # hand | seeded | feedback
  difficulty: easy
  tags: [aggregation, rbac-denial]
  outcome: {admin: allowed, analyst: allowed, viewer: refused}
  tables: [Customer]
  columns: [Customer.Country, Customer.CustomerId]
  order_matters: false
  sql: |
    SELECT Country, COUNT(CustomerId) AS customer_count
    FROM Customer
    GROUP BY Country
    ORDER BY customer_count DESC, Country
  rows:                             # written by regenerate, never by hand
  - {Country: USA, customer_count: 13}
  - ...
  plan: {...}                       # optional: the hand-written plan, for mode plans
Field Meaning id Unique in the suite question The natural-language question datasources The datasources the question is about. The routing scorer checks a run used exactly these. A case with sql names one status draft, approved or retired. Only approved cases run kind answer (the default, left out of the file) or routing: a case that says only where a question goes. A routing case has no sql, gets no result_match verdict and is left out of execution accuracy in every mode. An approved answer case that a role may answer must have sql; the loader rejects it otherwise origin hand (written by a person), seeded (drafted from a datasource's schema) or feedback (exported from a thumbs-up run) difficulty Optional: easy, medium or hard tags Free categories. A run can be narrowed to them, and the report gives accuracy per tag paraphrase_group Optional. Cases with the same intent share it and the same rows outcome Per role: allowed, refused, unanswerable or clarify. The case runs once per role named here tables, columns The tables the SQL reads, and the Table.Column names the answer needs. retrieval_recall scores against them order_matters Whether row order counts when rows are compared sql The reviewed SQL, in the datasource's dialect; null for an unanswerable case and for a kind: routing case rows The rows sql returns, as {column: value} maps. Written by regenerate, never typed by hand alt_sql, alt_rows Reviewed alternative answers and their rows plan Optional. A PlanModel written as data, which mode plans serves through its fake LLM. Mode plans needs one for every answerable case

The outcomes:

Outcome What the role should get allowed An answer. result_match then checks its rows refused The validator's refusal, with the generic message and no rows unanswerable The resolver's QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE clarify A request to narrow the question (status needs_clarification). This runs only with engine.evals.run(clarify=True); the outcome scorer passes it when the run asks and returns no rows

An approved case must have one alt_rows entry per alt_sql. An unanswerable case cannot have an alternative.

docs.title: Where suites live
docs.text:
evals.yaml names suites by path, relative to nl2sql.yaml. The suites the package ships are in nl2sql/evaluation/suites/, and nl2sql init --demo copies them into the demo's evals/ folder. engine.evals.load(path) and engine.evals.run([path]) also take a suite file directly.

The Chinook suite (suites/chinook.yaml) is 0.6's gold set (chinook_gold.yaml and chinook_gold_plans.yaml) with its keys renamed and nothing else changed:

Was Now datasource datasources expected outcome needed_tables, needed_columns tables, columns gold_sql, gold_result, alt_gold_sql, alt_gold_result sql, rows, alt_sql, alt_rows plans in chinook_gold_plans.yaml plan on each case

test_chinook_suite_holds_the_gold_data_unchanged pins a SHA-256 of every case's question, SQL, rows, alternatives, outcomes, tables, columns and plan, taken from the old files with the old loader. The Chinook suite describes it.

docs.title: The routing suite
docs.text:
suites/routing.yaml asks which of the demo's three databases (chinook, support, webanalytics) a question belongs to. Every case is approved, origin: hand, asked as admin, and names the datasources a right answer needs. None names tables, so in mode retrieval the routing scorer alone decides it. Its tags say where each case came from:

Tag Cases gold The Chinook suite's 43 answerable questions. Their answers are checked in chinook.yaml; here a recall miss cannot hide a routing one sample Each demo datasource's sample questions, as nl2sql init --demo writes them paraphrase, hand Questions written for routing and read against each datasource's schema, most about support and webanalytics. Ten carry reviewed SQL, with rows written by regenerate, so mode full checks those answers too

Every case without SQL is kind: routing, so mode full's execution accuracy is over the ten answered cases only. The suite's header names the cases with two defensible answers (support holds the same customers as Chinook), which a routing change may flip on purpose. | cross-database | Three questions that need two databases |

Every case also carries the names of the datasources it needs as tags, so --cases support runs every case about support, cross-database ones included. Mode plans cannot run the suite, since its cases have no plans. So the demo's evals.yaml names only chinook.yaml, and the routing suite is run by name:

nl2sql eval run --mode retrieval --suite evals/routing.yaml --out eval_routing.json   # no key: CI's gate
nl2sql eval run --mode full --suite evals/routing.yaml --max-cost 5                   # the release check

In mode retrieval a case passes when routing ranks one of its datasources first and shortlists all of them (settings.routing.candidates, cut at max_datasources). A few cases fail today; the baseline records where routing misses, and the gate allows no other case to start failing. The test bed's 1,200-table wide schema has routing cases of its own in the realdb job (tests/realdb/test_routing_wide.py), since they need the test bed's databases.

docs.title: The clarify suite
docs.text:
suites/clarify.yaml holds five approved cases about "sales", which the demo glossary leaves open: two terms list it as a synonym, revenue and invoiced total, so a planner that sees both names the phrase and the run ends needs_clarification. Each case expects clarify from admin and has no SQL: what the asker picks next is a person's choice, not a gold answer. The suite is copied by nl2sql init --demo but not named in evals.yaml, since its cases run only with clarification on:

engine.evals.run(suites=["evals/clarify.yaml"], clarify=True)

docs.title: The Pagila suite
docs.text:
suites/pagila.yaml holds 11 approved cases over the test bed's Pagila database (a datasource named pagila), which is past settings.retrieval.full_snapshot_max_tables, so the retriever has to choose tables. Each case is chosen so a table it needs is more than one join from the others, or the question's words are not near the table's name ("revenue" is not near payment): the smoke question "top 5 films by revenue in the top category" needs film, film_category, category, inventory, rental and payment. tables and columns are what the gold SQL reads, and test_pagila_suite_reads_the_tables_it_names keeps the two equal.

nl2sql init --demo does not copy it into the demo, which has no Pagila. The cases carry the rows that engine.evals.regenerate wrote from the gold SQL on the test bed's Pagila. After you edit a case, point a suite file at the test bed and run regenerate again, then review the rows, before a full run. Mode retrieval needs no rows.

CI runs the model-free floor on every pull request that touches the retriever (the realdb workflow, tests/realdb/test_pagila_retrieval.py) and gates it against the recorded baseline in benchmarks/retrieval/pagila/. The floor has no target; it only must not regress.

nl2sql eval run --mode retrieval --suite pagila.yaml --out eval_pagila.json   # no key: the floor, without the table selector
nl2sql eval run --mode full --suite pagila.yaml --max-cost 5                  # with the selector: every gold table should be sent

docs.title: Regenerating rows
docs.text:
rows and alt_rows are never typed by hand. After you add or edit a case, an alternative or any SQL, run:

engine.evals.regenerate("evals/mine.yaml")

For each approved case with SQL, regenerate asks the case's datasource adapter to run sql and every alt_sql. It goes through the engine's DatasourceRegistry, read-only and within the datasource's limits: the expected rows come from the same adapter questions run on. The rows are written back in the order the SQL returns them.

The returned RegenerateReport counts the result sets written, and lists in failed each case left unchanged and why:

  • the SQL failed;
  • the result was cut at the datasource's row limit;
  • a case with SQL names more than one datasource.

A suite the package ships (nl2sql/evaluation/suites/) is refused unless you pass allow_packaged=True. In an installed package it is not yours to rewrite: copy it into your project, as nl2sql init --demo does. The repo's own workflow passes the flag, from a checkout, after a reviewed alt_sql is added to suites/chinook.yaml.

The other cases are still written. The file keeps its leading comment lines and its layout, and the committed Chinook suite is byte for byte what regenerate writes.

docs.title: Drafts
docs.text:
A case that a machine wrote starts as a draft, and a draft never runs. nl2sql eval seed (engine.evals.seed) drafts cases from a datasource's schema, with origin: seeded (Benchmark your own database). nl2sql feedback export --good (engine.feedback.export(path)) writes each thumbs-up run as a draft case to a suite file of its own, with origin: feedback, the run's SQL, the datasources it read, and the rating role allowed.

To promote a draft:

  1. Check that the SQL answers the question.
  2. Fill in difficulty, tags, tables, columns and the outcome for each role.
  3. Set status: approved.
  4. Run regenerate to write its rows.

Drafts never replace reviewed cases. Seeding and export refuse these paths:

  • a suite the package ships;
  • a suite evals.yaml names;
  • any existing file that holds an approved case.

A file of drafts may be written again.

docs.title: The Chinook Suite
docs.text:
The Chinook suite holds 47 cases about the vendored Chinook database (nl2sql/datasets/chinook.sqlite). Each case has hand-written SQL, the rows that SQL returns, and a hand-written plan. Evaluations compare the engine's answers against it. It is a suite in the eval case format and runs through engine.evals.

File What it holds packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/suites/chinook.yaml The suite: the cases, their rows and their plans packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/suite.py EvalCase, EvalSuite, the loader and the writer packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/regenerate.py regenerate: the rows, through the datasource's adapter packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/run.py The three modes, prices and the cost cap packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/gold_llm.py The gold-plan fake LLM that mode plans runs on packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/scorers/ The scorer interface and the five built-ins packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/evaluator.py Row comparison (compare_results, column_picks, compare_results_lenient), which result_match reads on the run's terminal result (the combined result of a split question, not a sub-query's scan) packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/faithfulness.py Answer faithfulness: the written answer's numbers and names against the rows packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/report.py The report's boards: accuracy, intervals, pass^k, cost, latency packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/gate.py The regression gate's statistics: flips, McNemar's test, the checks packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/llm/prices.py The dated price table every call, mode full's included, is billed from packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/records.py Result records, comparable runs and the published pages packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/presets/ Named LLM configs to compare (*.yaml, shipped in the wheel) benchmarks/<kind>/<database>/ Committed result records (layout) packages/nl2sql/tests/unit/test_chinook_suite.py Key-free checks, part of the normal unit suite

docs.title: The cases
docs.text:
The fields are described in Cases and suites. For this suite:

  • The tags. tags come from a fixed list: single-table, filter, join, multi-join, aggregation, having, order-limit, offset, ties, date, paraphrase, keyword-in-question, keyword-in-value, data-range and value-matching. data-range marks a case that needs to know where the data ends ("the most recent month in the data"), and value-matching one that names a stored value in other words ("heavy metal" for 'Heavy Metal').
  • rbac-denial and unanswerable. rbac-denial marks exactly the cases some role is refused, and unanswerable the four the database cannot answer.
  • Every case is approved and hand written, about chinook. So the run is scored, and identified, by Chinook, whatever else the demo registers.
  • The outcomes follow the demo policy. outcome follows CHINOOK_POLICIES in nl2sql/datasets/chinook.py: a role gets refused when its scope does not allow one of tables, and allowed otherwise. An unanswerable case is unanswerable for every role.
  • Ties are broken on a key. Where ORDER BY has ties, sql breaks them on a key (CustomerId, Country and so on) so the result is deterministic, and the case carries the ties tag. When the tie is only about order, order_matters is false.

The data never changes. The suite was moved from 0.6's chinook_gold.yaml and chinook_gold_plans.yaml with only its keys renamed. test_chinook_suite_holds_the_gold_data_unchanged pins a SHA-256 of every case's question, SQL, rows, alternatives, outcomes, tables, columns and plan. A new accepted answer is a reviewed alternative, followed by regenerate; never an edit to the gold data.

docs.title: What the tests check
docs.text:
pytest packages/nl2sql/tests/unit/test_chinook_suite.py runs without an API key and checks that:

  • the data hashes to the pinned digest;
  • every case is approved and hand, on chinook;
  • ids are unique, and paraphrase groups share one result;
  • every table and column exists, and tables equals the tables in sql;
  • every role in outcome exists in the demo policy, and each outcome follows from it;
  • every answerable case has a plan, and no other case does. Each plan is a PlanModel that reads exactly tables and selects as many columns as rows has;
  • every alt_sql reads no table outside tables, returns between one and twenty-five rows, and is not the gold answer written again;
  • Chinook's twelve guided questions (CHINOOK_QUESTIONS) are included verbatim. The demo offers twenty in all; the other eight ask about support and webanalytics, which this suite does not cover.

tests/unit/test_eval_regenerate.py runs regenerate through the sqlite adapter and checks that the committed file is byte for byte what it writes.

docs.title: How a run is scored
docs.text:
Each case runs once per role in its outcome map, and each run is scored by the scorers. For result_match and outcome:

Outcome Passes when allowed Status success, one result set, and its rows equal rows or any alternative refused Status error, a SECURITY_VIOLATION whose message is the generic refusal (it names no table), and no rows unanswerable Status error, a QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE from the datasource resolver's answerability check, and no rows

Rows are compared by value, in selected column order:

  • Names and column order don't count. Column names and aliases are ignored, so SELECT Country AS c matches a gold Country column, and a result whose columns come in another order matches too: each gold column is answered by a distinct result column holding the same values. A mislabelled column fails, because its values differ, unless they equal another gold column's row for row (goals for and against, say): an accepted, rare limit. Rows must still line up across the matched columns.
  • Numbers match within 0.005, because gold values are rounded to two decimals.
  • A number matches a string that spells it, within the same tolerance, so '2009' is 2009: databases differ in which of the two they return for the same value.
  • A database decimal matches the number or string it spells, so a Decimal of 3094.78 is "3094.78": gold rows are stored as JSON.
  • Dates match their ISO strings. A date or datetime equals "2022-01-01T00:00:00Z", and a date-only label ("2022-01-01") equals that day's midnight in that datetime's own offset (2021-12-31T19:00-05:00 is not 2022-01-01), either way round. Two full datetimes are compared as instants, and a value with no timezone is read as UTC.
  • Other strings must be equal. Two strings compare as strings, so '2009' is not '2009.0'.
  • Row order counts only when order_matters is true.

docs.title: Strict and lenient accuracy
docs.text:
Every run is scored twice, and the report gives both, strict first.

Score What it is Strict The execution match above: the same columns (in any order) and the same rows; or the same rows with extra columns (see below) Lenient Every gold column is answered by some column of the result, wherever it sits

Strict is the honest headline. Lenient exists because most of what it forgives is shape a person would accept:

  • the same two names as FirstName, LastName or the other way round;
  • one extra key column;
  • a year labelled 2009-01-01 where the gold set writes 2009.

Academic and vendor practice has moved the same way. Spider 2.0 counts a prediction correct when every gold column vector appears in the result (paper). Defog's sql-eval falls back to subset_df, matching each gold column's values against some generated column with names, types and order ignored (post).

A run passes leniently when:

  • every gold column is matched, as a multiset of values, by a distinct column of the result, in any position, with column names ignored and the same numeric tolerance;
  • the rows of the matched columns then line up as the strict score requires, so values swapped between rows still fail;
  • the row count is equal, and row order still counts only when order_matters.

Two guardrails keep it from passing wrong answers:

  • A column cap. The result may carry at most max(2 x gold columns, gold columns + 2) columns: three for a one-column gold answer, four for two, six for three. Without it a SELECT * would pass by carrying the gold columns among many others. Databricks Genie counts any extra column as bad (docs), so a cap is the middle ground.
  • No constant columns. Once a result has more than one row, a column whose values are all the same -- all-null included -- may not answer for a gold column: a hard-coded literal has the right height and tells the gold column nothing. On a single row every column is constant, so the rule is off there.

One value normalisation is added, and only one: date and period labels. When a gold value is a YYYY, YYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD string and the predicted value is a date starting with it at a component boundary, the two are equal: '2009' matches '2009-01-01', and '2013-02' matches '2013-02-01'.

  • Only the gold side may be the shorter label.
  • Only strings are read this way: a number is a number, never a year.
  • Nothing else is normalised. Anything broader belongs in an alternative answer, which is reviewed per case and cannot silently widen.

Reordered columns and extra columns are the lenient readings that count as a pass in the strict score. A result passes result_match when some choice of its columns, in any order, equals the gold under the strict rules above; a result wider than the gold must also stay within the column cap, and a result of more than 12 columns is not searched for a reordering (the in-order match still applies). The record says which match it was (detail.match: strict, reordered, extra columns or extra columns, reordered). Period labels never pass this way; they stay lenient-only. The row count, every row value and, when order_matters, the row order are as strict as before. (Column order used to count dropped that rule, because a question asks for no column order and Spider-style execution checks ignore it.)

Lenient is a superset of strict by construction: everything strict accepts is accepted. It is not partial credit -- a case passes a score or it does not -- and there is no model in either score, so both stay reproducible. Every record carries status and lenient_status, so a case that passes one score and not the other is visible per case.

docs.title: Alternative answers
docs.text:
A question can have more than one right answer:

  • "Who are the top 5 customers by total spend?" is answered just as well with the name in one column as with FirstName and LastName side by side.
  • "What is the total revenue per year?" is answered with the year written 2009 or 2009-01-01.

alt_sql holds those other answers, one SQL each, and regenerate runs each one exactly as it runs sql. A run passes, strictly or leniently, when its rows match rows or any alternative.

This is how the field handles multiple right answers:

  • Snowflake has humans pick every correct answer out of several models' SQL (post).
  • LinkedIn reports that about 60% of its benchmark questions now have several answers, and that without them it "underreported recall by 10-15%" (post).
  • Spider 2.0 supports multiple gold files per task (paper).

docs.title: When to add one, and when not to
docs.text:
Prefer an alternative to loosening the comparator. An alternative is written down, reviewed once, and only ever affects the case it sits on. A looser rule applies to all forty-seven at once and can quietly start passing wrong answers. The lenient score is deliberately narrow for the same reason.

Add one when all of these hold:

  1. A real run produced it. Alternatives come from SQL a model actually wrote, not from shapes someone imagined it might write.
  2. A person has read the rows and would accept them as an answer to the question as written.
  3. It is the same question, from the same tables: an alternative may not read a table outside tables, and the test enforces that.
  4. It is deterministic -- ties broken on a key, as sql does.

Do not add one when the answer is a different question, however reasonable it looks. Two from the run this was built on, both refused:

  • "Where do our customers from Germany live?" answered with three distinct cities. It drops the customers, so it cannot say who lives where. The alternative kept for chinook_021 is the gold answer with the name in one column, not this.
  • "Who are the top customers by total spend?" answered with one row. "Top customers" is a list with no N; one row answers "who is the top customer", a different question. chinook_007 is not the same case: "which employees support the most customers" carries a superlative, and the one employee who holds the maximum is a fair reading of it, so that one is kept.

To add one:

  1. Write the SQL into alt_sql.
  2. From a checkout of the repo, run engine.evals.regenerate(CHINOOK_SUITE_PATH, allow_packaged=True) to write its alt_rows (CHINOOK_SUITE_PATH from nl2sql.evaluation.suite). The flag is needed because the suite lives in the package.
  3. Read the rows it wrote.
  4. Commit both.

Never type an alternative's rows by hand.

docs.title: Mode plans: gold plans through the code nodes
docs.text:
engine.evals.run(mode="plans") checks the nodes that are plain code -- the logical validator (including RBAC), the SQL generator and the executor -- with no model involved. Every answerable case has a hand-written plan (the typed AST the planner emits) that answers it.

A local FakeLLMServer (nl2sql/evaluation/gold_llm.py) answers every LLM call:

Node The fake answers Datasource resolver The case's datasources for a case with sql, and an empty list for an unanswerable one, so the resolver's refusal is what is scored Decomposer One sub-query whose expected columns are the plan's select aliases Planner The gold plan Refiner "Keep the same plan." Answer synthesizer A fixed sentence
