The key is written to the demo project's .env, replacing that provider's previous key and keeping the others, and the default moves to that provider. The running demo switches from replay to live without a restart: questions already running finish on the model client they started with, then the engine's LLM clients are rebuilt from the project's nl2sql.yaml (its llm.yaml), with the saved key given to them in memory rather than through the environment. Keys are write-only: no response, log line, trace or error carries one, only a masked form such as sk-...4f2a per provider. On a later start the precedence above still holds, so a key exported in your shell wins over a saved one, and every saved key is loaded so each step finds its own.

  • A provider and a model for each LLM step. One selector each for the answerability check (datasource_resolver), question splitter (decomposer), query planner (ast_planner), plan repair (refiner) and answer writer (answer_synthesizer). Each has a "Default" option that uses the top-level provider and model, then one group of models per provider. A provider with no saved key is listed but cannot be chosen, and a step already on a provider whose key is gone says so under its selector. A choice is written to llm.yaml under agents: with its provider, model and temperature. It takes the top level's endpoint and key when it is on the same provider, and names no key otherwise, so its own provider's variable is read. It takes effect on the next question, and a step put on another provider stays there when the default moves. The list is short on purpose. On 2026-09-20 each OpenAI model was sent the engine's parameters of the time (temperature=0, seed=42, strict json_schema) and worked with them, two of them only once the temperature was left out. The engine now asks every model for a tool call instead, as it already did for every node but the planner. That says the model accepts the engine's calls, not how well it plans, which is the evaluation's question:

    Model Written with gpt-5.4 (the default), gpt-5.4-mini, gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-mini, gpt-4o temperature: 0.0 gpt-5.5, gpt-5-mini temperature: null: they reject temperature 0, so a step on one runs at the model's default temperature and its answers vary more from run to run

    Claude's list was not probed on a real account; its temperatures follow Anthropic's documented rules:

    Model Written with claude-opus-5 (the default), claude-sonnet-5 temperature: null: both reject any temperature claude-haiku-4-5 temperature: 0.0

    The list lives in one place, VERIFIED_MODELS in nl2sql/llm/providers.py. It covers OpenAI and Anthropic for now: with an OpenRouter key or Ollama as the default the panel says the default has no model list, and offers only the other providers whose keys are saved. - Local only by default. Settings work only when the playground is bound to a loopback address (127.0.0.1, localhost, ::1). On 0.0.0.0 or any other address the panel says why it is off and the settings routes answer 403, because the playground has no login: a stranger who can reach it could swap in their own key, or spend on yours. Changes are also refused from another site's page (a foreign Origin), through a hostname that is not a loopback name, or in anything but JSON. - Hosted mode is a third state. With nl2sql-api serve --demo --hosted the page shows a key form and a Model for each step section that write only to this browser tab's sessionStorage; the settings routes stay refused because there is nothing on the server to save. Choosing a model needs nothing saved, so hosted mode keeps it: one key per provider and the model each step runs on travel with each question, in a header each. The Ask page there opens with the key form itself: pick a provider, paste the key and Use this key, under three facts about it -- Stored in this browser tab only, Sent with each question in a request header, Never written to disk, logs or traces. Nothing is held closed without a key: the guided questions the server has recordings for are marked and answer from a recorded run, labelled Recorded run, and any other question answers with a button to Settings to add a key. With recordings the key form is folded under Use your own key. Locally there is nothing to announce, and nothing is shown. See Hosted demo.

docs.title: The Retrieval inspector
docs.text:
Retrieval is the third page in the header nav. It embeds any text with the local model and runs the engine's own vector search against the live index: the pool of nearest entries with their similarity, the entries MMR picks in order, the score each won with, and what was dropped. There is no re-ranking model; the "re-ranking" is MMR, explained in Indexing.

  • Knobs. Picks (k, the pool is 4 * k), lambda (the engine uses 0.7; 1 is plain nearest-neighbour order, 0 favours entries unlike earlier picks), which entry types to include, and a datasource filter. After the first search, each change searches again. Each entry shows the text that was embedded for it.
  • Reading it. The picks in order, and the entries MMR passed over, sit above the pool as rows of chips. Each similarity has a bar placed within the pool's own range, nearest full and farthest empty: raw cosine scores bunch together, so this is what shows which entries are actually nearer.
  • Free. The embedder is local; nothing here calls the LLM.
  • For chunking experiments. Change the chunking, press Rebuild, search the same text, and diff the Copy as text output of the two runs: one fixed-width line per entry (rank, pick or drop, similarity, MMR score, type, name).
  • As a role. The search is made as the role chosen in Ask as, so the pool holds only the entries that role may read. The playground trusts the role the page sends; it does not verify who is asking.
  • Local only, like Settings and Rebuild, because it shows the index entries the role reaches, column statistics and sample values included: on a non-loopback --host it is off (POST /api/retrieval answers 403), and it refuses another site's page, a non-loopback hostname and anything but JSON.

A run's own retrieval is under Debug: open the datasource_resolver or schema_retriever row in the per-node table.

docs.title: Rating answers
docs.text: Below Cost & time, each answer asks Was this answer right?: ðŸ‘ Right or ðŸ‘Ž Wrong, with an optional note (Wrong number, Wrong table, Wrong filter, Missing rows, or your own words). The rating is saved in the demo's state store (.nl2sql/state.db) with the question, role, SQL, the model per step and the engine version; never the rows. It is local only, like Settings: on a non-loopback --host it is off. settings.feedback.enabled: false in the project's config turns it off. Read the ratings back, with the refusal, retry, error and plan-cache rates, from the CLI (below). See Feedback and Signals.

docs.title: 3. Use the demo from the CLI
docs.text:
Every command reads one config: --config PATH, else NL2SQL_CONFIG, else ./nl2sql.yaml. Paths inside it are relative to nl2sql.yaml, so from the demo folder (cd nl2sql-demo) no flag is needed; from anywhere else, add --config nl2sql-demo/nl2sql.yaml before the command.

# Run a query against the demo
nl2sql run "How many customers do we have, by country?"

# Ask as a role that is not allowed the answer
nl2sql run --role viewer "Who are the top 5 customers by total spend?"

# Plan and validate without touching the database
nl2sql run --no-exec "Which artist has the most albums?"

# Pin one datasource instead of letting the resolver pick
nl2sql run --ds-id support "How many support tickets are still open, by priority?"

# Re-index after editing the demo's config
nl2sql index

# Re-index one datasource only; the others' entries are left untouched
nl2sql index --datasource chinook

# After changing the embedding model: drop the old model's index
nl2sql index prune

# Check the install, the keys, and the engine: each datasource, each key, the index
nl2sql doctor

The two flags that name a datasource are not the same flag: run takes --ds-id, which pins the datasource and makes the resolver skip its search; index takes --datasource (-d), which chooses what to re-index.

The demo's settings.yaml sets traces: { mode: always }, so every run also writes a trace to .nl2sql/traces/ and prints its path. Inspect one with nl2sql trace show <file or trace id>, or re-run it on the recorded model answers with nl2sql trace replay <file>. See Debugging a Run.

Asking a question a second time on the same day reuses the first run's validated plan from the plan cache (in .nl2sql/state.db), so the SQL and rows are the same and the planner is not called; the playground's Debug view says "Plan from the plan cache". The plan is still validated for the role you ask as. To start fresh:

nl2sql cache clear

The playground's ratings, and the guardrail rates over every rated run and kept trace:

nl2sql feedback list               # the ratings, newest first
nl2sql feedback stats              # thumbs up/down, refusals, retries, errors, plan cache
nl2sql feedback export --good      # thumbs-up runs as draft eval cases, for review
nl2sql feedback clear              # delete every rating

export --good writes feedback_gold_drafts.yaml, a suite of draft cases. A person must review each draft, approve it and run engine.evals.regenerate before it runs; see Feedback and Signals.

Recording (scripts/record_demo_answers.py) turns the cache off (settings.pipeline.plan_cache is off in the engine it builds; the files are not changed), so every planner answer is captured. It also stops with exit 1, recording nothing, when the demo's indexing fails: a plain nl2sql demo keeps going and offers Rebuild, but answers recorded against no index would be the wrong ones. Only a question whose run succeeded (rows, an answer, no error) keeps its recordings; a failed run's are dropped, the question is listed as not recorded, and the command exits 1 after writing recordings.json with the rest. The file names the provider and the model that answered, and a replay reports that model -- in the usage ledger, the Debug pane and on the Pipeline page, tagged recorded -- rather than the one the replaying config names. See Determinism â†’ The plan cache.

The .env next to nl2sql.yaml is loaded by the CLI, nl2sql-api and nl2sql demo at startup, so doctor and run find a key kept only there; a variable already exported in your shell wins over the file. There is no --env flag and no .env.<name> lookup: one config folder, one .env.

run and index call engine.check() first. A datasource marked required: true that cannot connect stops them with the report (exit 1); any other one that fails is printed and left out of routing.

docs.title: Sample questions
docs.text:
The demo's datasource files carry twenty questions (sample_questions), the same ones the playground offers as guided questions -- a few as chips for the database the rail is showing, and all twenty behind N more, in one pile per database, each headed by the datasource id. Chinook's twelve come first, so the demo opens on familiar ground:

  • How many customers do we have, by country?
  • Who are the top 5 customers by total spend?
  • Which artist has the most albums?
  • What is the total revenue per year?
  • Which genre sells the most tracks?
  • What is the average invoice total by billing country?
  • Which employees support the most customers?
  • What is the longest track in each genre?
  • Which 5 customers bought the most jazz tracks?
  • What was the monthly revenue in 2013 for customers in the USA?
  • Which playlists contain tracks from more than three genres?
  • Who are the top customers by total spend?

Then four on support:

  • How many support tickets are still open, by priority?
  • Which support agents resolved the most tickets?
  • What is the average time to close a ticket, by category?
  • Which customers raised the most support tickets?

And four on webanalytics:

  • Which pages were viewed the most last year?
  • How many sessions came from each marketing channel?
  • What is the bounce rate by device type?
  • How many purchases were there per month in 2013?

None of them spans two databases, deliberately: the engine cannot answer such a question yet. The rail says so too, under the database switcher: each question is answered from one database, and joining across them is planned. Clicking a question from another pile moves the switcher to that database, so the schema on the left is the one the question is about.

They are also indexed, per datasource, each question as an entry of its own (schema.datasource_example, from sample_questions in its datasource file), beside the schema.datasource entry with the configured description. Routing votes with both, and with each datasource's tables and columns, which is how the resolver tells the three apart (see Routing). Re-index (nl2sql index) after editing them.

Whether a given question is answered correctly depends on the model; see Known limitations.

docs.title: Regenerating the demo
docs.text: nl2sql init --demo DIR --force overwrites the config files and all three databases under data/ with fresh copies; without --force it names the files that exist and writes nothing. It never touches .env, so a saved key survives, and it leaves the index under .nl2sql/ alone: run nl2sql index afterwards. nl2sql demo never rewrites an existing project's config (only llm.yaml, to point it at the mode it starts in); start a new --dir for a fresh one.

docs.title: The datasets that are not here
docs.text: --lite and --docker chose between a generated manufacturing dataset in SQLite and the same data in a Postgres/MySQL/MSSQL Compose stack. Both are gone: the manufacturing DDL declared no foreign keys, so it could not answer a join question, and it was the only dataset the test suite ran on. The Postgres, MySQL and MSSQL adapters are unaffected - they are product features, configured like any other datasource. The demo's three SQLite databases took their place. A question that has to read two of them at once is still not answerable: the engine plans each sub-query against a single datasource.

docs.title: Docker (REST API)
docs.text: Use this path when you want the HTTP API only.

docs.title: Build the image
docs.text:
From the repo root:

docker build -t nl2sql-api .

The Dockerfile is at the repo root. Its first stage builds the web app (nl2sql-ui); the second installs the local packages from the build context - packages/sdk, packages/nl2sql[postgres,mysql,mssql,duckdb,anthropic,otel] and packages/api - and serves the built app, so the build context has to be the repo root. For a running stack with a volume and API keys, see Docker Compose.

The root .dockerignore keeps that context to the sources the build actually needs - it drops .git, virtualenvs, docs/, site/, chroma_db/, data/, logs/ and stale build/, dist/ and *.egg-info directories.

docs.title: Adapters
docs.text: The image ships all five adapters' drivers (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server with Microsoft's ODBC driver 18, DuckDB, SQLite) and the Anthropic provider. One image, no slim variant.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The image sets NL2SQL_CONFIG=/etc/nl2sql/nl2sql.yaml. Mount a config folder there: nl2sql.yaml, the files it includes, and optionally a .env next to it, which the API loads at startup without overriding variables already set. Write one with nl2sql init (see Start a config).

Keep the index, state, traces and results on a volume: write storage.path from an environment variable, and mount the volume there.

# storage.yaml
path: "${env:NL2SQL_DATA_DIR}"

# api.yaml (nl2sql.yaml has  api: { file: api.yaml })
auth: static
static_role: admin      # one role for every request

api.auth: static pins the RBAC role for every request. The image runs nl2sql-api serve --host 0.0.0.0, which refuses to start while api.auth is the default, none, so the container needs api_keys, proxy or static. See Identity and API settings.

The routes that register datasources or LLMs and build or clear the index need a role listed in policies.admin_roles (default [admin]), so static_role: admin above allows them. See Admin routes.

docs.title: Run the API
docs.text:
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 \
  -v "$PWD/my-project:/etc/nl2sql:ro" \
  -v nl2sql-data:/data -e NL2SQL_DATA_DIR=/data \
  nl2sql-api

Provider keys come from the environment (-e OPENAI_API_KEY=...) or from the mounted .env. Before it serves, the API calls engine.check(): a datasource with required: true that cannot connect stops the container, and any other that fails is logged and left out. Build the index once with POST /api/v1/jobs/index, or with nl2sql --config my-project/nl2sql.yaml index against the same storage.

docs.title: API usage
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/query \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"question":"Top 5 customers by revenue last quarter?"}'

docs.title: Launch
docs.text:
nl2sql launch [DIR] takes you from "I have a database" to a working project in one sitting. It finds the database, asks for what is missing, tests the connection, writes the project, indexes it, profiles it and files five starter questions, then lets you review what it found. Every step is a package call (engine.datasources.scan, test, save, engine.index.build, engine.knowledge.profile, engine.dashboards.suggest_questions, engine.proposals), so Python and REST callers can do the same.

pip install "nl2sql-cli[web]"
nl2sql launch my-project

or, with nothing installed first:

uvx --from nl2sql-engine nl2sql launch my-project

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Meaning DIR The project folder (default .). Without a nl2sql.yaml there, launch writes a new project; with one, it adds one datasource to it --provider NAME The LLM provider and its default model for a new project (openai, the default, anthropic, openrouter, ...). An existing project keeps its own --as ROLE The admin role the launch acts as (repeatable). Default: the first of policies.admin_roles; under allow_all, none is needed. A role that is not in policies.admin_roles is refused before the first question --draft Also have the profiler model draft descriptions, under settings.profiler.max_cost_usd. The only step that calls a model --yes Accept nothing: write DIR/review.yaml (or the next free review-<n>.yaml, never over a file already there) for review in git instead of asking --no-ports Do not look for databases on local ports

docs.title: What happens
docs.text: Step What you see Find A numbered list: database files under DIR (two folders down), the DATABASE_URL environment variable, and servers listening on their default ports on 127.0.0.1 (PostgreSQL 5432, MySQL 3306, SQL Server 1433), then "Another database". Nothing connects while it looks. Fill A prompt for each field the finding could not fill. For "Another database" it is every field that is not advanced, with its default (a port, say), so a server on a non-default port can be set. A password is hidden. Name The datasource id, defaulting to the file's name. A name that cannot be a file name in datasources/ (con, a/b) is asked again. Test A connection test. On failure it prints the stage (network, auth, ...), the reason and the fix, and asks for every field again, what you typed as the default. Model key The provider's key from the environment, or asked (hidden). It is not checked with a call; your first question is the check. Write A new folder gets the whole project (nl2sql.yaml and a file per section, glossary.yaml); an existing project gets datasources/<id>.yaml. Secrets go to .env and the YAML holds ${env:NL2SQL_...} references. Index Builds the index, with progress. The first run downloads the local embedding model. Profile Joins the database does not declare and column roles, filed as proposals (Schema Profiler). Starter questions Five questions from the starter dashboard's templates, printed and filed as example proposals. Review Each waiting proposal: accept, reject, skip or edit. Next The nl2sql run command for the first starter question, and nl2sql demo --dir DIR to open the playground on your project. demo warns about an old engine only for a folder whose demo stamp is older, so a launched folder (it has no stamp) opens without a warning.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: A connection password and the model key are written to DIR/.env, which launch adds to .gitignore, and never to YAML. After writing, launch loads that .env and rebuilds the engine from the files it wrote, so the key and every ${env:...} reference resolve in the same run and the files are proven to load. A variable already set in your environment is never overridden, and a key already in the environment is used without being written. No password or key is printed, not in the candidates, an error or a summary.

docs.title: Review, and what --yes does
docs.text:
The profiler's findings and the starter questions wait in the review queue. Nothing a model or a template drafted reaches a prompt, the index or glossary.yaml until an admin accepts it. In the prompt, a accepts, r rejects, s (the default) leaves it for later and e edits its change as JSON object before accepting (anything else is skipped). An accepted item is written to glossary.yaml; run nl2sql index --refresh so it reaches the index. When DIR is not ., the commands launch prints carry --config DIR/nl2sql.yaml (and --as ROLE under roles).

With --yes, nothing is accepted. launch exports the open proposals to DIR/review.yaml; set each decision in a pull request and run nl2sql --config DIR/nl2sql.yaml review apply DIR/review.yaml --as ROLE.

docs.title: Drivers
docs.text:
An adapter whose driver is not installed is listed but cannot be used. launch prints the two fixes and stops: install it (pip install "nl2sql-engine[postgres]"), or, if you started with uvx, start again with the extra included (uvx --from "nl2sql-engine[postgres]" nl2sql launch). It does not install anything itself, because an install inside uvx's throwaway environment would not last.

launch is the one command that reads DATABASE_URL.

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text:
nl2sql mcp serves the engine to an MCP client, such as a desktop assistant or an IDE, over stdio, or with --http over HTTP behind API keys. The client gets three tools: ask, list_datasources and describe_table. It is built on the official mcp Python SDK and uses only the engine's public API, so it answers as engine.run_query does.

pip install "nl2sql-engine[mcp]"
nl2sql --config my-project/nl2sql.yaml mcp --role analyst

The server reads and writes the MCP protocol on stdin and stdout until the client closes the stream. Everything else, logs included, goes to stderr.

docs.title: Who is asking
docs.text:
stdio has no authentication: the person who started the process is the caller, and every tool call runs as the role they name.

Flag Meaning --role ROLE A role from policies.yaml (repeatable). The caller reads what any of its roles allows. --user ID The user id runs are recorded under (traces, the audit log, approvals) and conversations belong to. Optional: without it the user id is mcp.

Without --role, the caller has policies.default_role. With neither, the server refuses to start, because a caller with no role reads nothing:

Error: nl2sql mcp needs a role: pass --role <role> (repeatable), or set policies.default_role in nl2sql.yaml. A caller with no role reads nothing.

A role the policies do not define is refused the same way, naming the roles there are, and a policies.default_role that names no role stops the config from loading. With policies: {allow_all: true} (what nl2sql init writes) every caller reads everything, so no role is needed: the server starts and logs a warning that the client can read every table of every datasource. Under allow_all no role is defined, so any --role is refused as unknown.

docs.title: Connect a client
docs.text:
A client that launches stdio servers takes the command and its arguments. For example, in a client's JSON config:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "nl2sql": {
      "command": "nl2sql",
      "args": ["--config", "/path/to/my-project/nl2sql.yaml", "mcp", "--role", "analyst"]
    }
  }
}

The model's API key is read as for any command: from the environment, or the .env next to nl2sql.yaml.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text:
Every tool returns a structured result (JSON). A failure is a status and a code, never an exception's text: the details are in the server's log and the run's trace.

Tool Arguments Returns ask question (it must stand alone; optional only when sending a choice, which answers the pending question), conversation_id (optional: continue that conversation), datasource_id (optional: skip routing; only when starting one), choice (optional: the option id for a question that asked, see below) See below. list_datasources none {"datasources": [...]}: each one's id, type, description and status, for the datasources the caller's roles reach. describe_table datasource_id, table (its name, or schema.name) {"status": "ok", "table": {...}}: its columns (name, type, nullable, primary_key, description), foreign_keys, row_count and description, as engine.datasources.schema gives them.

ask returns:

Key Meaning conversation_id, turn, question The conversation this ask belongs to (a new one without a conversation_id), the turn's number in it, and the question that ran. status The run's status: success, plan_only, error, needs_approval, stopped, needs_clarification. answer {"summary", "content"}, or null when no answer was written. sub_queries Per sub-query: id, datasource_id, sql, columns, the first 20 rows, total_rows and truncated. truncated Whether any sub-query's rows were cut, at the preview or at the row ceiling. source Whether a verified query or a generated one answered. warnings Each one's code and message, under the same rule as errors. trace_id The run's trace. The full results are read by it with engine.results. errors When the run failed: each one's code, node and message. A refusal (SECURITY_VIOLATION) always carries the generic "You do not have permission to see the data this question requires.", whatever refusal_names_tables says. A hook's denial, a limit, a provider failure or an answer check keeps the engine's message; any other message names only its code and the trace, since it may carry an exception's text. approvals_needed When status is needs_approval: what a person must approve, as run_query returns it. stop When status is stopped: which limit stopped the run. clarification When status is needs_clarification: the phrase, and each option's id, label and plain-English explanation. The request itself stays in the conversation.

Each ask is a turn of a conversation owned by the caller: without conversation_id one starts, with it the question continues that conversation. The client's own model leads, so ask runs only the question, with no model call of its own; write each question so it stands alone. A conversation that is another user's, or does not exist, is CONVERSATION_NOT_FOUND; one running another turn is CONVERSATION_BUSY; one that has reached conversations.max_turns is CONVERSATION_TOO_LONG: start a new one. A datasource_id on a follow-up (it is set when the conversation starts), or no question and no choice, is INVALID_REQUEST.

A question that can be read more than one way is not run. The assistant shows the options to its user and calls ask again with the same conversation_id and choice="b", the id of the option picked; the engine runs that option's plan through the same checks as any plan, under the same role. A choice with no conversation_id, an id that is not an option of the pending question, or nothing pending is CLARIFICATION_INVALID; a request that the data or glossary has outdated is CLARIFICATION_STALE: ask again without a choice.

An exception out of the engine is {"status": "error", "errors": [{"code": "INTERNAL_ERROR", ...}]}, and logged.

docs.title: What a role cannot see
docs.text:
The caller sees only what its roles may read:

  • list_datasources leaves out a datasource none of its roles reaches.
  • describe_table answers a table its roles deny exactly as a missing one: {"status": "not_found", "message": "No table 'Customer' in datasource 'chinook'.", "tables": [...]}, where tables lists the tables it may read. A datasource it cannot reach answers not_found with no tables.
  • ask with a datasource_id the caller cannot reach answers DATASOURCE_NOT_FOUND, as for one that does not exist, without running. Without one, the run is refused by the engine's policy checks as any run is.
  • ask never names a denied table. The client is a third party, and a refusal that named the table would confirm it exists, so refusal_names_tables does not apply here: every refusal carries the generic message.

Two things can still give a table away, and are the operator's to manage:

  • The refusal's code. The message is generic, but the code is not. A plan that names a table the role may not read can end in SECURITY_VIOLATION, while a plan that names a table that does not exist fails a different check. The review of this server saw it with a role written as a deny list (the demo's analyst): a client that guesses table names can tell a denied table from a missing one by the code. This is how the engine's validator reports, not something the server adds.
  • The datasource's description. list_datasources returns each datasource's description from the config, verbatim, to every caller that reaches it. Do not name tables there that some role may not read.

docs.title: In Python
docs.text:
engine.serve_mcp(identity) serves the engine over stdio until the client closes the stream; nl2sql mcp builds the engine and calls it. Over stdio identity is required (a ValueError otherwise). nl2sql.mcp.server.build_server(engine, identity) returns the server (a FastMCP) if you need to run it yourself. identity is a UserContext, or a function returning one that is called on every tool call, inside the tool's guard: a function that raises gives INTERNAL_ERROR, never its exception's text. The engine stays yours to close.

The SDK's FastMCP settings read FASTMCP_* environment variables and the working directory's .env; every setting is passed explicitly when the server is built, so neither can change it.

from nl2sql import NL2SQL, UserContext

with NL2SQL.from_config("nl2sql.yaml") as engine:
    engine.serve_mcp(UserContext(roles=["analyst"]))

For HTTP, engine.serve_mcp(None, http=True) runs it with Uvicorn (host and port override mcp.http). identity is only used with mcp.auth: none. To build the app yourself, build_server(engine, identity, over_http=True) sets the server up for streamable_http_app(), and nl2sql.mcp.http.build_app(engine, identity) wraps it in the key check.

docs.title: Over HTTP
docs.text:
nl2sql keys create --as admin --user ana --role analyst --label laptop   # prints the token once
nl2sql --config my-project/nl2sql.yaml mcp --http                        # http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp

nl2sql mcp --http [--host H] [--port P] serves the same three tools at /mcp over the MCP SDK's streamable HTTP transport, stateless with JSON responses: each request stands alone, and a follow-up names its conversation_id. stdio stays the default. Without --host and --port the server uses mcp.http in mcp.yaml (see the mcp section):

# nl2sql.yaml
mcp: mcp.yaml

# mcp.yaml (every value shown is the default)
http:
  host: 127.0.0.1
  port: 8765
  path: /mcp
  allowed_hosts: ["127.0.0.1:*", "localhost:*", "[::1]:*", "127.0.0.1", "localhost", "[::1]"]   # Host headers accepted
  allowed_origins: []                              # browser Origins accepted
auth: api_keys            # api_keys | none (none: loopback only)

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
With auth: api_keys every request carries Authorization: Bearer <token>, a token from nl2sql keys create. The request runs as that key's user, tenant and roles; nothing is taken from the client, and --role and --user do not apply. Two keys in flight at once each get their own identity. A missing, malformed, unknown or revoked key is a 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer, and an mcp.denied event the audit observer keeps (the reason and a revoked key's id; never the token). Revoke a key and its next request fails.

auth: none runs every request as the one identity --role and --user name, as stdio does. It is for trying things out on your own machine: the server refuses to bind any address but loopback with it, and refuses to start when allowed_hosts lists a name that is not loopback (see below).

docs.title: Host, Origin and TLS
docs.text:
The SDK's DNS-rebinding protection refuses a request whose Host is not in allowed_hosts (entries are host or host:*) or whose Origin is present and not in allowed_origins. The default allows the loopback names only, so a server reached under another name needs that name:

http:
  allowed_hosts: ["mcp.example.com"]

The server speaks plain HTTP and the key is a bearer token, so anything that is not on your own machine needs TLS from a reverse proxy or a tunnel, and a remote chat app requires https. Keep the server on 127.0.0.1 and let the proxy face the network:

# Caddy: terminates TLS, forwards to the server
mcp.example.com {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8765
}

# or a tunnel
cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8765

The proxy or tunnel passes the public name as Host, so list it in allowed_hosts. Binding a public address directly (--host 0.0.0.0) is allowed with auth: api_keys only. For the same reason a proxy or tunnel needs auth: api_keys too: with auth: none the server refuses to start when allowed_hosts lists any name that is not loopback, since anyone who could reach that name would read as the one identity.

docs.title: Connect a client
docs.text:
A client that lets its user set a header works with keys: a desktop assistant's or IDE's config file, or a script using a model provider's remote MCP tool. For example, in a client's JSON config:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "nl2sql": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer nl2sql_<id>_<secret>" }
    }
  }
}

Keep the token in the client's secret store, not in a file you share. A chat app whose connector screen offers only OAuth does not work with keys; OAuth is the next step after 0.9. The hosted demo is not exposed over MCP.

Logs go to stderr. A request that fails to check a key (the state store is down) is a 500 and a log line, never the token.

docs.title: PyPI (Python API)
docs.text: Use this path when you want to embed NL2SQL directly in a Python application. See the Core API documentation at docs/api/index.md.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
# Core only
pip install nl2sql-engine

# install all available adapters. (Never prefer this, until you really need all adapters.)
pip install "nl2sql-engine[all]"

# Core with selected adapters
pip install "nl2sql-engine[postgres]"
pip install "nl2sql-engine[mysql,mssql]"   # [mssql] also needs Microsoft's ODBC Driver for SQL Server
pip install "nl2sql-engine[duckdb]"

# The browser playground behind `nl2sql demo` (adds fastapi + uvicorn).
# `[all]` does NOT include it -- `all` covers database drivers only.
pip install "nl2sql-cli[web]"

Running a query needs an LLM key; only indexing is key-free. See Known limitations.

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
The engine reads one config, nl2sql.yaml, and the files it includes. nl2sql init writes it (in Python, nl2sql.init_project("my-project") writes the same files); see Start a config with nl2sql init. Each section has its own page:

  • Datasources
  • LLMs
  • Embeddings
  • Policies
  • Storage
  • Secrets
  • Settings

docs.title: Building the engine in Python
docs.text:
from nl2sql import NL2SQL

with NL2SQL.from_config("nl2sql.yaml") as engine:   # or $NL2SQL_CONFIG, then ./nl2sql.yaml
    report = engine.check()                         # connects, and reports what is ready
    print(report)

Building the engine never connects to a datasource or calls a model. engine.check() does: it raises EngineNotReady when a datasource with required: true fails, and otherwise leaves a failed datasource out of routing. The library never reads a .env file; call python-dotenv yourself before from_config if you keep keys in one. See Public Facade for every way to build it, including a Config built in code and NL2SQL.demo(). Use the config for fixed, app-wide settings. Use runtime registration when you need to add datasources on a long-running process without restart.

docs.title: Datasource configuration
docs.text:
datasources/ holds one file per datasource; the file name is its id:

# datasources/my_postgres.yaml
type: postgres
description: Primary analytics DB.
connection:
  host: localhost
  port: 5432
  user: "${env:POSTGRES_USER}"
  password: "${env:POSTGRES_PASSWORD}"
  database: analytics
limits: { row_limit: 100, timeout_ms: 8000, max_bytes: 10485760 }

Install the adapter extras that match type:

pip install "nl2sql-engine[postgres]"

See Adapters for the full list of available adapters. See Datasource config for field definitions.

docs.title: LLM configuration
docs.text:
llm.yaml selects the model and any per-agent overrides:

# llm.yaml
provider: openai
model: gpt-5.4
temperature: 0.0
# api_key is optional: without it OPENAI_API_KEY is read.
agents:
  profiler: { model: gpt-5.4-mini }

To route chat through OpenRouter instead — one key for Anthropic, Google, Meta and hundreds of other models, with no extra dependency:

provider: openrouter
model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.5
temperature: 0.0

To use Claude on Anthropic's own API, with the system prompts prompt-cached, install the anthropic extra and point the config at it:

pip install "nl2sql-engine[anthropic]"

provider: anthropic
model: claude-opus-5
temperature: null          # Claude Opus 5 rejects a temperature

See LLM configuration → Anthropic.

A local Ollama daemon is configured the same way, with provider: ollama; how well a given local model handles the pipeline's structured output varies by model, so see LLM configuration → Ollama first.

Note that OpenRouter serves chat completions only. Embeddings are their own section: embeddings: { provider: local } (what nl2sql init writes) embeds with a key-free ONNX model, and provider: openai needs OPENAI_API_KEY. See Embeddings.

See LLM config for full schema details.

docs.title: Add a datasource at runtime
docs.text:
You can register a datasource programmatically without editing config files:

from nl2sql import NL2SQL, Datasource, Limits

engine = NL2SQL.from_config("nl2sql.yaml")
engine.datasources.add(Datasource(
    id="runtime_pg",
    type="postgres",
    description="Runtime Postgres datasource",
    connection={
        "host": "localhost",
        "port": 5432,
        "user": "postgres",
        "password": "${env:RUNTIME_PG_PASSWORD}",
        "database": "analytics",
    },
    limits=Limits(timeout_ms=8000, row_limit=100, max_bytes=10485760),
))

engine.index.build(["runtime_pg"])

The description is indexed as given, even though no file lists runtime_pg, and the datasource joins engine.config. Indexing makes no LLM call; the descriptions it indexes are the database's comments and your glossary's.

You can also add the datasources of another config:

from nl2sql import NL2SQL, load_config

engine = NL2SQL.from_config("nl2sql.yaml")
for datasource in load_config("other/nl2sql.yaml").datasources:
    engine.datasources.add(datasource)

docs.title: Replace the LLM at runtime
docs.text:
engine.llm.replace swaps the whole llm section in the running engine, as one step: it is validated as llm.yaml is, every agent's key must resolve, and questions already running finish on the old LLM.

from nl2sql import NL2SQL, LLM, AgentLLM

engine = NL2SQL.from_config("nl2sql.yaml")
engine.llm.replace(LLM(provider="openai", model="gpt-5.4",
                       agents={"ast_planner": AgentLLM(model="gpt-5.5")}))
engine.llm.list()["ast_planner"]["model"]   # 'gpt-5.5'

The llm section of another config:

from nl2sql import load_config

engine.llm.replace(load_config("other/nl2sql.yaml").llm)

docs.title: Policies configuration
docs.text:
policies.yaml defines which roles can access which datasources and tables:

# policies.yaml
default_role: viewer
admin_roles: [admin]
roles:
  admin:
    description: System Administrator
    allow: ["*"]
  viewer:
    description: Read-only access to the catalogue
    allow: ["my_postgres.public.products"]

{allow_all: true} (what nl2sql init writes) lets every caller read everything, for local use only. See Policies config for the allow and deny patterns and wildcards.

docs.title: Secrets configuration (optional)
docs.text:
A secrets section is only needed when you want to pull secrets from a provider other than the environment:

# secrets.yaml
providers:
  - id: azure-prod
    type: azure
    vault_url: "https://my-vault.vault.azure.net/"

A datasource then writes password: "${azure-prod:db-password}". See Secrets config for supported providers and fields.

docs.title: Run a query
docs.text:
from nl2sql import NL2SQL
from nl2sql import UserContext

engine = NL2SQL.from_config("nl2sql.yaml")
user_ctx = UserContext(user_id="user123", roles=["admin"])

result = engine.run_query(
    "Top 5 customers by revenue last quarter?",
    user_context=user_ctx
)

print(result.final_answer)
for sub_query in result.sub_queries:
    print(sub_query.datasource_id, sub_query.sql)

The QueryResult includes sub_queries (each with its generated sql), final_answer, errors, warnings, artifact_refs, and a trace_id for observability. Each sub-query carries a capped sample of its rows (rows); the full result set lives in artifact storage and is addressed through artifact_refs.

A question repeated on the same day reuses its validated plan from the plan cache (no planner call, same SQL and rows; still validated every time), and sub_query.plan_source says "cache". Turn it off with settings.pipeline.plan_cache: false; empty it with nl2sql cache clear. See Determinism → The plan cache.

docs.title: Lifecycle (configure → check → index → query)
docs.text:
1. Configure datasources, LLMs, and policies (nl2sql init).
  2. Build the engine and call engine.check().
  3. Index schemas at least once (and after schema changes).
  4. Run queries.

docs.title: Index schema (required)
docs.text:
engine.index.build(["my_postgres"])   # one datasource
engine.index.build()                  # every datasource

docs.title: Configure providers
docs.text:
Secrets providers are installed via extras and selected in the secrets section:

pip install "nl2sql-engine[aws]"
pip install "nl2sql-engine[azure]"
pip install "nl2sql-engine[hashicorp]"

See Configuration for the whole config, the environment variables it reads, and where each 0.4 file and variable went.

docs.title: Use the engine from Python
docs.text:
from nl2sql import NL2SQL, UserContext

engine = NL2SQL.demo()               # the bundled databases; reads OPENAI_API_KEY (or another provider's key)
engine.index.build()                 # once: builds the index under .nl2sql-demo/
# Your own config instead:  engine = NL2SQL.from_config("nl2sql.yaml")
result = engine.run_query(
    "How many customers are there?",
    user_context=UserContext(roles=["admin"]),
)

print(result.status)                  # "success", "error", "plan_only", or "" if nothing ran
for sq in result.sub_queries:
    print(sq.sql)
    print([c.name for c in sq.validation if c.passed])
    print(sq.rows.rows[:5] if sq.rows else "plan only")
print(result.final_answer["summary"] if result.final_answer else result.errors)

Building an engine never connects; engine.check() connects to each datasource and reports, and with NL2SQL.from_config(...) as engine: closes it. run_query also takes datasource_id and execute=False (plan and validate only). Pass a user_context with a role: with none the call currently raises a validation error, and a role the policy does not know is refused. QueryResult carries per sub-query the plan, checks, SQL, a capped row sample with the true total, status and retry count, and per run the status, errors, warnings, per-node timings, usage (LLM calls and tokens, and cost when llm.prices covers the model) and trace_path. Asking the same question again reuses the validated plan from the plan cache (sq.plan_source == "cache"), still validated for the caller's role.

Everything else on NL2SQL is a namespace: engine.datasources (list, get, add, remove, schema, test), engine.index (build, health, clear, inspect, inspect_defaults), engine.llm (list, get, providers, prices, replace, set_models), engine.policies (roles, allows, allowed, validate), engine.curated (validate, test), engine.results (manifest, page, csv), engine.feedback (record, list, stats, export, clear), engine.traces (get, replay) and engine.evals (load, run, regenerate, scorers); engine.about() describes the engine and each step of a run. The CLI, the MCP server and nl2sql-api use nothing else. See the public facade and examples/.

docs.title: From Source (Development)
docs.text: Use this path when you want to contribute or run the latest changes.

docs.title: Clone and install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/nadeem4/nl2sql.git
cd nl2sql

python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate

pip install -e packages/sdk -e "packages/nl2sql[postgres,duckdb]" -e packages/api -e "nl2sql-cli[web]"
pip install --group dev

These are the extras the full test suite needs (see CONTRIBUTING.md): postgres and duckdb supply the drivers the adapter tests import, and demo supplies the FastAPI/uvicorn server behind nl2sql demo. Add mysql or mssql for those drivers, or use [all] for every dialect driver (it does not include demo). There is no sqlite extra: that driver is in the standard library. pip install --group dev (pip 25.1 or newer) installs the PEP 735 dev group from the root pyproject.toml: pytest, pytest-randomly, pytest-timeout and httpx.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The engine reads one nl2sql.yaml. nl2sql init writes it, with each section in its own file, and nl2sql init --demo writes the demo's. See Start a config with nl2sql init and Configuration.

nl2sql init my-demo --demo
nl2sql --config my-demo/nl2sql.yaml index

docs.title: Run locally
docs.text:
CLI:

nl2sql --config my-demo/nl2sql.yaml run "How many customers are there?"

Python API:

python -c "from nl2sql import NL2SQL, UserContext; print(NL2SQL.from_config('my-demo/nl2sql.yaml').run_query('How many customers are there?', user_context=UserContext(roles=['admin'])))"

API service:

NL2SQL_CONFIG=my-demo/nl2sql.yaml nl2sql-api --port 8000

or in Docker:

docker build -t nl2sql-api .
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 -v "$PWD/my-demo:/etc/nl2sql" nl2sql-api

The image listens beyond localhost, so it needs api.auth set (api_keys, proxy or static) in the config; with the default none it exits at start-up. For a demo, add api: { auth: static, static_role: admin } to my-demo/nl2sql.yaml, or use the Compose stack, which ships api_keys.

See Docker (REST API) for adapter extras, the role settings and the data volume.

docs.title: Debugging a Run with Traces
docs.text:
A run trace is one JSON file that records everything a single question did inside the engine: every node execution in order (retries and parallel sub-queries included), the state each node read and the update it returned, its errors and warnings, and for every LLM call the exact messages sent, the raw response, the parsed result and the token usage. The final QueryResult is in it too.

The point is to run a failing question once, then debug it from the file: read it, print its timeline, or replay it through the pipeline without calling the model again.

docs.title: When a trace is written
docs.text:
Each engine reads these from the settings.traces section of its config, so two engines in one process trace by their own settings. The 0.4 variable each one is still set from by the CLI and the playground is in brackets.

Setting Default Meaning settings.traces.mode on_failure off, on_failure or always. settings.traces.sample_rows 50 Result rows kept in the trace. settings.traces.max_field_chars 20000 Longest string kept in a node's recorded inputs and outputs.

Traces are written through the trace store in storage.traces (see Storage). The built-in files store writes them to <storage.path>/traces/; nl2sql init puts storage.path in .gitignore. A trace store of your own (the TraceStore protocol in nl2sql_sdk.stores: write, get, purge) receives the whole document.

Traces are kept for the store's max_age_days, 14 days by default (traces: { type: files, max_age_days: 30 }). engine.storage.purge() deletes the older ones; nl2sql storage purge calls it, and nl2sql-api calls it at startup and once a day.

on_failure writes a trace when the run returned errors, needed a retry in any sub-query, had a node fail, or did not complete (timeout, cancellation, crash). A run that recovered on retry therefore still leaves a trace.

The demo's config (nl2sql init --demo) sets settings.traces.mode: always in its settings.yaml, so every playground question is traced.

The trace is recorded by a callback that run_with_graph attaches to every run, so the CLI, the Python API, the REST API and the playground all produce it. Writing a trace never fails a run; a write error is logged as a warning.

Where the file went is reported back:

  • QueryResult.trace_path (Python API) and trace_path in the REST /query response: the path, or null when no trace was written or the trace store is not the files store. trace_id is in the file name, and engine.traces.get(trace_id) reads the trace from any store. A trace records its asker (owner); with a user_context only that asker reads it, and with none the caller is the in-process operator (nl2sql trace).
  • nl2sql run prints Trace written to <path>.
  • The playground shows a Download trace link under Cost & time when Debug is on.

File names are <UTC timestamp>_<trace_id>.json, so a directory listing sorts by time.

docs.title: What is in the file
docs.text:
{
  "trace_format_version": 1,
  "trace_id": "159afe1f-3305-4907-903a-55495d040665",
  "started_at": "2026-09-21T16:48:37.324431+00:00",
  "finished_at": "2026-09-21T16:48:37.712202+00:00",
  "duration_s": 0.3878,
  "outcome": "completed",
  "failed": true,
  "error": null,
  "request": {"question": "How many customers are there?", "roles": ["admin"],
              "tenant_id": "default_tenant", "datasource_id": null, "execute": true, "clarify": true, "answer": true,
              "today": "2026-09-21"},
  "engine": {"version": "0.1.2", "git_sha": "2cfe121", "python": "3.13.14"},
  "llm": {"configured": {"default": {"provider": "openai", "model": "gpt-5.4", "temperature": 0.0}},
          "by_node": {"decomposer": "gpt-5.4", "ast_planner": "gpt-5.4", "refiner": "gpt-5.4",
                      "answer_synthesizer": "gpt-5.4"}},
  "settings": {"...": "the run's settings section: pipeline, retrieval, results, traces, schema, ..."},
  "limits": {"sample_rows": 50, "max_field_chars": 20000, "max_list_items": 200, "note": "..."},
  "nodes": ["... one entry per node execution, below ..."],
  "events": ["... the run's bus events, below ..."],
  "result": {"...": "the QueryResult, rows capped"}
}

request holds what a replay needs to ask the same question again: the question, caller (roles, tenant_id), datasource_id, and the execute, clarify and answer flags, plus today, the date the prompts were told.

events lists the run's own events in the order they were published (run.started, each node.started and node.finished with its sub_query_id, result.manifest, llm.call and the rest), every one but answer.delta, whose text the result holds whole. Each is the event as JSON: name, at, trace_id, tenant_id and data. The trace is written before the run's run.finished is published, so the list ends just before it; the trace's result is what that event summarises.

A log line written while the run was in flight carries the same trace_id, on the caller's thread and on every graph worker thread, so grepping the logs for a trace's id finds its lines (Events).

One entry of nodes (the planner's second attempt, from a run whose first plan named a column that does not exist; long values shortened here):

{
  "seq": 20, "end_seq": 21,
  "node": "ast_planner", "sub_query_id": "sq_9579d7d41aee", "attempt": 2, "parent": "sql_agent",
  "status": "ok",
  "started_at": "2026-09-21T16:48:37.683402+00:00", "duration_s": 0.0071,
  "inputs": {"sub_query": "...", "relevant_tables": "...", "errors": "...", "retry_count": 1},
  "outputs": {"ast_planner_response": "...", "reasoning": "...", "errors": []},
  "errors": [], "warnings": [], "exception": null,
  "llm_calls": [{
    "key": {"node": "ast_planner", "sub_query_id": "sq_9579d7d41aee", "attempt": 2, "call_index": 1},
    "model": "gpt-5.4",
    "params": {"model": "gpt-5.4", "temperature": 0.0, "seed": 42},
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "[ROLE]\nYou are a SQL Planner. ..."}],
    "prompt_sha256": "63ccb543...",
    "response": {"content": "{\"query_type\": \"READ\", ... \"column_name\": \"CustomerId\" ...}",
                 "tool_calls": [], "finish_reason": "stop", "model_name": "gpt-5.4"},
    "parsed": {"query_type": "READ", "...": "..."},
    "usage": {"input_tokens": 1, "output_tokens": 1, "total_tokens": 2, "...": "..."}
  }]
}
  • seq / attempt / sub_query_id: seq orders executions by start. The attempt counts per node and sub-query, so a retried planner is attempt: 2. Nodes inside the SQL agent carry parent: "sql_agent".
  • status: ok, warning (the node returned warnings, such as COLUMN_NOT_FOUND when strict columns are off), error (it returned an ERROR or CRITICAL error, raised, or an LLM call failed) or unfinished (it never ended: the run timed out or was cancelled first).
  • inputs are the state fields that node reads, not the whole graph state; outputs is the update it returned.

  • llm_calls: the messages exactly as sent, the model's raw answer (text content, or tool calls with their arguments), what the node parsed it into, and the usage record from TokenUsageCallback (the same record QueryResult.usage.calls reports). params holds what was sent: an agent configured with temperature: null has no temperature there, and llm.configured shows it as null. model is the model the provider says answered, per call, so per-node models show up per node in llm.by_node.

  • Plan cache hits. When a sub-query's plan came from the plan cache, its ast_planner entry has outputs.ast_planner_response.plan_source: "cache" and llm_calls: [] (zero planner tokens), and the validator, generator and executor entries follow as usual. The result shows the same thing as result.sub_queries[].plan_source and result.usage.plan_cache_hits. See Determinism → The plan cache.

docs.title: Retrieval
docs.text:
The datasource_resolver and schema_retriever entries carry a retrieval object in outputs: what the vector search retrieved and how MMR chose among it (the engine has no re-ranking model; see Indexing).

"retrieval": {
  "skipped": false,
  "query": "Tracks sold per genre, highest first\ngroup_by: genre name ...",
  "searches": [{
    "search": "tables",
    "filter": {"datasource_id": "chinook", "types": ["schema.table", "schema.metric"]},
    "k": 8, "fetch_k": 32, "lambda_mult": 0.7,
    "pool": [
      {"rank": 1, "id": "schema.table:[main].[Track]:<version>", "label": "[main].[Track]",
       "type": "schema.table", "datasource_id": "chinook", "table": "[main].[Track]", "column": null,
       "similarity": 0.5651, "distance": 0.8698,
       "picked": true, "pick_order": 1, "mmr_score": 0.5651, "redundancy": 0.0}
    ],
    "picks": ["<ids in the order MMR picked them>"],
    "dropped": ["<ids of the pool entries not picked>"]
  }],
  "tables": [{"table": "Track", "columns": ["Name", "GenreId"], "qualified": "[main].[Track]", "steps": ["vector"]}]
}

On a schema past settings.retrieval.full_snapshot_max_tables, each sent table carries steps: which of vector, glossary, selector and join_path added it, so a missed table can be traced to its cause (see the schema retriever).

  • query is the text actually embedded: the question for the resolver's routing, and for the schema retriever the sub-query's intent, filters, group-by, expected columns and metrics, one per line.
  • pool is every candidate, nearest first. similarity is the cosine similarity MMR uses; distance is Chroma's (squared L2). The resolver's routing searches record no distance: each ranks its pool by similarity alone (recorded as lambda_mult 1), and its picks are each datasource's best entry. pick_order is the order MMR picked in, mmr_score the score the pick won with, and redundancy its similarity to the closest earlier pick.
  • searches lists each search in order; the schema retriever runs tables (or columns when that finds nothing), then planning over the tables found. The resolver runs one search per routing signal (route.description, route.examples, route.curated, route.tables, route.columns) and ends with a routing record: each signal's datasource ranking (signals), the fused reciprocal-rank scores with each datasource's ranks (fused), the datasources kept (picks) and those dropped (dropped, with floor or limit), and the rrf_k, vote_k, candidates and floor_ratio used. See Routing.
  • tables (schema retriever) is what survived: the tables and columns sent to the planner.
  • skipped: true with a reason means no search ran: the schema is small enough to send whole (each of the demo's three schemas, at 11, 4 and 5 tables, always is), only one datasource is registered ("single datasource: vector search skipped", which the demo is not: it registers three, so the resolver searches on every question), the request named a datasource_id, or there is no vector store. The resolver's answerability check is an LLM call, so it is in that entry's llm_calls, not in retrieval.

The record carries entry ids and names, never an entry's embedded text, which for a column holds its statistics and sample values. A table the run's role may not read is never searched at all (the searches run over the readable tables only, and the filter records how many as searched_tables), so it never appears in the record. The record is built from the numbers MMR computes anyway, so it is always there and costs no extra search.

The file records what happened. A sub-query's status reflects its final attempt, so one that recovers on retry reports "success"; the failed attempts stay in the node entries and in the result's warnings.

docs.title: Redaction
docs.text:
Every trace is redacted before it is written, with no setting to turn it off:

  • every value any secret reference resolved to (${env:...} and the other secret providers), the configured API keys, and the values of environment variables whose names contain KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, CREDENTIAL, CONNECTION_STRING or AUTH;
  • anything shaped like a secret even if the engine never saw the value: sk-... style keys, Bearer ... tokens, the password in scheme://user:password@host, and password=, pwd=, secret=, api_key=, AccountKey=, token= pairs;
  • the string value of any key named like api_key, password, secret, authorization, access_key, connection_string or credential(s);
  • the settings snapshot is the settings section only, which holds no credential: keys live in the llm, embeddings and datasources sections as references, and their resolved values are redacted as above.

A test runs a real question with the fake key sk-test-not-a-real-key-1234 in the environment and asserts that string appears nowhere in the file. Redaction is pattern and value based, so treat a trace as internal: it contains your prompts, schema and a sample of result rows.

docs.title: Capping
docs.text: Node inputs and outputs, and the result, are capped so a trace stays readable: result rows (rows, and the aggregator's terminal_results) keep settings.traces.sample_rows rows, other lists keep 200 items, and strings keep settings.traces.max_field_chars characters. Every cut leaves a [truncated] marker saying how much was dropped. LLM messages and raw responses are never cut, because replay needs them whole; a planner prompt on Chinook is about 12 000 characters, and a whole trace is typically a few hundred kilobytes.

docs.title: Why this answer: the explanation
docs.text: Before reading a trace, read QueryResult.explanation: each sub-query's plan in plain English (its tables, joins and where each join came from, filters, groupings, measures and order), the glossary terms and rules its prompt carried, and the assumptions the answer made (a reading not chosen, a filter value replaced after VALUE_NOT_FOUND, a sanity warning, a result cut at the row cap). It is rendered from the typed plan with no model call, so it says what the SQL does, not what a model thinks it does; the planner's own reasoning is kept apart as planner_note. A result rebuilt from a trace (nl2sql trace replay, engine.traces) carries it too, since it is rendered from the same state. See Explanation.

docs.title: Reading a trace: nl2sql trace show
docs.text:
nl2sql trace show traces/20260921T164837755710Z_159afe1f-....json
nl2sql trace show 159afe1f-3305-4907-903a-55495d040665   # looks it up in the trace store (engine.traces.get)

It prints the question, then one row per node execution (nested SQL agent nodes indented) with sub-query, attempt, duration, tokens and status, then each error or warning, and marks the first failing node with >. A run with no failing node but a retry marks the first warning instead, since that is what set the retry off.

docs.title: Replaying a trace: nl2sql trace replay
docs.text:
nl2sql --config nl2sql-demo/nl2sql.yaml trace replay 159afe1f-3305-4907-903a-55495d040665

Replay runs the real pipeline again for the recorded question, roles and datasource, but every LLM call is answered from the trace. The engine's chat clients are pointed at an in-process transport, so no request reaches a model provider and no key is needed; the command reports how many recorded calls it served. It then compares the replayed QueryResult with the recorded one (ignoring ids, timings, usage and artifact paths) and says whether it matches.

  • Keying. Recorded answers are looked up by (node, sub_query_id, attempt, call_index), never by question text: a retried planner asks the same question twice and gets the answer it got the first time for that attempt, and parallel sub-queries cannot take each other's answers.
  • Divergence. If the replayed run asks for a call the recording does not have, or sends a prompt whose hash differs from the recorded one, replay stops at that call and reports Replay diverged at <node>, sub-query <id>, attempt <n>, LLM call <k>, with a diff of the prompt when it changed. If the run finishes without using a recorded call, that is reported too. This is information, not a crash: everything before that point ran as recorded.
  • Plan cache. Replay makes the LLM calls the recording made. If the recorded planner called the model, replay turns the plan cache off so that call is replayed rather than answered from a plan cached since. If the recorded run used the cache, replay uses it too, and reports a divergence (missing) when the cached plan has since been cleared.
  • Date. The planner and refiner prompts carry today's date, and the trace records it as request.today. Replay pins settings.pipeline.today to that date, so a trace recorded yesterday replays without diverging. A trace written before the date was recorded replays with the current setting.
  • Its own runtime. The pinned date, the plan cache choice and a zero retry back-off go into a config derived from the engine's (Runtime.derive), and the replay runs on a runtime built from it, with its own playback clients. The engine's config and LLMs are never changed, so a query running on the same engine meanwhile is unaffected. The replayed result is capped with that runtime's settings.traces sizes, as the recording was.
  • Exit code: 0 when the replayed result matches the recording, 1 on a divergence, a different result, or a datasource that cannot be reached.

docs.title: What replay can and cannot tell you
docs.text:
• Replay tests the code downstream of the model: parsing, validation, SQL generation, execution, aggregation. It is how you check a fix to that code against a real failure without spending tokens.
  • After a prompt change the recorded response is stale. Replay reports the node where the prompt diverged; one real run is needed to record a new trace.
  • The datasource must be reachable from where you replay, with the same configuration (the same --config). Replay says so and stops if it is not. Queries run again, so a database whose data changed gives a different result, and replay reports the difference.
  • The datasource resolver and schema retriever still run their vector search, which embeds the question with the configured embedding provider (the local model in the demo; with EMBEDDING_PROVIDER=openai that is an embeddings API call, not a chat model call).
  • Redaction applies to the recorded answers too: a model answer that contained something secret-shaped is replayed redacted.

docs.title: The playground
docs.text:
With Debug on, the per-node table under Cost & time puts a bar beside each node's time, sized to the slowest node, so the slow step stands out. Each node name opens that node's record from the trace: every attempt and sub-query, its errors and warnings, what it read and returned, and for LLM nodes the exact prompt, the raw response and the parsed result. Long text is folded. For the datasource_resolver and schema_retriever nodes it also shows the retrieval record as a table: the pool nearest first, picks marked with their MMR order, dropped entries greyed, the picks in order as a row of chips, and a second row naming the entries MMR passed over because they repeat an earlier pick. The Retrieval inspector at the top of the page runs the same search for any text (see the demo guide). The page fetches the trace from GET /api/trace/{trace_id}, which reads it with engine.traces.get: any id that is not a plain token is rejected before the trace store sees it, and the files store reads only files directly inside its folder, so ../ or an absolute path never reaches the filesystem.

Below the run, Was this answer right? records a rating keyed by the same trace id; nl2sql feedback stats reads the ratings together with the traces in <storage.path>/traces. See Feedback and Signals.

docs.title: Error Handling + Circuit Breaker
docs.text:
NL2SQL represents failures as structured PipelineError objects and propagates them through state. Retries are managed at the subgraph level, and a single circuit breaker provides fast-fail safety for vector retrieval.

One case cannot use state: LangGraph conditional-edge routers may only return routing decisions, so route_scan_layers() reports "no compatible subgraph found" by raising PipelineExecutionError (nl2sql.common.exceptions), an NL2SQLError carrying the PipelineError payload on .error. This propagates out of the router and is caught by run_with_graph(), which unwraps it and returns its PipelineError payload unchanged in GraphState.errors — preserving error_code (INVALID_STATE), severity, node and is_retryable; only unrecognised exceptions become UNKNOWN_ERROR.

docs.title: Error contract
docs.text:
PipelineError includes:

  • node, message, severity, error_code
  • provider and provider_response, set on a PROVIDER_* error (below), otherwise None
  • is_retryable derived from severity and error code

A query the database rejects is EXECUTION_FAILED when the adapter says the query itself was wrong (retried through the refiner) and DB_EXECUTION_ERROR when the database refused or could not run it (fatal). Common error codes include MISSING_SQL, EXECUTION_FAILED, PIPELINE_TIMEOUT, SECURITY_VIOLATION, QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE. VALUE_NOT_FOUND marks an empty result whose filter named a value its column does not have: retried once when a close value exists, otherwise a warning the answer reports (see ExecutorNode). RESULT_TRUNCATED marks a combine input that reached its datasource's row cap: an error for a join or compare, a warning for a union (see row cap before a combine). QUESTION_TOO_BROAD ends the run when the decomposition needs more than settings.routing.max_sub_queries sub-queries; it is never retried (see DecomposerNode). JOIN_KEY_TYPE_MISMATCH marks a join-key column whose type cannot be coerced to its declared one, such as a date declared a number; it is retried, asking for another column (see LogicalValidatorNode). JOIN_KEY_UNCONVERTED is a warning: join-key values that did not convert to the key's type and so joined nothing (see EngineAggregatorNode). JOIN_FAN_OUT marks an aggregate over rows a join repeated, confirmed by a probe: retried once under COUNT (the planner counts distinct values), a warning under SUM or AVG. ALL_NULL_COLUMN is a warning: a result column with no value. Both come from the answer sanity checks, which settings.pipeline.sanity_checks: false turns off. Four codes are declared for release 0.8 and not raised yet, none of them retried: NEEDS_CLARIFICATION (the question can be read more than one way; the result carries the options), CLARIFICATION_INVALID and CLARIFICATION_STALE (a choice passed back that is not one of the run's, or one the data or glossary has since changed under), and COST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED. COST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED is raised: the query is estimated to read more rows than the caller's cost rule allows, with over_limit: refuse; it is never retried, and the run's result carries no rows.

Six codes are declared for release 0.9. Conversations raise MODEL_STEP_INVALID and CONVERSATION_TOO_LONG, and the chat-tool runner raises the three tool codes; TILE_NEEDS_FIXING is not raised yet (dashboard refresh). MODEL_STEP_INVALID (the conversation agent's step did not validate after its parse retries), CONVERSATION_TOO_LONG (more than conversations.max_turns turns) and TILE_NEEDS_FIXING (a dashboard chart's stored plan no longer validates) are never retried. TOOL_FAILED (a chat tool raised), TOOL_NOT_APPLICABLE (a warning: the tool cannot apply to that turn) and UNKNOWN_CHAT_TOOL (a name that is not enabled) are carried on a conversation step. Their lookup errors are exceptions of the facade: ConversationNotFound, ConversationBusy, DashboardNotFound and WorkspaceNotFound (all LookupError), and NotIndexed, NoTiles, WorkspaceNotEmpty, ScheduleTooFrequent, SecretValueInConfig and ConnectionInvalid (a connection that does not validate; its problems list each as {path, message}) (all ValueError), in nl2sql.common.errors.

Every one of them derives from nl2sql.NL2SQLError as well as from its built-in, so except LookupError still works. NL2SQLError carries code, message, fix (or None) and status, the HTTP status the exception means: 404 for ConversationNotFound, DashboardNotFound, WorkspaceNotFound, ResultNotFound, TraceNotFound and ApprovalNotFound (NOT_FOUND); 409 for ConversationBusy and DashboardBusy (CONFLICT); 403 for NotAuthorized (also a PermissionError); 422 for the ValueError ones, MissingProviderKey, and InvalidArgument (INVALID_ARGUMENT), which the dashboard and workspace methods raise for a wrong argument (an empty name, a duplicate, an unknown chart or filter). ReviewError maps its own code the same way (NOT_FOUND 404, FILE_CHANGED 409, the others 403). REPLAY_MISS and APPROVAL_NOT_GRANTED are new ErrorCodes, never retried; nothing raises them yet.

A run that goes on carries what its answer should say in QueryResult.warnings, a list of RunWarning (code, node, message, sub_query_id, detail; see Warnings). An earlier attempt's error that a retry replaced is there too, with detail.recovered true.

ErrorCode carries only codes something can produce. Eleven members that no code path raised were removed (MISSING_GROUP_BY, INVALID_ALIAS_USAGE, JOIN_MISSING_ON_CLAUSE, INVALID_DATE_FORMAT, INVALID_NUMERIC_VALUE, EXECUTION_ERROR, PERFORMANCE_WARNING, SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, PHYSICAL_VALIDATOR_FAILED, EXECUTION_TIMEOUT, INTENT_VIOLATION); a code nobody can emit is a promise to a caller the engine never keeps. SAFEGUARD_VIOLATION is kept although nothing raises it yet: it has a caller-facing message in SAFE_ERROR_MESSAGES, so it is a declared refusal path. test_boundary_tidy_ups.py asserts the rule.

A run that hits the global timeout returns PIPELINE_TIMEOUT and an answer: the apology is written where the answer synthesizer writes its own, so QueryResult.final_answer carries it. It used to be written to a top-level state key that result_from_state never read, so every caller through the SDK and the REST route saw final_answer: null with only the error code.

QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE (severity ERROR) comes from the datasource resolver when its answerability check finds that no datasource the role may read can answer the question, such as "what is the weather in Paris?". The run ends before the decomposer: no decomposer, planner, refiner or synthesizer call is made, QueryResult.status is error, and the message tells the user the question can't be answered from the connected data. The check is told to answer "answerable" when unsure. See DatasourceResolverNode.

docs.title: Provider failures
docs.text:
When the model provider refuses or fails a call, the LLM node that made it (datasource resolver, decomposer, AST planner, refiner, answer synthesizer) reports it through nl2sql.llm.failures.provider_error instead of its own failure code, so every caller (SDK, REST API, playground) gets the same entry. classify_provider_error reads the OpenAI and Anthropic SDK exceptions by shape (the anthropic SDK is an optional extra, so it is never imported), looking through what the exception was raised from:

error_code when message (for OpenAI) PROVIDER_AUTH_FAILED HTTP 401, or 403 "OpenAI rejected the API key." PROVIDER_RATE_LIMITED HTTP 429 "OpenAI rate limited the request." PROVIDER_QUOTA_EXCEEDED HTTP 429 with insufficient_quota "OpenAI says this API key has no quota left." PROVIDER_TIMEOUT the SDK's timeout, or HTTP 408 "OpenAI did not answer in time." PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE a connection error, or HTTP 5xx "OpenAI could not be reached." / "OpenAI had a server error and could not answer." PROVIDER_MODEL_UNAVAILABLE HTTP 404, or model_not_found "OpenAI does not offer the configured model to this API key."
  • message is one sentence naming the provider. It never carries the key (masked or not), a Python repr, or the node's own label.
  • provider is the provider as a person names it (PROVIDER_LABELS in llm/providers.py): Anthropic for the Anthropic SDK, otherwise the preset whose endpoint the call went to. A base_url no preset names is "The model provider".
  • provider_response is the provider's own words, such as HTTP 401 (invalid_api_key): Incorrect API key provided: [redacted key]. ..., for a "provider response" disclosure. redact_keys replaces anything key-like (a bearer token, an sk-/pk-/rk- key whole or masked, any unbroken run of 32 or more letters, digits, - or _) with [redacted key]. The error of a failed call in usage.calls is redacted the same way.
  • Every PROVIDER_* code is fatal (is_retryable is false): a refinement retry would make the same call to the same provider with the same key.
  • An HTTP 400 is not classified. It is a request the engine built wrongly, or a model refusing a parameter, and the node's own error explains it better.

run_with_graph()'s fallback applies the same classification, so a provider failure that escapes its node is not UNKNOWN_ERROR.

docs.title: Model output invalid
docs.text:
Every structured call retries an answer that does not parse, up to the agent's parse_retries times (see Parse-and-retry). When the last answer still does not parse, wires.structured() raises StructuredOutputError, and provider_error reports it as MODEL_OUTPUT_INVALID:

The ast_planner agent's answer did not match PlannerAnswer after 2 attempts. Set another
structured_output for it (tool_calling, json_schema or json_mode), or use a stronger model.
  • The agent is the node that made the call (or, outside a run, the agent whose client it was).
  • The last answer's validation errors are in details, which is not sent to callers; the trace has every attempt in the node's llm_calls.
  • It is not fatal: like the node's own failure codes, the run's usual retry path still applies.

docs.title: Circuit breaker
docs.text:
create_breaker() configures pybreaker.CircuitBreaker instances with observability hooks. The system defines exactly one:

  • VECTOR_BREAKER (fail_max=5, reset_timeout=30)

Retrieval calls in the Retriever are wrapped with VECTOR_BREAKER. It is the only breaker instance the system defines: LLM calls and SQL execution are not breaker-guarded, and their failures surface as PipelineError values in state.

docs.title: Failure flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Node[Pipeline Node] --> Error[PipelineError]
    Error --> State[GraphState.errors]
    State --> Retry{is_retryable?}
    Retry -->|yes| Refine[RefinerNode / retry loop]
    Retry -->|no| Stop[Terminate branch]

See ../architecture/failure_recovery.md for failure domains, retry scope, and recovery limitations.

docs.title: Cancellation and timeouts
docs.text:
• run_with_graph() enforces a global timeout (Settings.global_timeout_sec).
  • Cancellation is honored through a per-run nl2sql.common.cancellation.CancellationToken, passed to the graph via config["configurable"]["cancellation_token"], so cancelling one run never affects another.
  • run_with_graph() never raises: cancellation, timeout, routing failures and unexpected crashes all come back as PipelineError values in state. A PipelineExecutionError is unwrapped so its original error_code survives; only genuinely unrecognised exceptions become UNKNOWN_ERROR.

docs.title: Source references
docs.text:
• Error contracts: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/common/errors.py
  • Circuit breaker: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/common/resilience.py
  • Retry logic: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/subgraphs/sql_agent.py
  • Cancellation: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/common/cancellation.py

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Everything the engine does is published as an event on its event bus: each step of a question, its result manifest, its answer as it is written, and how it ended; and model calls, policy denials, hook decisions, index builds, purges and LLM swaps. Two readers see them:

  • The caller who asked the question sees their own run's events on engine.stream_query, from a caller-safe allow-list. nl2sql-api's POST /query/stream, the playground and nl2sql run all read this stream.
  • An operator sees every event of every run, and the engine's own, through engine.events.subscribe.

docs.title: The event
docs.text:
from nl2sql import Event   # nl2sql_sdk.events.Event: pydantic and the standard library only

event.name       # "node.finished", from the catalog
event.at         # when, in UTC
event.trace_id   # the run's id (QueryResult.trace_id); None for an engine event no run caused
event.tenant_id
event.data       # JSON-ready; the catalog's model for this name
event.sse()      # "event: <name>\ndata: <the whole event as JSON>\n\n"

trace_id is the id a run has everywhere: the result (QueryResult.trace_id), its saved results (engine.results.page), its trace (engine.traces.get) and its log lines all join on it.

No event carries result rows, sample values, keys or header values. The question and the answer text are carried, and may contain values from the data.

docs.title: The catalog
docs.text:
